3.q: In project scheduling terms, what does the technique of time boxing primarily help a project team to control?
o: The reporting format used for progress updates
The quality standards applied to the outputs
The number of stakeholders that are consulted
The elapsed time devoted to a piece of work
3.w: Time boxing controls the elapsed time given to a piece of work by fixing the period and flexing scope within it.

3.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical use of a risk register?
o: Recording the agreed response for each risk
Tracking the status and ownership of identified risks
Authorising payments to the project's suppliers
Providing a basis for reviewing risks at meetings
3.w: The register manages information about risks; authorising supplier payments is a financial and procurement matter, not a register function.

3.q: A new appraisal system must be handed to HR within six weeks. What best distinguishes this project from HR's business-as-usual work?
o: The HR department holds greater control over the project budget
The project has a defined end date and delivers a unique output
The project exists to support HR's routine daily operations
The project is concerned only with engaging its stakeholders
3.w: A project delivers a one-off output within defined constraints and then closes, whereas HR's ongoing work is repeatable business-as-usual.

3.q: Why might an organisation choose to manage several related projects together as a programme rather than entirely separately?
o: To achieve coordinated benefits that the individual projects could not deliver alone
To remove the need for any individual project to have its own objectives
To guarantee that each project finishes strictly within its own isolated budget
To convert temporary project work into permanent operational business activity
3.w: A programme coordinates related projects so that combined, aligned benefits are realised that separate projects could not deliver individually.

3.q: How can a project leader who consistently models the standards and behaviours they expect influence their team?
o: It transfers leadership responsibility to the team
It guarantees that no conflict will ever arise
It sets a clear example that encourages similar behaviour and effort
It removes the need for any team ground rules
3.w: Leading by example sets the standard others follow, encouraging the behaviour and effort that support performance.

3.q: A project logs each deliverable, tracks its versions and controls access to it. Which discipline does this describe?
o: Quality assurance
Change control
Benefits management
Configuration management
3.w: Identifying, versioning and controlling deliverables is configuration management.

3.q: What is a disadvantage of using physical noticeboards for communication on a project?
o: They provide real-time chat features for participants
They rely on people being present in person to see updates
They can be edited and updated remotely with ease
They automatically create a backup of their content
3.w: Physical noticeboards are static and only reach those who can access them in person.

3.q: What principally happens during the transition phase of a typical linear project life cycle?
o: The high-level idea is assessed for viability and strategic fit
Detailed plans, schedules and budgets are produced and baselined
The main deliverables are designed, built and progressively tested
Outputs are handed over to users and the project is formally closed
3.w: In the transition phase the outputs are handed over into use and the project is closed down.

3.q: One product is basic but meets every requirement; another is elaborate but misses several. Which better demonstrates quality?
o: The elaborate product, because it offers more features
Neither, because quality cannot be compared between products
The basic product, because it conforms to its requirements
The elaborate product, because it clearly cost more to build
3.w: Quality is conformance to requirements, so the basic product that fully meets its requirements demonstrates quality.

3.q: Stakeholder analysis shows a group of community residents to have low influence but high interest. What is the recommended approach?
o: Avoid all engagement until after delivery
Monitor them only if they raise a concern
Manage them closely and involve them in every decision
Keep them informed through regular updates and consultation
3.w: Low-influence, high-interest stakeholders should be kept informed to maintain support and prevent misinformation.

3.q: Under the communication plan, status updates are issued every Monday by 10 a.m. What does this help the project manager achieve?
o: Freedom from attending project governance meetings
Predictable updates that build stakeholder confidence
Automatic generation of procurement requests
The removal of any need to produce progress reports
3.w: Predictable, scheduled updates keep stakeholders informed and build confidence in how the project is being controlled.

3.q: Why might an organisation choose to conduct a project audit while the project is still being delivered?
o: To test the completed deliverables for technical faults
To confirm compliance and highlight improvements while action is still possible
To cancel the project before any more money is committed
To sign off the final benefits review with the sponsor
3.w: A mid-project audit can surface issues early, allowing corrective action to be taken while the project is still underway.

3.q: Which of the following is a typical output of the quality control process on a project?
o: Records of inspections and test results for the deliverables
The quality management plan produced for the whole project
The schedule of independent process audits to be carried out
The list of quality standards the project will adopt
3.w: Quality control produces inspection and test records for deliverables; the other items are outputs of quality planning or assurance.

3.q: Beyond simply naming suppliers, what does a well-considered procurement strategy aim to achieve for a project?
o: The elimination of every risk associated with using suppliers
The detailed daily task schedule for the internal project team
A guarantee that no external suppliers will be needed at all
Value for money and a sound, consistent approach to sourcing external work
3.w: A procurement strategy aims to secure value for money through a sound, consistent approach to sourcing external work.

3.q: Early in the design phase a team produces an estimate with a tolerance of around plus or minus 40%. What does this represent in the estimating funnel?
o: A confirmed contingency figure
A final, validated estimate
A preliminary, high-level estimate
A detailed bottom-up estimate
3.w: Wide tolerances such as plus or minus 40% are typical of the preliminary, high-level estimates near the top of the funnel.

3.q: A project manager creates an organisational breakdown structure (OBS). What is the main purpose of this tool?
o: To record the project's detailed work breakdown structure
To show the reporting relationships and lines of authority
To define the project's risks and their planned responses
To set out the methods used to communicate with stakeholders
3.w: An OBS sets out the project's organisational hierarchy, showing roles, reporting relationships and lines of authority.

3.q: At handover, the sponsor asks for evidence that the project met its objectives. Which element should the project manager refer to?
o: The communication plan produced during delivery
The success criteria agreed at project initiation
The work breakdown structure for the project
The procurement strategy used for the project
3.w: The success criteria agreed at initiation provide the benchmark against which achievement of the objectives is judged at closure.

3.q: A newly logged issue has just been assessed for its impact. According to the process, what happens at the next stage?
o: Its probability of occurring is analysed and scored
It is logged in the issue register before any assessment
It is identified and recorded for the very first time
It is resolved, or escalated if it is beyond the manager's authority
3.w: After assessment, the process moves to resolving the issue or, where it exceeds the manager's authority, escalating it.

3.q: Which estimating technique is best suited when detailed information is unavailable and a quick estimate is needed?
o: Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
Parametric estimating
3.w: Analogous estimating provides a quick, high-level estimate based on past projects when detailed data is not yet available.

3.q: Which of the following is a common challenge when building a project team?
o: Ensuring that every member has an identical working style
Relying on communication being clear from the first day
Balancing team members' roles, personalities and availability
Removing every difference in members' skills and experience
3.w: Forming a cohesive team requires balancing individuals' roles, personalities, skills and availability.

3.q: Which of the following statements best defines communication in the context of a project?
o: The process of completing and filing project documentation
A control activity used only during the planning phase
The exchange of information between people to reach shared understanding
The transfer of technical data solely to the project sponsor
3.w: Communication in projects is the exchange of information to achieve shared understanding and alignment among those involved.

3.q: A team leader gives regular, specific and constructive feedback to team members. What effect is this most likely to have?
o: It reduces the leader's own accountability for the outcome
It removes the need for any recognition or reward
It helps members improve and sustains strong performance
It fixes the project's deployment baseline permanently
3.w: Regular constructive feedback helps team members learn and adjust, sustaining and improving their performance.

3.q: Within a single iteration of an iterative life cycle, which set of activities is typically carried out?
o: Closure and disbanding of the entire project team
Procurement of all materials with no further planning needed
A one-off concept phase followed by permanent operations
Planning, building and reviewing an increment of the solution
3.w: Each iteration repeats a compact set of plan-build-review activities to produce an increment.

3.q: Which pairing correctly matches the terms 'risk' and 'issue' to their defining feature?
o: Risk = has occurred; issue = might occur
Risk = might occur; issue = has occurred
Risk = certain benefit; issue = certain threat
Risk = external only; issue = internal only
3.w: A risk is a possible future event that might occur, whereas an issue is something that has already happened.

3.q: A project manager wants to anticipate how their new team's behaviour will change as it matures. Which model is most relevant?
o: Belbin's team roles
A PESTLE analysis
A responsibility assignment matrix
Tuckman's stages of team development
3.w: Tuckman's model describes forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning, helping anticipate how a team develops over time.

3.q: What is a major risk of using unstructured methods such as instant messaging for decisions?
o: They ensure the team complies with governance requirements
They leave no audit trail to trace how decisions were made
They improve the clarity of the project's agreed scope
They enforce formal stakeholder approval of every decision
3.w: Informal chats often bypass documentation, making it difficult to trace how and why decisions were taken.

3.q: What is the main benefit of using traffic light (RAG) status in project progress reports?
o: It conceals emerging issues from the stakeholders
It communicates status simply using clear visual cues
It replaces the project's earned value calculations
It removes the need for any narrative reporting
3.w: RAG status gives a quick, visual indication of performance, making status easy to grasp and supporting rapid decision-making.

3.q: Which two dimensions are typically used in an influence/interest matrix for stakeholder analysis?
o: Influence and interest
Support and opposition
Cost and time
Risk and reward
3.w: The matrix maps stakeholders by their power to affect the project (influence) and their level of concern (interest).

3.q: A senior manager commissions a check on whether a project complies with corporate governance requirements. Which process is this?
o: Conducting a project audit
Planning the project's risk responses
Realising the project's benefits
Carrying out quality control
3.w: A project audit is the formal assessment of a project's compliance with governance, processes and policies.

3.q: An issue has occurred within a project. Which process is used to resolve it?
o: Configuration management
Change control
Issue management
Risk management
3.w: Issue management is the structured process for recording, assessing and resolving problems once they have occurred.

4.q: A risk recorded earlier in the project has now actually happened. In project terminology, what has it become?
o: An assumption
An issue
A milestone
A constraint
4.w: When a risk materialises it becomes an issue: a problem that has occurred and now requires management action.

4.q: A team leader coaches members to build the skills their roles require. How does this most likely influence performance?
o: It removes the need to plan the project schedule
It makes the team dependent on external suppliers
It shifts accountability for the benefits to operations
It strengthens capability and confidence, improving future output
4.w: Coaching develops skills and confidence, raising the team's capability and its future performance.

4.q: A team both authorises a requested change and then updates the version record of the affected deliverable. Which two disciplines have they used?
o: Configuration management only
Quality assurance, then benefits management
Change control only
Change control, then configuration management
4.w: Authorising the change is change control; updating the deliverable's version record is configuration management.

4.q: Which of the following is a potential drawback of virtual communication methods?
o: They provide the same rich body-language cues as meeting in person
They remove every difficulty associated with differing time zones
They always ensure the confidentiality of shared information
They can suffer technical problems and reduced personal connection
4.w: Virtual tools can create barriers through technical limitations and weaker non-verbal engagement.

4.q: What is the primary purpose of change control within project scope management?
o: To adjust the project's budget in line with the latest forecasts
To allow changes to proceed without approval to maintain momentum
To develop the initial scope statement at the start of the project
To assess and then approve or reject proposed changes to scope
4.w: Change control is the formal process for assessing proposed changes and deciding whether to approve or reject them before implementation.

4.q: How does working in fixed time boxes help a team guard against work expanding without limit?
o: The immovable deadline forces the work to be contained within the period
It fixes the scope so that nothing can ever be added
It allows the deadline to move whenever more work appears
It removes the need to prioritise any of the work
4.w: The fixed, immovable deadline contains the work within the period, guarding against uncontrolled expansion or scope creep.

4.q: What distinguishes genuine leadership from merely instructing a team to comply?
o: It relies on enforcing rules so people obey through instruction
It concentrates on producing detailed progress reports
It focuses on allocating resources evenly across all tasks
It motivates people to commit willingly towards shared goals
4.w: Leadership motivates people to commit willingly to shared goals, rather than securing mere compliance through instruction.

4.q: Which statement best defines quality control in a project setting?
o: Training the team members in various quality methods
Planning how the required quality will be assured
Monitoring results to check they comply with standards
Identifying lessons learned from earlier quality issues
4.w: Quality control monitors and inspects project outputs to confirm they meet the specified requirements.

4.q: What is a recognised disadvantage of physical, paper-based communication on a project?
o: It promotes instant feedback between the sender and the recipient
It is ideally suited to sending urgent updates at short notice
It is difficult to update and distribute quickly when things change
It is the most secure communication option in every situation
4.w: Paper-based communication is slow to amend and circulate, which is a disadvantage in a fast-changing project environment.

4.q: Which of the following is a common responsibility of a project management office (PMO)?
o: Providing assurance and support across multiple projects
Owning and controlling the project budget
Managing the scope and deliverables of each project
Acting as the primary user of the deliverables
4.w: A PMO offers governance, assurance, reporting and consistent support across projects or programmes.

4.q: Which of the following best summarises the key purpose of project management?
o: To take the place of business-as-usual activities
To help organisations deliver change and achieve specific objectives
To increase permanent headcount in operational areas
To standardise routine reporting across all departments
4.w: Project management enables organisations to deliver change and meet specific time, cost and quality objectives.

4.q: Within a hybrid approach, which work is best suited to the iterative element of the life cycle?
o: Fixed infrastructure that must be installed in a strict, unchanging order
Regulatory documentation that cannot be altered once it is approved
Foundational elements whose design is settled before delivery begins
Evolving features that benefit from repeated user feedback and refinement
4.w: The iterative element suits uncertain, evolving requirements that improve through successive cycles of feedback and refinement.

4.q: After a change, the team confirms that the new deliverable matches the approved configuration. Which activity is this?
o: Configuration planning
Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration identification
4.w: Verification and audit confirm that items conform to their approved configuration and that changes were made correctly.

4.q: What is a primary benefit of producing regular project progress reports for the sponsor?
o: They replace the project's risk register entirely
They remove the need to engage with project stakeholders
They finalise the agreed scope of the project
They inform sponsor decisions and enable timely intervention
4.w: Regular reports give the sponsor visibility of status, risks and deviations, supporting informed decisions and proactive corrective action.

4.q: A city-centre event project faces growing scrutiny over its impact on local air quality and pollution. Which PESTLE category does this most relate to?
o: Technological
Environmental
Political
Legal
4.w: Pollution, air quality and sustainability concerns fall under the environmental category of PESTLE.

4.q: In Belbin's model, which team role is most associated with exploring opportunities outside the team and developing external contacts?
o: Resource Investigator
Coordinator
Implementer
Team Worker
4.w: The Resource Investigator is an outgoing networker who explores opportunities and brings in ideas and contacts from outside the team.

4.q: Which statement correctly reflects the relationship between a risk and an issue on a project?
o: An issue can always be prevented through effective mitigation planning
A risk is always a negative event that will harm the project
A risk and an issue are always recorded within the same register
An issue represents a realised risk or a newly arising problem
4.w: An issue is something that has happened now, arising either from a risk that has materialised or from a new event, unlike a risk which is uncertain.

4.q: Which of the following best describes the role of decision gates within quality management?
o: They replace all other assurance activities
They confirm each phase meets its standards before progressing
They ensure only the final output is reviewed
They remove the need to engage with stakeholders
4.w: Decision gates support quality by confirming that the objectives and standards for a phase are met before progressing.

4.q: A colleague asks what 'hybrid life cycle' means. Which explanation is correct?
o: Delivering the entire project through a single fixed sequence of phases
Running the same iterative cycle continuously until funding is exhausted
Handing the project between two organisations at the halfway point
Blending linear and iterative approaches within one project's delivery
4.w: A hybrid life cycle blends linear and iterative methods so each part of the work uses the most suitable approach.

4.q: A team is given two weeks to complete as much as possible from a defined set of features. Which technique is being used?
o: Critical path calculation
Time boxing
Milestone tracking
Float analysis
4.w: This is time boxing: the duration is fixed at two weeks while the scope achieved within it is allowed to vary.

4.q: A new team member asks how the discipline of project management should best be defined in practice.
o: The steady supervision of recurring departmental duties within fixed annual budgets
The organising of resources purely to reduce day-to-day operational running costs
The application of knowledge, tools and techniques to deliver objectives within agreed constraints
The prioritising of competing initiatives to reflect the organisation's changing strategy
4.w: Project management applies knowledge, tools and techniques to deliver objectives within the constraints of time, cost and quality; the distractors describe operations and portfolio activity.

4.q: A project manager uses a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM). What is the key benefit of using this tool?
o: It tracks the financial cost incurred against each project phase
It allocates the packages of work to their related deliverables
It shows who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed
It breaks the project schedule down into its individual tasks
4.w: A RAM, often using RACI, maps who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each task, giving clear role accountability.

4.q: Infrastructure must be delivered in a fixed sequence, while software features are released in cycles based on user feedback. Which life cycle is being used?
o: Iterative
Extended
Hybrid
Linear
4.w: A hybrid life cycle combines a linear approach for predictable work with an iterative approach for work that benefits from feedback.

4.q: Keeping a logistics project aligned to the sponsor's strategic vision is best described as an example of what?
o: One of the fundamental purposes of project management
A post-project review conducted after handover
A portfolio management responsibility above the project
A quality assurance activity carried out independently
4.w: Ensuring the project stays aligned to organisational strategy and the sponsor's objectives is a core purpose of project management.

4.q: What is the main purpose of applying resource optimisation techniques when planning a project schedule?
o: To set the thresholds at which changes must be formally approved
To define how the project team will communicate with its stakeholders
To forecast how inflation will affect the overall project budget
To use resources efficiently and avoid periods of over- or under-allocation
4.w: Resource optimisation adjusts the schedule so that resource demand is balanced, avoiding overloads and idle periods.

4.q: A project manager sequences activities and sets their timings before delivery begins. Which project management activity is being carried out?
o: Scheduling
Risk analysis
Quality control
Benefits management
4.w: Determining the timing and sequence of activities, and the resources needed, is the purpose of scheduling.

4.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between benefits and outputs?
o: Benefits are the measurable value achieved through using the outputs
Benefits are the deliverables that the project creates
Outputs always exceed the benefits they produce
Outputs are the future outcomes that are derived from benefits
4.w: Outputs are what the project delivers; benefits are the measurable value that arises from using those outputs.

4.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between the project sponsor and the project manager?
o: The sponsor sets direction and governance while the manager delivers
The sponsor manages daily delivery while the manager sets strategy
The two roles operate independently with no formal relationship
The sponsor handles finance while the manager makes technical choices
4.w: The sponsor provides strategic direction and governance, while the project manager delivers the project within those boundaries.

4.q: Which statement best describes how scope is managed differently in linear and iterative projects?
o: Linear projects fix scope early, whereas iterative projects adapt it over time
Linear projects define scope late, whereas iterative projects define it early
Both linear and iterative projects fix their scope only at project closure
Iterative projects rely on strict change control, whereas linear projects stay flexible
4.w: Linear projects establish scope early in the life cycle, whereas iterative projects refine it throughout delivery.

4.q: What is the main purpose of the closure phase in a typical linear project life cycle?
o: Designing and building the deliverables
Reviewing performance and capturing lessons learned
Approving the project business case
Training the operational end users
4.w: Closure reviews project performance, captures lessons learned and hands over responsibility for realising the remaining benefits.

5.q: What does a flexible deployment baseline allow a team to do in an iterative project?
o: Avoid the need for governance reviews
Work without any documentation or tracking
Respond to evolving user needs as they emerge
Make changes without any impact on the project
5.w: A flexible baseline lets an iterative team remain responsive to changing requirements while still planning and tracking work.

5.q: During delivery a team reviews whether its agreed working procedures are being applied consistently across all workstreams. Which process is this?
o: Quality control
Quality assurance
Change control
Benefits management
5.w: Reviewing whether agreed processes and procedures are being applied is a quality assurance activity.

5.q: A charity is running a time-limited fundraising campaign. Why is managing it using project management principles appropriate?
o: Because the campaign forms part of routine operations
Because fundraising is a continuous, repeatable task
Because project management suits one-off, goal-focused initiatives
Because the campaign has no defined end point
5.w: Project management is designed for temporary initiatives with clear objectives and a defined end, which fits the campaign.

5.q: A new CEO cancels two projects, starts three, and groups related initiatives into one programme. Which type of management is being applied?
o: Programme assurance
Change control
Portfolio management
Operational leadership
5.w: Prioritising, terminating and initiating initiatives across the organisation to reflect strategy is portfolio management.

5.q: Which of the following best describes how a cost breakdown structure (CBS) supports effective budget control on a project?
o: By setting out the project's overall decision-making structure
By showing the cost associated with each part of the project
By categorising the project's scope into functional units
By assigning named individuals to each of the project tasks
5.w: By attributing costs to each project element, the CBS lets the project manager monitor and control spending against the budget.

5.q: How does quality control contribute to the successful delivery of a project?
o: By verifying that outputs meet defined standards before they are accepted
By ensuring that the plans align closely with the users’ needs
By selecting the most appropriate project delivery methodology
By communicating agreed changes to the project’s stakeholders
5.w: Quality control checks outputs against defined standards before acceptance, reducing rework and helping ensure deliverables are fit for purpose.

5.q: Why can two stakeholders usually agree on whether a deliverable has quality when its requirements are clear?
o: Because quality is judged objectively against the agreed requirements
Because quality depends only on each person's individual taste
Because quality is decided solely by the deliverable's price
Because quality always means the highest specification possible
5.w: With clear requirements, quality can be judged objectively against them rather than by subjective opinion.

5.q: What is a major benefit of using virtual communication tools on a project?
o: They guarantee strong cohesion among all team members
They prevent technical problems from disrupting the project
They enable collaboration across different locations and time zones
They remove the need to engage with project stakeholders
5.w: Virtual communication allows geographically dispersed teams to collaborate effectively regardless of location.

5.q: Throughout the life of a project, who holds overall ownership of the business case and its continued validity?
o: The project sponsor
The project manager
The project team
The end users
5.w: The sponsor owns the business case and is accountable for ensuring the investment remains justified throughout the project.

5.q: Why can virtual tools such as shared whiteboards be advantageous for collaborative planning?
o: They remove the need to keep any project documentation
They are inherently more secure than meeting in person
They prevent disagreement between the project's stakeholders
They allow asynchronous contributions from remote participants
5.w: Shared online tools support collaboration even when participants are not all available at the same time.

5.q: A team colour-codes its risks red, amber and green to show their severity. What is this an example of?
o: Qualitative risk analysis
Quantitative risk analysis
Configuration management
Critical path analysis
5.w: Ranking risks by descriptive categories such as red, amber and green is a form of qualitative risk analysis.

5.q: Following project handover, who is normally accountable for tracking whether the intended benefits are actually realised?
o: The project sponsor or designated benefits owner
The finance administrator who managed the budget
The lead supplier who provided the deliverables
The project manager who led the delivery work
5.w: Benefits are usually realised after the project has closed, so accountability passes to the sponsor or a designated benefits owner identified in the business case.

5.q: As sponsor, what should you do if the business case is found to be no longer valid during delivery?
o: Pause the project and update the business case for governance review
Instruct the team to continue with the work regardless
Increase the project's scope to add further value
Remove the project's risk management procedures
5.w: The sponsor must keep the business case valid; if it is not, work should be paused and approval sought for any change.

5.q: What is the defining feature of the way phases are arranged in a linear project life cycle?
o: Phases can be reordered freely according to team preference
Each phase is largely completed before the next one begins
All phases run in parallel from the very start of the project
Phases repeat in short cycles until the customer is satisfied
5.w: A linear life cycle runs its phases sequentially, with each substantially finished before the next starts.

5.q: How does a hybrid life cycle mainly differ from a purely iterative life cycle?
o: A hybrid abandons all upfront planning in favour of continuous change
A hybrid is always shorter and cheaper than an iterative approach
A hybrid never gathers stakeholder feedback during delivery
A hybrid keeps predefined linear phases for part of the work, unlike a fully iterative approach
5.w: Unlike a purely iterative life cycle, a hybrid retains fixed linear phases for the parts of the work that are stable.

5.q: Why is risk management important to the successful delivery of a project?
o: It removes the need for stakeholders to be involved in the project
It ensures that all project issues are completely avoided altogether
It guarantees that the project will succeed and meet every objective
It allows uncertainties to be identified and controlled before they occur
5.w: Risk management enables uncertainties that could affect objectives to be identified, assessed and responded to proactively.

5.q: What is a key limitation of using email as a communication method?
o: It is the most suitable channel for urgent decision-making
It is not actually a written form of communication
It lacks tone and non-verbal cues, so it can be misread
It always ensures an immediate two-way exchange of views
5.w: Emails can be misinterpreted because they carry no tone of voice or body language.

5.q: A sponsor is concerned that high inflation and rising interest rates could affect a capital investment project. Which PESTLE category applies?
o: Legal
Technological
Economic
Environmental
5.w: Inflation and interest rates are economic factors, which directly influence a project's cost and viability.

5.q: A PMO balances resource allocation and risk exposure across a suite of unrelated IT and marketing projects. What is being demonstrated?
o: Operational management
Programme governance
Portfolio management
Project assurance
5.w: Balancing investment, resources and risk across unrelated projects to serve organisational strategy is portfolio management.

5.q: When explaining project management to stakeholders unfamiliar with the discipline, which description would be the most accurate to give?
o: The application of processes and skills to deliver a project's objectives
The routine oversight of established services to keep them running smoothly
The selection of investments to balance the organisation's limited resources
The coordination of several related projects to achieve one strategic change
5.w: Project management is the application of processes and skills to deliver the project's objectives; the remaining options describe operations, programme and portfolio management respectively.

5.q: Which of the following is a common tool used to carry out quality assurance?
o: Product inspections of the deliverables
Change request logs for the project
Issue registers maintained by the team
Peer reviews of the processes used
5.w: Peer reviews of processes support quality assurance by verifying that agreed procedures are being applied.

5.q: Analysis places a senior regulator as high influence but low interest in day-to-day detail. How should they be engaged?
o: Kept satisfied with concise, high-level updates rather than routine detail
Sent every operational report so nothing is ever withheld from them
Left entirely uninformed until the project has been formally closed
Given full control over prioritising the project team's daily tasks
5.w: High-influence, low-interest stakeholders should be kept satisfied with proportionate, high-level information rather than routine detail.

5.q: How does configuration identification differ from status accounting within the configuration management process?
o: Identification defines and references the items; status accounting records their state and history
Identification records change history; status accounting assigns each item a reference
Both assign references, but only one audits the schedule
Both record change history, but only one plans the budget
5.w: Identification defines and labels the configuration items, whereas status accounting maintains the ongoing record of their status and changes.

5.q: External stakeholders report that they are not receiving relevant project information. Which document should the project manager review first?
o: The risk register's list of threats and their owners
The quality plan's checklists and acceptance criteria
The communication plan's stakeholder list and distribution schedule
The benefits register's expected outcomes and measures
5.w: The communication plan defines who should receive which information and when, so its stakeholder mapping and schedule are the first thing to check.

5.q: Why are estimates at the top of the estimating funnel less accurate than those produced later?
o: Because the risk register has not yet been created
Because detailed scope and task data are not yet available
Because all projects rely on top-down budgeting at that point
Because agile approaches avoid planning at that stage
5.w: Early estimates rest on assumptions and high-level inputs because the detailed scope and work breakdown structure do not yet exist.

5.q: Why must a project's baseline be updated once an approved change has been implemented?
o: So that performance is measured against the current, agreed configuration
So that the change avoids needing any authorisation
So that the original change request can be permanently deleted
So that no further changes can ever be requested
5.w: The baseline is updated so future performance is measured against the current, agreed configuration reflecting the change.

5.q: A project manager finds that a key resource is assigned to several tasks on the same day. Which technique should resolve this?
o: Milestone tracking
Scope definition
Earned value analysis
Resource levelling
5.w: Resource levelling reschedules activities to resolve over-allocation, accepting that the end date may be affected.

5.q: At which points in the life cycle do the sponsor and project manager jointly review the business case?
o: Only once the project has been formally closed
Solely at the point a change request is raised
At project initiation and at key decision gates
Only after the benefits have been fully realised
5.w: They review the case together at initiation and at decision gates to confirm the justification remains valid.

5.q: Which action is most appropriate during the risk closure stage of the risk management process?
o: Reviewing the outcomes and updating the lessons learned
Increasing the project's contingency budget for reassurance
Converting each closed risk into a formal change request
Assigning new owners to risks that have already expired
5.w: Closure involves recording outcomes and capturing lessons learned to improve risk handling on future projects.

5.q: A developer implements a software change from an informal request, and it later proves incompatible with existing modules. Which process breakdown occurred?
o: Stakeholder mapping was not kept properly up to date
Change control was bypassed and configuration was not enforced
Quality control was applied too heavily to the work
Risk escalation was skipped during the delivery phase
5.w: The change was not authorised through change control and was not verified or integrated through configuration management, so both controls failed.

6.q: A project is defined as being undertaken to achieve planned objectives. In what terms are these objectives usually expressed?
o: Outputs, outcomes or benefits
Routine, repeated daily tasks
Departments, functions or teams
Profits, dividends or returns
6.w: Planned objectives on a project are defined in terms of outputs, outcomes or benefits, distinguishing a project from operations, programmes and portfolios.

6.q: A product meets every technical specification, yet customer feedback is negative. What most likely went wrong?
o: The deployment baseline was disregarded
The success criteria did not include user satisfaction
Too much emphasis was placed on iterative delivery
Stakeholders were engaged too frequently
6.w: Success criteria focused only on technical outputs can omit qualitative measures such as user satisfaction.

6.q: Within a project, what is the primary responsibility of the project governance arrangements?
o: To carry out the day-to-day technical tasks defined in the work packages
To provide the framework of oversight, authority and accountability for the project
To gather user feedback after each iteration is completed
To produce the deliverables that make up the final product
6.w: Project governance provides the structure of oversight, decision-making authority and accountability within which the project is directed and controlled.

6.q: A project leader uses team feedback to improve work processes and decision-making. What effect is this likely to have?
o: It weakens the leader's authority over the team
It enhances team ownership and improves performance
It increases conflict between team members
It undermines the project's governance arrangements
6.w: Involving the team in shaping decisions creates a sense of ownership that improves engagement and output.

6.q: A developer finds that a technical constraint will prevent on-time delivery of a feature. What should they do next?
o: Raise the issue with the project manager and suggest options
Withdraw from the task and await reassignment
Notify the project sponsor of the problem directly
Escalate to the governance board for a decision
6.w: Team members are expected to raise emerging issues with the project manager and collaborate on possible solutions.

6.q: Which of the following best describes the responsibility of a project team member?
o: Providing specialist skills and completing assigned tasks
Defining and owning the project business case
Approving transitions between project phases
Authorising procurement contracts with suppliers
6.w: Team members apply their specialist skills to complete assigned work packages and report progress to the project manager.

6.q: A product breakdown structure sets out the main product, its subassemblies and its components. Why is this useful to the project manager?
o: It identifies which work packages are behind schedule
It clarifies exactly what the project must deliver
It shows who is responsible for each delivery
It allocates team members to each activity
6.w: The PBS defines and visualises all elements of the final product, clarifying exactly what the project must deliver.

6.q: Which situation is the strongest reason for a project to adopt a hybrid life cycle?
o: Some parts are predictable while others need flexibility
All requirements are fixed and fully understood
The product is simple, small and repetitive
The customer has minimal involvement in delivery
6.w: Hybrid life cycles are chosen when some components need firm, predictive control while others benefit from adaptive delivery.

6.q: What is a key benefit of agreeing a procurement strategy at the start of a project?
o: It removes the need to monitor suppliers once contracts are signed
It gives a structured, consistent approach to acquiring goods and services
It replaces the need to produce a business case for the project
It guarantees that internal resources are always selected in preference
6.w: An early procurement strategy provides a consistent, transparent framework for obtaining resources and services externally.

6.q: At a project board meeting, stakeholders are found to disagree on what constitutes project success. What is the most likely cause?
o: Lessons learned were not reviewed
Too much time was spent on procurement
The project budget was exceeded
Success criteria were not clearly defined and agreed at the start
6.w: When success criteria are not defined and agreed early, stakeholders interpret success differently, causing misalignment.

6.q: A team has implemented a change, but its effects on cost and schedule were never recorded. Which change control step was most likely omitted?
o: Approval by the project sponsor
Impact assessment
Configuration verification audit
Change request logging
6.w: Impact assessment identifies the cost, time, quality and risk effects of a change and must precede approval and implementation.

6.q: A project manager must brief forty stakeholders in different offices within an hour. Which method offers the strongest advantage here?
o: A virtual broadcast or video conference to all of them
A handwritten memo pinned to each noticeboard
A printed newsletter posted to each office
A one-to-one face-to-face meeting with each person
6.w: A virtual broadcast reaches many dispersed stakeholders simultaneously and quickly, its key advantage over the alternatives.

6.q: Once a change has been implemented, what is a key final step in the change control process?
o: Monitor the impact and confirm alignment with project objectives
Notify the members of the wider supply chain
Archive all unused change request forms immediately
Submit the change again for a further round of approval
6.w: A post-implementation review confirms the change has delivered the intended benefit and remains aligned with the project's objectives without adverse side effects.

6.q: An organisation with strong risk management is more likely to achieve its project objectives. Why is this the case?
o: Risk management removes every possible threat before it can occur
Risk management removes the need for a project sponsor
Risk management guarantees delivery below the approved budget
Uncertainty is actively managed, improving the chance objectives are met
6.w: Actively managing uncertainty improves the likelihood that the project's objectives are achieved.

6.q: How does starting scope definition with a product breakdown structure help ensure completeness?
o: It confirms who will approve changes to the schedule
It fixes the project budget before any products are known
It ensures all required deliverables are identified before the work is planned
It removes the need to produce a work breakdown structure
6.w: Identifying all deliverables in the PBS first ensures the work needed to create them can be planned completely, reducing missed scope.

6.q: In configuration management, what does the term 'configuration item' typically refer to?
o: A stakeholder's preferred method of receiving communication
A deliverable or document that is placed under version control
A resource that has been assigned across several tasks
A task that lies on the project's overall critical path
6.w: A configuration item is any product, deliverable or document that is identified and controlled through the configuration management process.

6.q: A diagram breaks a new aircraft into fuselage, wings and avionics, then into their sub-parts. Which structure is this?
o: Cost breakdown structure
Organisational breakdown structure
Product breakdown structure
Work breakdown structure
6.w: A product breakdown structure decomposes the final output into its major products and their component parts.

6.q: A team identifies that early supplier delivery could let them finish sooner and plans to take advantage. Which purpose of risk management does this show?
o: Exploiting opportunities as well as managing threats
Avoiding the need to update the risk register
Eliminating all uncertainty from the schedule
Recording issues after they have already occurred
6.w: Risk management addresses positive uncertainty too, so planning to capture a beneficial outcome is exploiting an opportunity.

6.q: Before delivering a major milestone presentation, why would a project manager consult the communication plan?
o: To review the supplier's procurement performance
To approve an outstanding change request to scope
To confirm the audience, delivery method and timing of the update
To reassess the risk thresholds and escalation triggers
6.w: The communication plan defines the who, what, how and when of key information sharing, so it confirms how the milestone update should be delivered.

6.q: A supplier requests a change to a component because of a manufacturing constraint, so the project manager raises a change request. Which process decides whether the change is accepted?
o: Change control
Scheduling optimisation
Risk escalation
Scope definition
6.w: Change control is the formal process used to evaluate a change request and decide whether the change to scope should be accepted.

6.q: During delivery, who is best placed to confirm whether a new process will actually be workable in daily operation?
o: The project sponsor
The end users
The project governance board
The finance department
6.w: End users operate the outputs day to day, so they are best placed to confirm the solution is usable and fit for purpose.

6.q: Which of the following is least likely to be a genuine stakeholder in a project management plan?
o: A supplier with no involvement in the project
The project sponsor authorising the plan
The end users who will operate the output
The team members delivering the work packages
6.w: A stakeholder has an interest in or is affected by the project; a supplier with no involvement has no such stake in the plan.

6.q: A project manager applies Tuckman and Belbin, but a colleague expects them to remove all team problems. What is the correct view?
o: The models guide team development but do not guarantee a problem-free team
The models ensure the team never reaches the storming stage
The models fix the project's budget and schedule automatically
The models make leadership of the team unnecessary
6.w: The models guide team development and role balance but do not guarantee a problem-free team; leadership is still required.

6.q: During testing, a defect is discovered that prevents the product from being deployed. How should this be classified?
o: As an issue, because it has occurred and must be resolved
As a risk, because it may affect deployment later
As a baseline, because it defines the tested product
As an assumption, because it was expected during testing
6.w: The defect has already occurred and is blocking deployment, so it is an issue that must be managed to resolution.

6.q: Two teams run the same product, one linearly and one iteratively. What difference in scope management should be expected?
o: The linear team changes scope daily; the iterative team never alters it
Neither team applies any control over scope changes
The linear team fixes scope early; the iterative team reprioritises it each cycle
Both teams leave scope entirely undefined until handover
6.w: Linear fixes scope early, while iterative reprioritises it repeatedly as the solution develops.

6.q: How does a time-boxed activity differ from a conventionally scheduled activity in terms of what is fixed and what flexes?
o: Both its scope and its end date are entirely fixed at the outset
Its scope is fixed and its end date flexes to suit the remaining work
Its end date is fixed and its scope flexes, rather than time flexing to fit scope
Neither its scope nor its end date is ever actually defined
6.w: In time boxing the end date is fixed and scope flexes; conventional scheduling instead lets the timeline extend to fit the scope.

6.q: After a prototype is built it undergoes several tests to confirm it meets the client's requirements; which process is this part of?
o: Risk management activity
Quality assurance of processes
Quality control of outputs
Change management activity
6.w: Quality control includes testing outputs to confirm they meet the required standards and client expectations.

6.q: What is a key difference between resource levelling and resource smoothing?
o: Levelling adjusts quality, whereas smoothing adjusts cost
Levelling may change the critical path, whereas smoothing does not
Levelling applies only to Agile, whereas smoothing applies to linear
Smoothing adds team members, whereas levelling removes them
6.w: Levelling can extend the schedule and alter the critical path, whereas smoothing works within float and preserves the end date.

6.q: In a linear project with scope locked at the concept phase, a client requests a significant change during delivery. How is this typically handled?
o: It is implemented without review to avoid delay
It is added straight into the next delivery sprint
It is deferred until the benefits realisation phase
It is assessed through a formal change control process
6.w: Linear projects manage changes to a fixed scope through a formal change control process to maintain control of the project.

6.q: Resource levelling and resource smoothing are the two main examples of which scheduling activity?
o: Resource optimisation
Critical path analysis
Change control
Configuration management
6.w: Resource levelling and smoothing are the two principal resource optimisation techniques used within scheduling.

7.q: A chart divides a project into 'design', 'build' and 'test', each split into smaller work packages. Which structure is this?
o: Product breakdown structure
Cost breakdown structure
Responsibility assignment matrix
Work breakdown structure
7.w: A work breakdown structure decomposes the total work of a project into progressively smaller, manageable work packages.

7.q: A supplier misses a key delivery, so the project manager records it and assigns it to the procurement lead. Which stage of issue resolution is this?
o: Analysis of the issue's impact on objectives
Identification and assignment of the issue
Closure of the issue once it is verified
Resolution of the issue through corrective action
7.w: Logging the issue and giving it an owner are part of the initial identification and assignment stage of the resolution process.

7.q: A modest, low-cost component performs exactly as its specification demands. How should its quality be judged?
o: Poor, because it is inexpensive and simply designed
Good, because it meets its requirements and is fit for purpose
Poor, because it lacks additional premium features
Impossible to judge without knowing its market price
7.w: Because it meets its requirements and is fit for purpose, the component is of good quality regardless of cost.

7.q: Why can face-to-face communication be less effective in certain project delivery environments?
o: It provides too much written documentation for the team
It can be impractical for dispersed teams or tight schedules
It excludes body language from the exchange of information
It removes the need to consider cultural sensitivities
7.w: For geographically dispersed or fast-moving projects, arranging in-person meetings can be costly and time-consuming.

7.q: A benefit review finds that only part of the forecast savings were achieved; what should the organisation do?
o: Analyse why the benefits were not fully realised
Treat the whole project as a complete failure
Cancel all future benefit reviews entirely
Ignore the results because the project has closed
7.w: The gap between expected and actual benefits should be analysed and captured as lessons learned for future projects.

7.q: Which estimating method is most suitable for a project with high uncertainty in its early planning stage?
o: Analytical estimating
Parametric estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
7.w: Analogous estimating gives rough early estimates based on prior projects when detail is minimal and uncertainty is high.

7.q: A senior stakeholder questions whether recent product updates were properly authorised. Which combination of processes evidences both approval and controlled implementation?
o: Change control and configuration management
Scheduling and stakeholder management
Benefits management and procurement
Risk management and issue tracking
7.w: Change control provides the record of approval, while configuration management shows the change was applied and tracked correctly.

7.q: A high-impact risk was reduced by early action, and the manager records this in the register. Why does this matter?
o: It automatically triggers a review of the team's performance
It provides an audit trail of the risk treatment actions taken
It ensures the stakeholder matrix is kept fully up to date
It activates a formal contract change notice with suppliers
7.w: Recording responses and their outcomes in the register provides transparency and an audit trail that supports future learning.

7.q: Stakeholder analysis identifies a group as both highly influential and highly resistant. What should the engagement strategy prioritise?
o: Reassigning them to a different project
Proactively engaging them to understand concerns and seek alignment
Sending them brief updates by email only
Ignoring them unless they choose to escalate
7.w: Highly influential yet resistant stakeholders must be actively engaged to reduce opposition and secure buy-in.

7.q: What challenge might a project manager face when leading a team spread across multiple geographic locations?
o: Standardising tools that are already uniform everywhere
Reducing over-involvement from the team
Reconciling differing cultures and communication styles
Coping with excessive face-to-face interaction
7.w: Differences in culture and communication style can cause misunderstanding and tension, requiring the leadership approach to be tailored.

7.q: A team identifies all the key deliverables that must be placed under version control. Which configuration management activity is this?
o: Verification audit
Configuration planning
Configuration identification
Status accounting
7.w: Configuration identification determines which items are to be controlled and labels them so they can be managed.

7.q: Why does an approach based on time boxing depend heavily on clear prioritisation of the work to be done?
o: Because the scope is fixed and therefore cannot ever be reduced
Because prioritisation removes the need to set any deadline at all
Because the period is simply extended to accommodate all of the work
Because only the highest-priority items can be guaranteed within the fixed period
7.w: With time fixed, prioritisation ensures the most valuable items are completed first, as not all scope can be guaranteed in the period.

7.q: A team member consistently struggles with their workload. How can the leader best influence performance positively?
o: Ignore the issue in order to protect team morale
Remove the member from the team immediately
Provide support, coaching or mentoring to the member
Publicly highlight the member's poor performance
7.w: Effective leaders support struggling team members to build their capability and confidence rather than penalising them.

7.q: How does a communication plan help ensure stakeholders receive consistent information even when different team members send updates?
o: It requires the project manager personally to send every single message
It replaces the need for a project schedule during delivery
It prevents team members from ever contacting stakeholders directly
It defines the agreed messages, channels and timing that everyone follows
7.w: By defining agreed messages, channels and timing, the plan keeps information consistent regardless of which team member issues it.

7.q: Which of the following would you typically expect to find within a procurement strategy?
o: Preferred contract types and the criteria for evaluating suppliers
The models used to support development of the project team
The amount of float available on each of the project's tasks
The categories used to prioritise the identified project risks
7.w: A procurement strategy defines how suppliers will be chosen, including preferred contract types and evaluation criteria.

7.q: A project manager compares actual cost and progress against the plan approved before delivery to identify variances. What are they comparing against?
o: The risk register
The deployment baseline
The stakeholder analysis
The quality plan
7.w: Variances are measured against the deployment baseline, the approved plan for scope, cost and schedule.

7.q: Having developed a targeted engagement plan from stakeholder analysis, what is the next logical step?
o: Cancel all project communications until delivery begins
Implement the engagement activities aligned to each stakeholder profile
Replace the risk assessments with stakeholder assessments
Assign the delivery tasks to the project sponsor
7.w: The analysis and plan lead into delivering the engagement activities so communication stays relevant and timely for each group.

7.q: Beyond control, what wider benefit does transparent progress reporting bring to a project's stakeholders?
o: It builds stakeholder confidence and trust
It ensures no changes are ever requested
It removes the sponsor from the governance chain
It abolishes the need for a communication plan
7.w: Open, accurate reporting builds stakeholder confidence and trust in the project's management and direction.

7.q: During a gate review of the business case, what is the project manager's main role?
o: To determine the project's strategic alignment
To provide updates on justification and delivery feasibility
To chair the project governance board
To formally approve continued investment in the project
7.w: The project manager supplies delivery information that helps the sponsor present the case for continuation; approval rests with governance.

7.q: How does the risk analysis stage differ from the risk identification stage?
o: Both stages only find risks, but identification also selects the responses
Identification finds the risks, whereas analysis assesses their probability and impact
Both stages only assess impact, but analysis is done after closure
Identification assesses probability and impact, whereas analysis simply lists the risks
7.w: Identification discovers and records the risks; analysis then evaluates each one's probability and impact so they can be prioritised.

7.q: Which sequence best represents the stages of a typical risk management process?
o: Concept, definition, delivery and handover
Logging, escalation, resolution and reporting
Identification, assessment, response and closure
Planning, execution, monitoring and closure
7.w: A typical risk management process runs from identification, through assessment (analysis) and response, to closure.

7.q: Compared with a standard linear life cycle, what does an extended life cycle mainly change?
o: It shortens the concept phase so that the delivery phase can start much sooner
It lengthens the timeline after delivery to realise benefits and, later, dispose of the asset
It repeats the delivery phase in short cycles until stakeholders are satisfied
It merges the definition and delivery phases into a single continuous phase
7.w: The extended life cycle chiefly adds time after delivery, continuing through benefits realisation to the eventual disposal of the asset.

7.q: Midway through delivery a previously minor stakeholder gains significant influence. What does this imply for stakeholder analysis?
o: It should be ignored because the original analysis is now fixed
It should be revisited so engagement reflects their changed position
It shows analysis is only ever useful before the project starts
It means engagement should stop until the project is closed
7.w: Stakeholder analysis is iterative; as positions change it is revisited so engagement remains effective.

7.q: Members of a team with mixed experience are in conflict over task ownership. Which leadership challenge does this represent?
o: Slow approval cycles within governance
Inadequate quality assurance activity
Undefined roles and unclear expectations
Poor negotiation during procurement
7.w: Conflict over ownership usually signals unclear roles, and it is the leader's task to clarify expectations and responsibilities.

7.q: Why is it important to consider success criteria during the handover phase of a project?
o: To benchmark actual outcomes against the planned objectives
To allow the project budget to be closed early
To reassign the project team more quickly
To ensure the client signs off regardless of delivery quality
7.w: At handover, success criteria are used to confirm that deliverables and outcomes meet the agreed objectives.

7.q: Why do organisations apply project management to unique, time-limited pieces of work?
o: To ensure the work continues indefinitely as part of routine operations
To guarantee that the work encounters no risks or unexpected events
To achieve the defined objectives within agreed time, cost and quality constraints
To keep the project team occupied until a permanent role becomes available
7.w: The key purpose of project management is to achieve the project objectives within the agreed constraints, typically time, cost and quality.

7.q: Why is risk management considered a proactive discipline throughout the delivery of a project?
o: It focuses purely on logging issues after they occur
It records lessons learned solely at project closure
It only reacts once problems have already materialised
It anticipates and addresses uncertainty before it affects objectives
7.w: Risk management is proactive because it identifies and responds to uncertainty before it can affect project objectives.

7.q: During delivery, which task most directly reflects what a project team member is responsible for?
o: Deciding whether the project should proceed past each gate
Championing the project at senior board level
Completing assigned work packages to the required standard
Approving the project's business case before work starts
7.w: Project team members are responsible for carrying out the assigned work packages and producing outputs to the required standard.

7.q: A project manager explains why a linear deployment baseline feels more rigid than an iterative one. Which explanation is correct?
o: Linear fixes it early, while iterative refines it each iteration
Both fix the baseline rigidly before any delivery starts
Both leave the baseline entirely open until closure
Iterative fixes it early, while linear evolves over time
7.w: A linear life cycle establishes a firm baseline early, whereas an iterative life cycle refines the baseline across successive iterations.

7.q: Compared with business as usual, project work is generally characterised by higher levels of which factor?
o: Uncertainty, because the outputs are unique
Repetition, because the tasks are standardised
Stability, because the team is permanent
Predictability, because the work is routine
7.w: Because projects deliver unique outputs, they carry greater uncertainty and risk than the routine, repeatable work of operations.

8.q: What is a likely consequence of a project running no quality management at all?
o: Deliverables may fail to meet requirements and prove unfit for purpose
The project's scope becomes permanently fixed
All of the project's risks are automatically eliminated
Stakeholder communication is no longer required
8.w: Without quality management, deliverables risk failing requirements and being unfit for purpose.

8.q: Why is carrying out quality planning during the early stages of a project so important?
o: It guarantees the fastest possible project delivery
It removes the need to communicate with stakeholders
It reduces the budget the project will require
It defines how outputs will be verified against requirements
8.w: Quality planning establishes clear verification criteria, reducing rework and increasing confidence in delivery.

8.q: What is a key advantage of using time boxing in project delivery?
o: It ensures delivery is prioritised within a fixed timeframe
It guarantees that the full scope will always be delivered
It removes the need for configuration management activities
It extends deadlines to allow further stakeholder approval
8.w: Fixing the time forces prioritisation and focus, improving predictability of delivery within the agreed period.

8.q: Which feature most clearly distinguishes an iterative life cycle from a linear one in terms of its phases?
o: Its phases are repeated to develop the solution incrementally
Its phases are always carried out by external suppliers
Its phases are performed strictly once in a fixed order
Its phases exclude any form of review or feedback
8.w: The defining difference is repetition of phases to build the solution incrementally rather than a single pass.

8.q: A plan lists the executive board against a monthly summary report. Which attribute of the communication is this defining?
o: The frequency
The medium
The audience
The sender
8.w: Naming the executive board as the group to receive the report defines the audience for that communication.

8.q: In a linear life cycle, a board reviews whether the project should move into its next phase; what is this review called?
o: A stakeholder review
A decision gate
A post-project review
A formal quality audit
8.w: A decision gate is a review point used to decide whether a project should proceed to the next phase.

8.q: In what way does an effective risk management process improve decision-making on a project?
o: It replaces the need for a project board to make decisions
It removes uncertainty so no judgement is required
It ensures decisions are only made at project closure
It provides a structured understanding of threats and opportunities to inform choices
8.w: By assessing threats and opportunities, risk management gives decision-makers a structured basis for informed choices.

8.q: In an iterative project life cycle, what typically happens at the end of each development iteration?
o: The final product is signed off and the project closes
Stakeholder feedback is gathered to shape later iterations
All remaining risks are transferred to suppliers
The business case is rewritten from scratch
8.w: Each iteration ends with a review that gathers stakeholder feedback, informing and adapting the next iteration.

8.q: During an overseas product launch, the team flags that new tax legislation has been enacted. Which PESTLE category does this relate to?
o: Technological
Sociological
Environmental
Legal
8.w: New legislation, including tax law, falls under the legal category of PESTLE, which covers the laws and regulations affecting a project.

8.q: Which description best reflects the level and focus of a project's procurement strategy?
o: A high-level plan for how a project will source what it needs externally
A detailed cost estimate for every item the project will purchase
A log of goods received and inspected against their specifications
A list of the internal skills the project team already possesses
8.w: A procurement strategy is the high-level approach to sourcing externally, not a detailed estimate, receipt log or skills list.

8.q: What must happen before a change can be applied to a project's baseline?
o: Declaration of a change freeze across the project
Renegotiation of the relevant supplier contract
Deletion of the affected configuration item
Formal approval through the change control process
8.w: No change should be applied to a baseline until it has been formally assessed and approved through change control.

8.q: The project management plan is agreed between the project manager and which party who approves it on behalf of the organisation?
o: The project team members
The external suppliers
The end users
The project sponsor
8.w: The PMP is owned by the project manager but approved by the sponsor, who represents the organisation's interests.

8.q: Which configuration management activity ensures that only approved changes are made to configuration items?
o: Configuration planning
Configuration identification
Status accounting
Configuration control
8.w: Configuration control ensures that changes to controlled items follow the correct review and approval process before being made.

8.q: Within a project, who is normally responsible for developing and maintaining the project management plan?
o: The end users, who receive and operate the project’s final outputs
The project team members, who deliver the work packages defined within it
The project sponsor, who owns the business case on behalf of the organisation
The project manager, who develops and maintains it throughout delivery
8.w: The project manager owns and maintains the project management plan, which sets out how the project will be delivered on behalf of the sponsor.

8.q: What is a risk of stakeholders relying solely on written communication such as reports?
o: Reports are the ideal channel for resolving emotional conflict
Reports encourage immediate two-way dialogue between parties
Reports may be misinterpreted or ignored without discussion
Reports remove all ambiguity as soon as they are issued
8.w: Written reports can be overlooked or misunderstood, particularly where there is no chance to seek clarification.

8.q: A sprint ends before all of its assigned tasks are finished. In a time-boxed approach, what happens next?
o: The team is formally penalised for missing the target
The sprint is extended until every task is complete
The incomplete tasks are permanently abandoned
The remaining work is re-prioritised for a future sprint
8.w: Time boxing fixes the time, so unfinished work is reassessed and, if still needed, carried forward and re-prioritised.

8.q: A council forms a temporary team to build a new leisure centre, disbanding it once the centre opens. Which characteristic marks this as a project?
o: The output is identical to previous deliverables
The endeavour is transient with a defined end point
The team and funding are permanent and ongoing
The work repeats on a fixed monthly cycle
8.w: A project is transient, having a defined beginning and end, after which the temporary organisation is disbanded.

8.q: A project holds a face-to-face kick-off meeting with key stakeholders. What is a genuine advantage of this approach?
o: It removes the need for any later follow-up communication
It lowers the travel and venue costs for the project
It speeds up the project's procurement decisions
It helps build trust and stronger relationships early on
8.w: Face-to-face interaction helps build relationships, trust and alignment at the start of a project.

8.q: Which statement best describes the difference between a product owner and a project sponsor?
o: The sponsor provides strategic oversight, while the product owner manages feature value
The product owner approves gateway reviews, while the sponsor delivers the outputs
The sponsor manages the backlog, while the product owner controls the funding
The product owner owns the business case, while the sponsor manages delivery tasks
8.w: The sponsor secures funding and strategic alignment, whereas the product owner focuses on feature value and customer priorities.

8.q: A communication plan entry reads: 'monthly, by email'. Which two attributes of the communication does this define?
o: Frequency and medium
Audience and purpose
Sender and audience
Purpose and frequency
8.w: 'Monthly' defines the frequency of the communication and 'by email' defines its medium.

8.q: Halfway through a critical online review, the connection repeatedly drops out. Which disadvantage of virtual communication does this show?
o: It always takes far longer than a face-to-face meeting
It leaves no possibility of recording the session
It depends on reliable technology and stable connectivity
It can never involve more than two participants
8.w: Virtual communication depends on reliable technology and connectivity; technical failures can disrupt or degrade the exchange.

8.q: Which estimating tolerance would you most expect to find towards the bottom of the estimating funnel?
o: Around plus or minus 40%
Around plus or minus 50%
Around plus or minus 25%
Around plus or minus 10% or less
8.w: The bottom of the funnel reflects higher confidence and more detailed information, so tolerances narrow to around plus or minus 10% or less.

8.q: Why does stakeholder analysis help a project manager use limited engagement time efficiently?
o: It highlights where to focus effort by ranking influence and interest
It confirms that all stakeholders require identical levels of contact
It replaces the need for a communication plan later in delivery
It transfers responsibility for engagement to the project sponsor
8.w: By ranking influence and interest, analysis shows where engagement effort will have most value, allowing resources to be focused.

8.q: Which of the following best describes a benefit of conducting stakeholder analysis?
o: It improves communication planning by aligning strategy to stakeholder needs
It guarantees that every stakeholder will support the project
It removes the need for a separate risk management plan
It ensures that only internal stakeholders are involved
8.w: Understanding influence and interest allows communication and engagement to be aligned to each group's needs.

8.q: What is the main objective of risk analysis in project management?
o: To approve outstanding change requests more quickly
To assess the likelihood and impact of each identified risk
To transfer every identified risk to external suppliers
To remove all uncertainty from the project's plans
8.w: Risk analysis evaluates how likely each identified risk is to occur and how much it would affect the project's objectives.

8.q: Which sequence best represents the typical flow of a change control process?
o: Approve, escalate, configure, then define
Assess, approve, implement, then review
Implement, review, approve, then log
Reject, implement, report, then close
8.w: A change is first assessed for impact, then formally approved, implemented in a controlled way, and finally reviewed to confirm the outcome.

8.q: Which communication method best allows immediate two-way feedback and interpretation of tone and body language?
o: Posting to a shared online drive
Holding a face-to-face meeting
Distributing a printed newsletter
Exchanging threads of email
8.w: Face-to-face communication is the richest method, providing direct dialogue and non-verbal cues.

8.q: In critical path analysis, what is true of the activities that lie on the critical path?
o: They each hold generous amounts of spare float
They may be delayed freely without consequence
They have zero float and cannot be delayed
They are optional and can be removed if needed
8.w: Critical path activities have zero float; delaying any of them extends the overall project duration.

8.q: In project management, what is the primary purpose of adopting an extended project life cycle?
o: To shorten the overall delivery timescale
To reduce resource usage during development
To manage post-project benefits and performance
To avoid further stakeholder engagement
8.w: The extended life cycle continues beyond handover to ensure benefits are realised and performance is monitored over time.

8.q: A plan is being produced to set out how requirements will be confirmed throughout delivery; which process does this describe?
o: Quality control of outputs
Quality assurance of processes
Change control of the scope
Quality planning for the project
8.w: This is quality planning, which decides how quality will be measured and verified before work is carried out.

9.q: Quality planning is best described as which type of activity within quality management?
o: An activity concerned only with closing the project
A proactive activity that sets standards before delivery
A reactive activity carried out only after defects appear
An activity limited to auditing supplier processes
9.w: Quality planning is proactive, establishing the standards and approach to quality before delivery begins.

9.q: Why is the temporary nature of a project important to the way it is managed?
o: It ensures defined objectives are delivered within a bounded time frame
It removes the need for any stakeholder involvement during delivery
It guarantees the team can immediately be reused on other work
