It aligns all delivery activity strictly to the financial year
9.w: Being time-bounded focuses the project on achieving its specific objectives within defined constraints rather than continuing indefinitely.

9.q: What is a benefit of using instant-messaging platforms within a project team?
o: They support fast, informal exchanges that aid quick decisions
They remove the need for the team to hold any meetings
They create a formal, legally binding record of decisions
They eliminate the difficulties caused by differing time zones
9.w: Instant messaging enables rapid, informal collaboration, which is useful for fast-moving issues.

9.q: A sponsor asks what benefits management will contribute once the new system is operational. What is the best answer?
o: It will close the project's contracts with its suppliers
It will track and confirm that the expected improvements are actually achieved
It will approve any further changes to the system's scope
It will build and test the remaining system components
9.w: Benefits management tracks and confirms that the expected improvements are actually realised once the output is in use.

9.q: Which leadership behaviour is most likely to improve team commitment and output?
o: Avoiding all feedback in order to prevent conflict
Withholding key information to retain control
Setting unrealistic targets to push performance
Encouraging collaboration, openness and shared decision-making
9.w: Inclusive leadership builds trust and a sense of ownership, leading to stronger commitment and better results.

9.q: A sponsor wants one document setting out why the project is worth doing and what it will cost. Which document meets this need?
o: The business case
The quality plan
The risk register
The communication plan
9.w: The business case explains why the project is worthwhile, presenting its justification, costs, benefits and risks in a single document.

9.q: While revising the project management plan, a project manager notices there has been no input from the senior supplier. What risk does this pose?
o: Delivery capability and logistics could be misaligned
The project may receive excessive funding
Stakeholder interest will rise unexpectedly
The benefits are likely to be over-delivered
9.w: Without supplier input the plan's delivery logistics may be unrealistic or misaligned with the supplier's capacity.

9.q: An office build is estimated by applying a known cost per square metre to the floor area. Which estimating method is being used?
o: Expert judgement
Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
Parametric estimating
9.w: Parametric estimating applies a known cost per unit to a measured quantity to derive the total estimate.

9.q: Why is it important to establish project success criteria during the initiation phase?
o: To remove the need to prepare a business case
To allow the project to be closed sooner
To allocate individual tasks to team members
To define clear performance expectations that guide later decisions
9.w: Defining success criteria early gives a basis for measuring progress, guiding decisions and managing stakeholder expectations.

9.q: A client insists a release must launch on a fixed date, accepting that some lower-priority features may not be ready. Which technique fits?
o: Resource levelling
Critical path analysis
Time boxing
Analogous estimating
9.w: Holding the launch date fixed while allowing lower-priority features to drop is time boxing.

9.q: Which of the following best describes quality assurance within a project?
o: Identifying the risks that the project faces
Monitoring adherence to the quality processes used
Checking finished deliverables against the standards
Defining the acceptance criteria for outputs
9.w: Quality assurance ensures that the quality management processes are being followed and remain effective.

9.q: A delivery partner disputes the agreed timeline partway through the project. Which document validates the originally agreed plan?
o: The stakeholder matrix
The change control log
The deployment baseline
The communication strategy
9.w: The deployment baseline holds the agreed timeline and is the authoritative reference for resolving such disputes.

9.q: What is the purpose of the estimating funnel in project planning?
o: To identify the benefits associated with each deliverable
To select the most competitive supplier for the work
To measure the performance of the project team
To progressively narrow cost and time estimates as more information becomes available
9.w: The estimating funnel refines estimates and reduces tolerance over time as project knowledge increases.

9.q: Which of the following best describes the escalation step in the issue resolution process?
o: Recording the lessons learned after the issue is resolved
Logging the issue formally when it is first identified
Raising the issue beyond project authority for a decision
Assigning the issue to a stakeholder for resolution
9.w: Escalation is used when an issue exceeds the project manager's authority and requires a decision from a higher level of governance.

9.q: Why is it important that project outputs are fit for purpose?
o: To impress stakeholders during the project's review meetings
To shorten the overall duration of the project's activities
To meet quality objectives and deliver value to the customer
To reduce the planning resources needed by the project
9.w: Outputs that are fit for purpose satisfy the project's quality objectives and deliver the intended value to the customer.

9.q: How do change control and configuration management jointly relate to a project's baseline?
o: Neither of the two processes has any bearing on the project's baseline
Both freeze the baseline permanently so that it can never be altered
Configuration management authorises baseline changes; change control archives the previous plan
Change control authorises amendments to the baseline; configuration management records the updated, controlled baseline
9.w: Change control governs whether the baseline may be amended; configuration management maintains the record of the controlled, updated baseline.

9.q: A previously effective team shows falling enthusiasm and less clarity of purpose. To which earlier Tuckman stage is it most likely reverting?
o: Adjourning
Forming
Norming
Storming
9.w: Teams can slip back to norming when motivation or shared clarity declines, requiring the leader to re-establish focus.

9.q: A team specifies tolerances for the appearance, function and durability of a new product; which phase are they most likely in?
o: Quality planning for the product
Formal scope definition work
Stakeholder engagement activity
Quality control of the product
9.w: Defining tolerances and acceptance measures for deliverables is a key part of quality planning.

9.q: Which of the following would a communication plan typically specify about each message?
o: The exact cost of producing each report
The project's detailed technical specification
The intended audience for the message
The supplier's contractual penalties
9.w: A communication plan defines who each message is for, alongside its content, method, frequency and responsibility.

9.q: A project team meets regularly to review threats and plan responses before they occur. What core purpose of risk management does this serve?
o: Reducing the impact of uncertainty on project objectives
Transferring all responsibility for outcomes to the sponsor
Recording issues only after they have disrupted delivery
Guaranteeing that the original plan will never change
9.w: Regularly reviewing and responding to threats in advance reduces the impact of uncertainty on the project's objectives.

9.q: A configuration management plan is produced during initiation. What does this plan typically include?
o: A list of the approved external procurement providers
Roles, responsibilities, item tracking methods and audit schedules
The benefits realisation strategy for the whole project
A detailed cost breakdown of each individual task
9.w: The configuration plan defines the framework for managing items, including who is responsible, how items are tracked, and when audits occur.

9.q: Which of the following is most likely to support effective communication on a project?
o: Delaying all project updates until the project reaches closure
Engaging stakeholders and delivering consistent, timely messages
Changing the communication approach at frequent intervals
Giving the delivery team only verbal instructions
9.w: Effective communication depends on engaging stakeholders and sharing consistent, timely information.

9.q: What is the main purpose of a deployment baseline once a project moves into delivery?
o: To provide a fixed reference against which progress and variance are measured
To record the names and contact details of all project stakeholders
To list the recognised standards that the deliverables must comply with
To capture the lessons learned for use on future similar projects
9.w: The deployment baseline serves as the benchmark for monitoring performance and identifying variances during delivery.

9.q: Which stage directly follows the approval of a change in a typical change control process?
o: Log the original change request
Assess the change's impact
Implement the change and update the baseline
Reject the change request
9.w: Once authorised, the change is implemented and the affected baseline and records are updated to reflect it.

9.q: Which of the following is a core responsibility of the project manager?
o: Chairing the project steering group
Owning the business case and justifying the benefits
Authorising the release of project funding
Managing delivery against time, cost and quality
9.w: The project manager is responsible for delivering the project within the agreed constraints of time, cost and quality.

9.q: A team completes a cycle of planning, building and reviewing, then begins the same activities again. Which life cycle does this reflect?
o: A linear life cycle
An extended life cycle
An iterative life cycle
A hybrid life cycle
9.w: Repeating the same set of activities over successive cycles is the defining feature of an iterative life cycle.

9.q: Why is scope in a linear project usually captured in a detailed baseline agreed before delivery starts?
o: So that stakeholders need not be consulted during planning
So that the team can alter deliverables freely without any record
So that scope can be decided only after the product is built
So that any later change can be measured against an agreed, approved reference
9.w: A fixed scope baseline gives an agreed reference so later changes can be assessed and controlled against it.

9.q: Which sequence correctly orders the deliverable focus across a linear life cycle?
o: Handover first, then build, then definition, then the concept
A working product, then plans, then an idea, then handover
An idea, then detailed plans, then the build, then handover
Plans, then the concept, then handover, then the build
9.w: The linear life cycle progresses from concept (idea), to definition (plans), to deployment (build), to transition (handover).

9.q: A communication plan records why each message is sent, such as 'to maintain sponsor confidence'. Which attribute is this?
o: The purpose of the communication
The frequency of the communication
The medium of the communication
The recipient of the communication
9.w: Recording the reason a message is sent defines its purpose within the communication plan.

9.q: During a review, a project manager updates the status of several risks in the register. Why is keeping it current important?
o: It guarantees no new risks will ever emerge
It transfers all risks to the project sponsor
It ensures decisions are based on up-to-date risk information
It removes the need to hold any further reviews
9.w: A regularly updated register keeps risk information current, so responses and decisions reflect the project's actual exposure.

10.q: On a supplier contract with staged deliverables, milestones are frequently used to trigger which of the following events?
o: The identification of new project-level risks
Automatic changes to the project's agreed scope
Staged payments once agreed points are reached
The levelling of over-allocated project resources
10.w: Milestones mark agreed points of achievement and are often used contractually to trigger staged payments on their completion.

10.q: A key decision made verbally in a corridor is later disputed because nobody wrote it down. Which drawback of informal verbal communication is shown?
o: It reaches too many recipients at once
It is too slow for urgent matters
It often leaves no permanent record
It relies entirely on stable technology
10.w: Informal verbal communication frequently leaves no documented record, making agreements hard to confirm later.

10.q: Which of the following is the range of outcomes a decision gate can authorise for a project?
o: Continue to the next phase, amend the plan, or stop the project
Only continue, since a gate can never stop a project
Only stop, since a gate cannot allow continuation
Reassign the entire project team to other work
10.w: A decision gate can decide to proceed, amend or stop, not merely authorise continuation.

10.q: A sponsor asks what project management is fundamentally there to accomplish on their initiative. What is the best reply?
o: To guarantee the initiative faces no risks or changes whatsoever
To deliver the initiative's objectives successfully within the agreed constraints
To keep the initiative running indefinitely as a routine service
To maximise the number of tasks the team completes each week
10.w: The key purpose of project management is the successful delivery of the initiative's objectives within its agreed constraints.

10.q: Why is it important to establish a deployment baseline before project execution begins?
o: It enables scope, cost and time to be measured and controlled
It removes the need to produce a business case
It provides the content for marketing the project
It satisfies post-project reporting obligations only
10.w: The deployment baseline provides the reference against which performance is measured and change is controlled during delivery.

10.q: What is the primary purpose of a risk register in project management?
o: To record and manage identified risks and their planned responses
To record the availability of staff across the project
To maintain the project's formal change control log
To monitor the day-to-day tasks of the project team
10.w: The risk register is the tool used to document identified risks, their status and their planned responses.

10.q: On a project, what distinguishes genuine communication from merely transmitting information to a group of recipients?
o: The seniority of the person sending the message
The volume of information contained in the message
The choice of digital rather than printed channels
The receiver's feedback confirming the message is understood
10.w: Feedback that confirms the message has been understood turns one-way transmission into genuine, effective communication.

10.q: A team assumes a 'quality' product must be the most expensive and feature-rich option. Why is this view mistaken?
o: Quality has no connection to the customer's stated needs
Quality requires deliberately exceeding every stated requirement
Quality is only ever judged by the project's total cost
Quality means meeting the agreed requirements, not maximising features
10.w: Quality is about meeting the agreed requirements and fitness for purpose, not about cost or maximising features.

10.q: A project passes a risky component to a specialist third party under contract. Which risk response is being used?
o: Acceptance
Mitigation
Transfer
Avoidance
10.w: Transfer shifts responsibility for a risk to another party, commonly through a contract or insurance.

10.q: What is meant by the term 'time boxing' in project management?
o: Fixing the time allocated to an activity and allowing scope to vary within it
Assigning extra resources to the activities with the longest durations
Holding a reserve of unused time to draw on during emergencies
Extending the project deadline to accommodate additional scope changes
10.w: Time boxing fixes the duration of an activity or phase, with the scope delivered varying to fit within the allotted time.

10.q: A project's main server crashes, halting all progress. How should this event most accurately be classified?
o: As a risk, because it may affect the schedule
As a constraint, because it limits progress
As a milestone, because it marks an event
As an issue, because it has already occurred
10.w: The crash has already happened and is affecting delivery, so it is an issue to be managed and resolved rather than an uncertain future risk.

10.q: A retailer plans to enter an unfamiliar overseas market. How would a PESTLE analysis help the project manager assess this move?
o: By revealing external influences in that market that could create risks or opportunities
By defining the acceptance criteria for the finished product
By allocating the project's work packages to named team members
By recording the internal costs of each project deliverable
10.w: PESTLE examines the external environment, exposing market-specific risks and opportunities the project must plan for.

10.q: Uncontrolled additions to the agreed work are steadily expanding a project beyond its plan. Which discipline is intended to prevent this?
o: Resource management
Quality management
Scope management
Risk management
10.w: Controlling additions to the agreed work, and so preventing scope creep, is a core purpose of scope management.

10.q: Your project is one of eight coordinated under a wider business change programme. What is the role of programme management here?
o: To coordinate and align related projects for greater benefit
To focus only on your project's budget and schedule
To monitor health and safety across the organisation
To take over the duties of the individual project sponsors
10.w: Programme management coordinates and aligns related projects so they contribute to wider, shared business benefits.

10.q: Which of the following would you least expect to find within a project communication plan?
o: The format and frequency of routine status reports
A record of decisions already taken on the project
The preferred communication channel for each stakeholder
The individuals responsible for issuing project updates
10.w: A communication plan is a forward-looking tool; a record of decisions already taken belongs in a separate decision log.

10.q: Within a business case, the expected benefits are weighed against which two factors to justify proceeding with the investment?
o: The costs and the risks of the investment
The schedule bar chart and the communication plan
The team structure and the individual reporting lines
The test scripts and the recorded defect logs
10.w: A business case justifies the investment by weighing the expected benefits against its costs and risks; schedules, team structures and test records are not what the benefits are balanced against.

10.q: Which statement best describes the purpose of quality management within a project?
o: To avoid the need for any configuration control
To provide contingency against time overruns
To remove every risk that the project might face
To ensure deliverables are reviewed against agreed criteria
10.w: Quality management ensures outputs are assessed against agreed standards and are suitable for their intended use.

10.q: Within the discipline of benefits management, a 'benefit' is most accurately defined as what?
o: A risk that has occurred and now requires resolution
A tangible product created by the project's delivery work
A task that must be completed before another can begin
A measurable improvement resulting from an outcome, seen as advantageous
10.w: A benefit is a measurable improvement, arising from an outcome, that is perceived as advantageous by stakeholders.

10.q: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of quality assurance on a project?
o: Inspecting and correcting individual defective deliverables
Providing confidence that the processes can deliver the required quality
Checking that the agreed processes are being followed
Giving objective, independent evidence about how the work is done
10.w: Inspecting and correcting individual deliverables is quality control; assurance is process-focused and provides confidence.

10.q: A project manager is drafting a communication plan. Which content should it include to ensure messages reach the right people?
o: The organisational charts of unrelated internal departments
The licence terms of the software used on the project
Stakeholders, methods, frequency and communication responsibilities
The catering preferences for the project's regular meetings
10.w: A communication plan sets out who receives information, how and when it is shared, and who is responsible for sharing it.

10.q: A quality control check finds that several components fail to meet the specification; what should happen next?
o: Ignore the failures because most components passed
Adjust the original scope to match the output
Change the requirements to suit the output
Report the failure and decide on corrective action
10.w: Non-conformance found in quality control should be reported so that corrective action can be taken to meet the standard.

10.q: Which of the following is the strongest success criterion for a new healthcare IT system?
o: Users agree the system improves the patient experience
Every stakeholder is invited to the project meetings
No existing member of staff changes their role
All project invoices are settled within thirty days
10.w: An outcome-focused, user-centred measure such as improved patient experience reflects the benefits the project is intended to deliver.

10.q: Why is it inappropriate for a project sponsor to delegate ownership of the business case entirely to the project manager?
o: Delegating it would automatically cancel the project's approved funding
The project manager is not permitted to view the business case at any stage
The project manager already owns the project's risk and quality registers
Ownership must remain with the sponsor, who is accountable for the investment's benefits
10.w: The sponsor owns the business case because they are accountable for realising the investment's benefits; that ownership cannot be handed to the project manager.

10.q: During development of the project management plan, which stakeholder is most involved in defining scope and quality requirements?
o: The project sponsor
The team leader
The project governance board
The product owner
10.w: The product owner articulates what needs to be delivered and sets the associated quality expectations.

10.q: A newly formed team works entirely remotely and rarely meets in person. Which leadership challenge is most likely to arise?
o: Building rapport and trust without regular face-to-face contact
Preventing the team from using any digital tools
Ensuring members never communicate outside meetings
Guaranteeing that no member needs any direction
10.w: Remote working makes building rapport and trust harder without the regular face-to-face contact that fosters it.

10.q: During delivery, a team finds that the original success criteria are no longer relevant. What is the best course of action?
o: Abandon the criteria and rely on team discretion
Continue using the original criteria regardless
Replace the criteria without consulting stakeholders
Revise and formally agree the updated criteria with key stakeholders
10.w: Success criteria must stay relevant and should be updated through agreed change control involving key stakeholders.

10.q: Because a time box cannot be extended, what is the likely fate of the lowest-priority items if time runs short?
o: They automatically become the highest-priority items
They are delivered by lowering the required quality
They are dropped or deferred to a later time box
The time box is lengthened until they are all finished
10.w: With the deadline fixed, the lowest-priority items are dropped or deferred to a later time box rather than the period being extended.

10.q: Why is a project audit usually carried out by people independent of the delivery team?
o: So the assessment of compliance with processes is objective and unbiased
So the delivery team can approve its own results
So the benefits can be measured long after handover
So the next phase is automatically authorised
10.w: Independence lets a project audit assess process compliance objectively, free from the delivery team's bias.

10.q: A stakeholder does not receive project updates because of a gap in the communication plan. What was most likely left out?
o: The earned value baseline agreed for the project
The storage location of the archived project data
The stakeholder's preferred method and required frequency
The project's formal change control process
10.w: A communication plan specifies who receives what information, when and how, so omitting these details can create gaps.

10.q: A target of a 30% reduction in complaint-handling time is set for your project. How does this relate to benefits management?
o: It is a deliverable produced during the project
It is a risk mitigation measure
It is a benefit that must be tracked and realised after delivery
It is a constraint placed on the project
10.w: The reduction is a measurable benefit that must be tracked and realised to demonstrate the project's value.

11.q: Why might resource smoothing alone fail to resolve a serious over-allocation of resources?
o: Because it always pushes the completion date far into the future
Because it deletes tasks from the schedule to reduce demand
Because it ignores the project's float when moving activities
Because it only moves tasks within float and cannot exceed the end date
11.w: Smoothing is constrained by the end date and float; where demand still exceeds capacity, levelling may be needed instead.

11.q: A team member regularly offers original, unorthodox ideas and creative solutions during workshops. Which Belbin role best describes them?
o: Completer Finisher
Team Worker
Plant
Shaper
11.w: The Plant is the creative thinker who generates novel ideas and imaginative solutions to the team's problems.

11.q: During which stage of the issue resolution process is the effect of the issue on project objectives determined?
o: Closure
Analysis
Resolution
Identification
11.w: The analysis stage examines the severity and implications of the issue for the project's objectives before deciding how to address it.

11.q: In a typical iterative life cycle, why are development activities repeated rather than completed only once?
o: To progressively evolve and improve the product through successive cycles
To fix the full scope and budget before any work starts
To avoid producing any documentation until the final release
To remove the need for stakeholder involvement during delivery
11.w: Repetition lets the product evolve incrementally, incorporating feedback with each cycle.

11.q: How does leadership differ from management within a project environment?
o: Leadership focuses on scheduling, while management inspires the team
Leadership sets the vision and direction, while management ensures delivery
Leadership handles procurement, while management handles risk
Leadership and management are effectively identical in project delivery
11.w: Leadership provides vision and inspires others, whereas management concentrates on planning, control and execution.

11.q: A planner links dependent activities to find the longest path through the network. What are they determining?
o: The minimum time in which the project can be completed
The total cost of all the project's resources
The number of stakeholders needing consultation
The quality standards for each deliverable
11.w: The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent activities, which determines the shortest possible project duration.

11.q: What is the main output produced by the quality planning process on a project?
o: A project closure report
A project risk register
A change control log
A quality management plan
11.w: The quality management plan sets out how quality will be defined, managed and verified throughout the project.

11.q: Midway through a busy period, a manager treats a unique system upgrade exactly like routine operations. Why is this approach likely to fail?
o: Routine operations demand far more governance than projects
The upgrade's uniqueness and finite scope need project management
The upgrade cannot involve any of the operational staff
Operations and projects require exactly the same controls
11.w: A unique, time-bounded upgrade requires project management disciplines, which differ from the steady controls used for business as usual.

11.q: In an extended project life cycle, what typically triggers the final termination or disposal phase?
o: The delivery phase producing the project's outputs
The delivered asset reaching the end of its useful life
The very first benefit being realised in operation
The business case first being approved by the sponsor
11.w: The termination or disposal phase begins once the asset has reached the end of its useful life and its benefits are exhausted.

11.q: Which statement correctly reflects how a project issue should be treated once it has been identified?
o: It must be actively managed and resolved, and escalated where necessary
It should be ignored until it possibly occurs at some later point
It should be recorded only within the project's risk register
It should be treated as a guaranteed benefit for the project
11.w: An issue is a current problem requiring active management, resolution and, where appropriate, escalation; it is not a future or beneficial event.

11.q: A key risk recorded in the project's risk register has now materialised. What should happen next?
o: It should be ignored because it has already been analysed
It should be closed and recorded as a completed milestone
It should be deleted from the risk register without further action
It should be reclassified as an issue and managed accordingly
11.w: Once a risk actually occurs it becomes a current problem, so it is reclassified as an issue and handled through the issue management process.

11.q: A project's main server crashes during a product launch. What should the project manager do first?
o: Replace the server without recording what happened
Log the issue and assess its impact on the project
Escalate the problem straight to the project sponsor
Cancel the launch until the server is restored
11.w: The first step is to formally log the issue and assess its impact so that an informed decision on the response can be made.

11.q: A PMO analyst finds that three portfolio projects are reporting schedule delays and inconsistent risk data. What is the most appropriate PMO action?
o: Replace the affected project managers without delay
Compile the performance data and escalate the trends to governance
Cancel the three projects that are reporting delays
Take over delivery responsibility for the projects
11.w: The PMO monitors and reports performance trends so that governance bodies can make informed decisions.

11.q: Which statement best reflects a purpose of risk management that goes beyond simply avoiding threats?
o: It removes all uncertainty from the project
It also identifies and helps exploit potential opportunities
It guarantees the project will finish under budget
It transfers accountability for outcomes to suppliers
11.w: Risk management addresses uncertainty in both directions, seeking to exploit opportunities as well as reduce threats.

11.q: A team member regularly supports colleagues, smooths over disagreements and helps keep the group harmonious. Which Belbin role best fits?
o: Specialist
Shaper
Coordinator
Team Worker
11.w: The Team Worker is supportive and diplomatic, helping to maintain cohesion and ease friction within the team.

11.q: A project manager works with stakeholders to agree the quality requirements before delivery begins; which process is this?
o: Change control of the scope
Quality control of the outputs
Quality planning for the project
Progress reporting to sponsors
11.w: Quality planning identifies the quality requirements and determines how they will be met before execution begins.

11.q: A new starter asks what separates an issue from an assumption in project terms. Which explanation is correct?
o: An issue is a problem that has occurred; an assumption is something taken to be true for planning
An issue is a benefit; an assumption is a cost to be recovered
An issue and an assumption mean effectively the same thing
An issue is a future possibility; an assumption is a current problem
11.w: An issue is a problem that has already occurred, whereas an assumption is something accepted as true for planning purposes; they are different concepts.

11.q: What is the main benefit of extending a project life cycle to include a benefits realisation phase?
o: It fixes the delivery budget more tightly before any work is allowed to begin
It confirms that the intended benefits are actually achieved once the outputs are in use
It allows the requirements to be changed freely throughout the delivery phase
It reduces the number of governance decision gates the project must pass through
11.w: Adding a benefits realisation phase lets the organisation confirm the forecast benefits are delivered in operational use.

11.q: Which of the following is most characteristic of business-as-usual rather than of project work?
o: Producing a unique output using temporarily assigned resources
Delivering a defined scope within a fixed time frame
Delivering repetitive tasks and services on a continuous basis
Following a phased life cycle to achieve set objectives
11.w: Business-as-usual maintains ongoing, repeatable services and functions, unlike the unique, time-bounded outputs of a project.

11.q: An estimate for a new school is based on a similar previous school build, adjusted slightly for inflation. Which estimating method is this?
o: Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
Parametric estimating
11.w: Using a comparable completed project as the basis for an estimate, with minor adjustment, is analogous estimating.

11.q: How does a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) help to reduce duplication of effort on a project?
o: By ranking the project's activities in their order of criticality
By defining the communication channels between the stakeholders
By assigning each member of the team to a specific budget code
By clarifying who is responsible and accountable for each task
11.w: By assigning clear responsibility and accountability, the RAM prevents overlap and confusion about who should do each task.

11.q: A project board rejects a change after assessment shows high cost for limited benefit. What does this demonstrate about change control?
o: It speeds up delivery through early implementation
It removes the need for any stakeholder input
It ensures that only beneficial changes are implemented
It supports uncontrolled changes to the project scope
11.w: Change control applies formal evaluation so the project is protected from changes that are unnecessary or harmful to its objectives.

11.q: At what point in the estimating funnel is a detailed bottom-up estimate typically produced?
o: Immediately after the contract is signed
When the full scope and work breakdown structure are available
After the post-project review is complete
At the initial project concept stage
11.w: Bottom-up estimating requires a detailed scope and work breakdown structure, which are available mid-to-late in the funnel.

11.q: Why is delivering far beyond the agreed requirements not necessarily a sign of quality?
o: Quality is measured solely by how much is delivered
Quality always improves whenever more features are added
Quality is unrelated to the requirements set for the deliverable
Quality is about meeting requirements, so over-delivery can waste resources
11.w: Since quality means conformance to requirements, delivering beyond them (gold plating) adds no quality and can waste resources.

11.q: What is the key difference between parametric estimating and analogous estimating when producing a project estimate?
o: Parametric relies on expert opinion, while analogous applies statistical formulae
Parametric is used only at handover, while analogous is used only at initiation
Parametric suits iterative projects only, while analogous suits linear projects only
Parametric uses historical per-unit data, while analogous compares whole completed projects
11.w: Parametric estimating scales historical cost or duration per unit, whereas analogous estimating draws on the overall data from a similar completed project.

11.q: Why can leading a team drawn from several different departments be challenging for a project manager?
o: Members may have divided loyalties and competing priorities
Members always share identical objectives and priorities
Members never require any form of communication
Members automatically report only to the project manager
11.w: Cross-functional members often answer to home managers too, creating divided loyalties and competing priorities.

11.q: Which of the following is a key responsibility of the project sponsor?
o: Writing the detailed work breakdown structure
Maintaining the day-to-day project issue log
Producing the project communication plan
Approving key decisions and owning the business case
11.w: The sponsor provides direction, owns the business case and approves the major decisions and investment for the project.

11.q: What is a common disadvantage of relying on face-to-face communication in a project?
o: It can incur higher costs through travel and scheduling
It is too formal to be used in iterative environments
It limits the opportunities for participants to give feedback
It reduces the level of trust between team members
11.w: Although effective for building trust, face-to-face communication can be costly and time-consuming to arrange.

11.q: How does benefits management differ from simply producing and delivering a project's outputs?
o: It focuses on realising the value the outputs are meant to create
It concentrates only on producing the outputs to specification
It ends the moment the outputs are handed over to users
It ignores the outcomes and measures only delivery on time
11.w: Outputs enable outcomes and benefits; benefits management focuses on realising the value rather than merely producing outputs.

11.q: Which of the following is a typical activity carried out during quality planning?
o: Identifying the residual risks remaining after responses are applied
Monitoring the changing attitudes of the project’s stakeholders
Defining the acceptance criteria that deliverables must meet
Approving the procurement contracts entered into by the project
11.w: Quality planning determines the standards and acceptance criteria that deliverables must meet and how quality will be achieved.

12.q: A new data protection regulation takes effect during your design phase. Which analysis would help you understand its implications for the project?
o: A lessons-learned report
PESTLE analysis
A RAID log
Monte Carlo simulation
12.w: PESTLE assesses how external legal and political factors, such as new regulation, may affect the project.

12.q: How does quality assurance differ from quality control in the delivery of a project?
o: Assurance checks that processes are followed, while control inspects the outputs
Assurance inspects the deliverables, while control defines the standards
Assurance applies only to iterative projects, while control applies to linear ones
Assurance happens after delivery, while control happens before planning begins
12.w: Quality assurance provides confidence that the correct processes are being followed, while quality control checks the resulting deliverables against standards.

12.q: A communication model describes a sender, a message, a medium and a receiver. Which further element makes it effective?
o: A more senior sender issuing the message
A longer, more detailed written message
Feedback confirming the message has been understood
A larger distribution list for the message
12.w: Feedback closes the loop between sender and receiver, confirming shared understanding and making communication effective.

12.q: A project was delivered on time and within budget, yet a stakeholder claims it was not successful. What most likely caused this disagreement?
o: The risk register was not kept up to date
The project board was disbanded too early
Lessons learned were not formally recorded
Success criteria were not clearly defined and agreed at the start
12.w: Without clear, agreed success criteria at the outset, stakeholders can hold conflicting views of what constitutes success.

12.q: Why is a structured issue management process valuable to a project manager?
o: It fixes the project scope so no changes are ever needed
It ensures problems are logged, assessed and resolved consistently
It replaces the need for a risk register entirely
It guarantees the project will finish under budget
12.w: A structured process ensures issues are captured, evaluated and resolved in a consistent, controlled way.

12.q: At handover, the operations team asks how it will be judged whether the project met its goals. What should they be shown?
o: The agreed project success criteria
The project communication plan
The project risk register
The project stakeholder map
12.w: The agreed success criteria are the standard against which the project's achievement of its goals is judged at handover.

12.q: On an agile project, which responsibility most clearly belongs to the product owner rather than the project manager?
o: Managing the project's overall budget and schedule
Reporting overall delivery progress to the project board
Prioritising the backlog so it reflects the greatest user value
Securing the resources needed for the delivery team
12.w: The product owner owns and prioritises the backlog to maximise value delivered to users, distinct from the project manager's delivery oversight.

12.q: A project manager prepares a one-page summary schedule for executives showing only the key dates. What are these key dates called?
o: Baselines
Dependencies
Work packages
Milestones
12.w: Key dates shown on a summary schedule are milestones, giving senior stakeholders a high-level view of progress.

12.q: One manager plans and controls the work; another energises and directs the people. Which is chiefly exercising leadership?
o: The manager who plans and controls the work
The manager who energises and directs the people
Both equally, because leadership simply means administration
Neither, since the two activities are identical
12.w: Leadership is about energising and directing people towards a vision, whereas planning and controlling the work is management.

12.q: A project manager describes a deliverable as being of 'high quality'. What does 'quality' mean in the context of a project?
o: That it meets the agreed requirements and is fit for purpose
That it was completed ahead of its planned schedule
That it includes more features than were originally specified
That it exceeds recognised industry standards for the sector
12.w: In APM terms, quality means the deliverable conforms to its agreed requirements and is fit for its intended purpose.

12.q: In an agile project a stakeholder maintains the product backlog and decides which features are developed next. Which role is this person performing?
o: Project sponsor
Scrum master
Product owner
Project manager
12.w: The product owner owns the backlog and maximises value by deciding the order in which features are delivered.

12.q: Which statement best describes the purpose of the estimating funnel within a project?
o: It maps the costs of each resource against the responsible stakeholders
It limits the number of estimates that may be produced to three
It illustrates how the accuracy of estimates improves as the project matures
It applies only within iterative project environments that use sprints
12.w: The estimating funnel shows that estimates become more accurate and their range narrows as more information becomes known through the life cycle.

12.q: Once a work breakdown structure is complete, which subsequent planning activity does it most directly enable?
o: Selecting the project's governance board
Approving the project's business case
Realising the project's long-term benefits
Estimating and scheduling the identified work packages
12.w: The WBS defines manageable work packages that can then be estimated, scheduled and assigned for control.

12.q: A project team has begun openly disagreeing as members assert their opinions and challenge each other's roles. Which Tuckman stage is this?
o: Forming
Storming
Norming
Performing
12.w: Storming is characterised by conflict as members assert their views and challenge roles and leadership.

12.q: A leader creates an environment where team members feel trusted and encouraged to share ideas. What is this most likely to improve?
o: Team performance and innovation
The quality of the risk register
The accuracy of the project budget
The logistics of the project location
12.w: Trust and inclusion encourage collaboration and allow teams to perform at their best.

12.q: Team members are unsure who is accountable for each work package, causing duplicated effort. Which tool should the project manager use?
o: A cost breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
A risk breakdown structure
A critical path network
12.w: A RAM clarifies who is responsible and accountable for each work package, reducing gaps and duplication.

12.q: A project manager reviews economic, legal and environmental trends affecting a new facility. What is the purpose of examining these together?
o: To confirm the internal budget allocation for the facility
To build a rounded picture of external influences on the project
To assign responsibilities to the facility's construction team
To measure the quality of the facility's finished components
12.w: Considering these factors collectively, as in PESTLE, gives a rounded view of the external environment shaping the project.

12.q: A change in organisational strategy puts a project at risk of cancellation. Who is responsible for deciding whether it should continue?
o: Project sponsor
Project manager
Product owner
Project planner
12.w: The sponsor assesses continued strategic alignment and has the authority to continue or cancel the project.

12.q: Selecting the type of contract and reimbursement approach for external work forms part of which project document?
o: The responsibility assignment matrix
The procurement strategy
The work breakdown structure
The issue log
12.w: Contract and reimbursement types are decisions set out within the procurement strategy.

12.q: At which point in the change control process is a change formally accepted or rejected?
o: Before the change request is logged
At the authorisation stage, after the impact has been assessed
Only after the change has already been implemented
During the project's closure phase exclusively
12.w: A change is formally accepted or rejected at the authorisation (decision) stage, once its impact has been assessed.

12.q: A colleague asks you to complete the sentence 'scope management is the process of...' using correct terminology.
o: ...reporting progress regularly to the project's various stakeholders
...allocating the people and equipment needed for the project's activities
...identifying and mitigating the threats that could affect the project
...defining, controlling and delivering the required work of the project
12.w: Scope management is the process of defining, controlling and delivering the required work; the distractors describe resource, risk and communication activities.

12.q: Which outcome would a well-run quality management approach be expected to deliver?
o: A guarantee that no risks will ever materialise
Deliverables that reliably conform to their specifications
A permanent freeze on the project's approved budget
An automatic increase in the size of the project team
12.w: Effective quality management produces deliverables that reliably conform to their specifications.

12.q: Why is knowing the critical path valuable when managing a project's timescale?
o: Because activities on it can slip without any effect
Because delay to any of its activities delays the whole project
Because it lists every risk recorded in the register
Because it removes the need to monitor other activities
12.w: Activities on the critical path have no float, so any delay to them directly delays the project completion date.

12.q: A project leader is described as providing 'direction'. What does this element of leadership involve?
o: Setting a clear vision and guiding the team towards shared objectives
Logging every risk that could affect the project outcome
Approving invoices submitted by the project's suppliers
Updating the configuration status of controlled items
12.w: Providing direction is the leadership function of setting a vision and guiding the team towards shared objectives.

12.q: Several related projects are managed together to improve customer service and maximise value. What are they collectively part of?
o: A portfolio
A business case
A programme
A risk register
12.w: A programme is a group of related projects managed in a coordinated way to deliver benefits not available from managing them individually.

12.q: A team reviews trends in renewable-energy legislation to see how they could shape a new facility's design. Which tool are they most likely using?
o: SWOT analysis
PESTLE analysis
MoSCoW prioritisation
Cost-benefit analysis
12.w: PESTLE analysis identifies and assesses external factors, such as legislation, that could influence project outcomes.

12.q: Within the project, programme and portfolio hierarchy, which level is most directly concerned with aligning investment to organisational strategy?
o: Portfolio management
Work package management
Programme management
Project management
12.w: Portfolio management is the level most directly focused on aligning the organisation's investment in projects and programmes with its strategy.

12.q: Which statement best describes analytical, or bottom-up, estimating as used to produce a project estimate?
o: Producing a top-down figure based on the overall size of the project
Building a total estimate by summing the estimated costs of individual tasks
Comparing the project with a previous initiative of broadly similar scope
Reaching a figure through repeated rounds of anonymous expert consensus
12.w: Analytical, or bottom-up, estimating totals the estimates for individual tasks or work packages to produce an overall project estimate.

12.q: Which of the following is most likely to be a portfolio management responsibility?
o: Selecting the right mix of projects to align with strategy
Ensuring two related projects are delivered in sync
Monitoring an individual project's risk register
Defining the detailed scope for a single project
12.w: Portfolio management ensures the right projects and programmes are chosen and prioritised to meet strategic goals.

12.q: A manager claims that project management is simply 'getting the work done'. Which correction is the most accurate?
o: It is the informal delegation of tasks to whoever happens to have spare capacity
It is the day-to-day running of a settled service once it has been established
It is the ongoing ranking of investments to match the organisation's overall strategy
It is the planned application of processes and skills to achieve defined objectives
12.w: Project management is a planned, structured application of processes and skills to defined objectives, not informal task allocation, operations or portfolio prioritisation.

13.q: Before a project is authorised, what is the main reason an organisation requires a business case to be produced?
o: To justify the investment by setting out its costs, benefits and risks
To list every task and dependency needed to build the product
To assign the day-to-day responsibilities across the whole project team
To record the detailed technical design of the final project deliverable
13.w: The business case justifies the investment by presenting the costs, benefits, risks and options, providing the basis for the decision to proceed.

13.q: Which of the following statements best defines the term 'benefits management' in a project context?
o: The production and testing of the project's outputs before handover
The identification, planning, tracking and realisation of a project's benefits
The scheduling of tasks so the project finishes by its agreed deadline
The control of changes to the project's approved scope baseline
13.w: Benefits management is the identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation of the benefits a project is intended to deliver.

13.q: Which of the following statements most accurately captures the central focus of the quality planning process?
o: Identifying the quality criteria and the means to satisfy them
Measuring completed products against their specification
Reviewing whether agreed procedures are being applied
Escalating issues that exceed the manager's authority
13.w: Quality planning focuses on defining the quality criteria to be met and the methods and resources used to satisfy them.

13.q: A business case presents only one delivery option. What weakness does this introduce?
o: It demonstrates that the approach is more agile
It removes the need for any stakeholder input
It automatically makes the project easier to fund
It limits consideration of alternatives and weakens the justification
13.w: Without alternatives to compare against, the case cannot demonstrate that the chosen option delivers the best value.

13.q: How does effective risk management support communication within a project?
o: It removes the need to hold regular project team meetings
It removes the need to hold a contingency budget in reserve
It gives the team a shared understanding of potential challenges and responses
It allows difficult decisions to be deferred until project closure
13.w: Risk management aligns the team around known uncertainties and agreed responses, supporting open and transparent communication.

13.q: Why is the closure stage important within the issue resolution process?
o: It confirms the issue is resolved and records any lessons learned
It assigns the issue to an owner for the very first time
It decides whether the issue should be escalated further
It determines the issue's likely impact on the schedule
13.w: Closure confirms the issue has been dealt with and captures lessons that may help on future work.

13.q: Understanding that a team is at Tuckman's storming stage, how should a project manager use this insight?
o: By disbanding the team and starting again
By helping resolve conflict and clarifying roles and goals
By stepping back entirely and giving no direction
By assuming the team is fully mature and self-managing
13.w: At the storming stage, conflict emerges, so the leader should facilitate resolution and clarify roles and objectives.

13.q: How can a well-run risk management process increase stakeholder confidence in a project?
o: By showing threats are being identified and actively managed
By promising that no risks will ever occur
By hiding potential threats from the project board
By removing the need for any progress reporting
13.w: Demonstrating that risks are being systematically identified and managed reassures stakeholders that the project is under control.

13.q: A project manager prepares a Gantt chart to show when specific tasks will be carried out. Which aspect of scheduling does this support?
o: Financial and cost reporting
Task sequencing and time planning
Assignment of team roles
Identification of project risks
13.w: A Gantt chart is a scheduling tool that displays the order of tasks and when each is planned to take place.

13.q: An agile team adapts its backlog regularly throughout delivery. What does this indicate about scope management on the project?
o: Scope is left undefined until testing begins
Scope is adapted continuously as the project evolves
Scope is fixed and unchanged after the concept phase
Scope is fully defined at the start and then locked
13.w: Regular backlog refinement reflects iterative scope management, in which scope adapts to evolving priorities and feedback.

13.q: Specifying that updates will be shared 'via video call' in a communication plan defines which attribute?
o: The frequency of the update
The owner of the update
The medium of the update
The audience of the update
13.w: Stating the channel, such as a video call, defines the medium or method of communication within the plan.

13.q: A team uses a RACI matrix and a stakeholder register to inform its communication plan. What benefit does this bring?
o: Roles and responsibilities are reflected in tailored communication
The overall project schedule is noticeably shortened
Procurement is then able to proceed without any oversight
The need to carry out risk assessments is removed
13.w: Drawing on a RACI matrix and stakeholder register ensures each communication is directed to the right person in the most appropriate way.

13.q: What characteristic must an event have before it can be classed as a project risk?
o: It must be uncertain and capable of affecting the project's objectives
It must lie entirely outside the project team's ability to control
It must occur only during the execution phase of the project
It must be guaranteed to happen at some point during the project
13.w: A risk must be uncertain and able to affect objectives, whether positively or negatively.

13.q: A team lists activities like 'write code' and 'run tests' but never identifies the deliverables these produce. Which structure is missing?
o: An organisational breakdown structure
A cost breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
A product breakdown structure
13.w: The product breakdown structure identifies the deliverables; without it the team risks planning work without confirming what it must produce.

13.q: What is meant by 'quality' in the context of a project?
o: Delivering outputs that meet the agreed requirements and are fit for purpose
Providing the most technically advanced solution available
Meeting customer expectations regardless of the agreed scope
Completing every task well ahead of its planned deadline
13.w: Quality is defined as meeting the specified requirements and ensuring the output is fit for its intended purpose.

13.q: How can appropriately delegating authority and trusting team members influence a project team's performance?
o: It always slows delivery because decisions take longer
It can increase ownership and motivation, improving output
It removes the leader's responsibility for the results
It prevents team members from developing new skills
13.w: Appropriate delegation builds ownership and motivation, which tends to improve the team's output.

13.q: A team uses a product breakdown structure (PBS) to represent the end product. What is its primary purpose in scope management?
o: To allocate costs to individual project activities
To estimate the overall schedule for the project
To define the deliverables that make up the final product
To assign team members to each project task
13.w: A PBS breaks the end product down hierarchically to define the deliverables that make up the final product.

13.q: An operations manager notes their team's output rarely changes month to month. How does this contrast with a project team's work?
o: A project team also produces unchanging monthly output
A project team has no need to manage any resources
A project team operates without any start or end date
A project team works towards a defined, finite objective
13.w: A project pursues a defined objective within a finite timeframe, unlike the steady, continuous output of operations.

13.q: In APM terms, the potential of an event to affect the achievement of objectives is known as what?
o: A risk
A benefit
A dependency
An issue
13.w: Risk is the potential of an event or situation to affect the achievement of objectives.

13.q: Why is a risk described as 'uncertain' rather than definite?
o: Because it can never affect the project's objectives
Because it is always guaranteed to occur eventually
Because it may or may not happen in the future
Because it has already happened and been recorded
13.w: Risk carries uncertainty: it is a possible future event that may or may not materialise.

13.q: A sponsor wants assurance that the methods being used are capable of producing acceptable outputs. Which activity provides this?
o: Quality control, by inspecting each finished item
Quality assurance, by evaluating whether processes are sound
Configuration management, by controlling document versions
Risk management, by logging threats to delivery
13.w: Quality assurance evaluates whether the processes are capable of delivering acceptable outputs, giving the sponsor confidence.

13.q: How do milestones assist a project manager specifically when reporting the status of a project to its stakeholders?
o: They provide clear reference points showing whether delivery is on track
They record the full technical specification of each project deliverable
They set out the communication methods to be used for each group
They list the individual costs of every one of the project's activities
13.w: Milestones give clear, recognisable reference points against which achievement can be reported, showing stakeholders whether delivery is on track.

13.q: A project team documents its overall approach to using external suppliers before any contracts are signed. What have they produced?
o: A configuration management plan
A procurement strategy
A benefits realisation plan
A stakeholder engagement matrix
13.w: Documenting the overall approach to sourcing from external suppliers is the procurement strategy.

13.q: A responsibility assignment matrix is typically created by combining which two structures?
o: The work breakdown structure and the organisational breakdown structure
The product breakdown structure and the benefits map
The communication plan and the procurement strategy
The cost breakdown structure and the risk register
13.w: A RAM maps the work packages of the WBS against the people or teams in the OBS to assign responsibilities.

13.q: A complex product must be delivered by combined IT and engineering teams. Which action best demonstrates project management?
o: Applying methods and tools to plan, execute and control delivery
Hiring additional administrative staff for routine services
Documenting every staff role across the whole organisation
Processing staff annual leave requests through a central team
13.w: Applying structured methods, processes and tools to plan and control the delivery is the essence of project management.

13.q: A project manager wants to anticipate how the wider environment might influence a new venture. Which analysis best serves this purpose?
o: A responsibility assignment matrix mapping tasks to team roles
A PESTLE analysis of political, economic, social and other external factors
A work breakdown structure decomposing the project's deliverables
A risk register listing only internal delivery threats
13.w: PESTLE is used to scan the external environment, whereas the other tools address internal work, roles or logged threats.

13.q: Critical path analysis shows a task that can be delayed without affecting the overall project timeline. What is this an example of?
o: Float
Budget slippage
Configuration drift
Scope creep
13.w: Float, or slack, is the amount of time an activity can be delayed without affecting the project's completion date.

13.q: Which configuration management activity maintains records of each item's current state and its history of changes?
o: Status accounting
Configuration planning
Verification audit
Identification
13.w: Status accounting keeps the records showing the current status and change history of each configuration item.

13.q: Why might a project manager create a product breakdown structure before a work breakdown structure?
o: To create a baseline budget for the project
To determine the cost of the individual tasks first
To assign team members to their roles early on
To establish a shared understanding of the product to be delivered
13.w: The PBS clarifies the deliverables required, giving a shared understanding of the product so that the WBS can be built around it.

13.q: Early feedback on a new IT system shows that users are confused by the interface wording. Which action best supports successful adoption?
o: Reassign the technical work to the users themselves
Transfer the concern to the sponsor as a risk
Arrange further end user engagement and training
Update the project governance plan
13.w: Engaging and training end users after handover helps embed the solution and maximise the benefits realised.

14.q: Why is quality assurance often carried out by people independent of the delivery team?
o: So that the delivery team is relieved of all quality responsibility
So that inspection of the final product can be skipped entirely
So that the schedule can be shortened by removing reviews
So that confidence in the processes is objective and unbiased
14.w: Independence gives quality assurance objectivity, providing unbiased confidence that processes are sound.

14.q: An estimate based on an industry-average unit cost is challenged as insufficiently accurate. How could its accuracy best be improved?
o: By breaking the work down and applying analytical estimating
By relying on expert guesswork instead
By substituting an analogous estimate
By adding a fixed contingency percentage
14.w: Analytical, bottom-up estimating improves accuracy by evaluating each component individually rather than applying a single average rate.

14.q: What is the main purpose of a decision gate within project governance?
o: To approve the contracts held with suppliers
To assess whether the project should continue
To carry out the lessons learned sessions
To delegate new work packages to the team
14.w: Decision gates provide control points where continuation of the project is reviewed against performance and objectives.

14.q: Which of the following is not part of managing a project?
o: Identifying and managing project risks
Resolving issues that arise during delivery
Continuously delivering an ongoing business function
Communicating with project stakeholders
14.w: Project management concerns temporary, defined outputs; the continuous delivery of a business function is business-as-usual, not project work.

14.q: What is the primary purpose of issue management within a project?
o: To develop contingency plans for anticipated external risks
To estimate the overall duration of the project's activities
To record, evaluate and resolve events that have already occurred
To identify and assess possible future threats to the project
14.w: Issue management provides a structured approach to capturing, assessing and resolving events that have already happened during the project.

14.q: In which phase of a typical linear life cycle is the project scope first defined and documented?
o: The delivery phase
The handover phase
The concept phase
The benefits realisation phase
14.w: The concept phase establishes the early definition of scope as part of the initial planning of the project.

14.q: How does a communication plan help a project manager direct communication effort where it is most needed?
o: By fixing the project scope so that no updates are required
By removing the need to report progress to the sponsor at all
By requiring every stakeholder to receive identical daily updates
By matching the type and frequency of information to each audience's needs
14.w: The plan matches information type and frequency to each audience, so the project manager focuses communication effort where it is most needed.

14.q: A post-project review finds that weak stakeholder engagement led to missed requirements; what should be done with this insight?
o: Ignore it because the project has now closed
Use it to place blame on the stakeholders
Delete it to protect the project's reputation
Document it as a lesson learned for future projects
14.w: Lessons learned should be captured and shared so that stakeholder engagement improves on future projects.

14.q: How does a cost breakdown structure (CBS) help a project manager with tracking project costs?
o: By allocating a named team member to each individual task
By linking a cost to each element of the project's scope
By listing the decision gates set throughout the project
By recording the lessons learned from earlier projects
14.w: The CBS links costs to defined elements of scope, allowing the project manager to track actual spending against the budget.

14.q: An organisation groups related projects under one change initiative and separately reviews all initiatives for strategic fit. Which two disciplines are described?
o: Programme management then project management
Portfolio management then programme management
Project management then programme management
Programme management then portfolio management
14.w: Grouping related projects to deliver a shared change is programme management; reviewing the whole collection for strategic fit is portfolio management.

14.q: What is the purpose of configuration verification within the configuration management process?
o: To review supplier invoices submitted during the delivery phase
To redefine the project budget once the baseline has been agreed
To approve the protocols used for stakeholder communication
To confirm that configuration items match their approved specifications
14.w: Verification and audit confirm that configuration items conform to their approved specification and that records accurately reflect their status.

14.q: Why must configuration management and change control operate together on a project?
o: To assign the members of the team to their delivery roles
To allow the project to eliminate the use of baselines
To ensure changes are properly evaluated, approved and implemented
To remove the need for any formal documentation of change
14.w: Change control evaluates and approves changes, while configuration management ensures they are consistently applied and documented.

14.q: A proposed change is rejected because it would create inconsistencies with existing components. Which process supported this decision?
o: Risk assessment
Schedule management
Quality assurance
Configuration management
14.w: Configuration management maintains the integrity and consistency of the product, so it can identify a change that would conflict with existing items.

14.q: A sponsor complains they only hear about problems once they are severe. Which reporting improvement would most directly address this?
o: Reporting exclusively on completed deliverables
Reporting only when the sponsor formally requests it
Reporting only at the project's closure stage
Reporting progress regularly with early variance alerts
14.w: Regular reporting with timely variance information gives early warning, preventing problems from being discovered only when severe.

14.q: Why is effective leadership important to team performance within a project environment?
o: It motivates the team and supports collaboration towards shared goals
It guarantees that project risk will be completely eliminated
It removes the need for the team to hold any meetings
It ensures that all project contracts are signed on time
14.w: Leadership sets direction and motivates and aligns individuals so that the team works collaboratively towards the project’s shared goals.

14.q: What advantage does a physical display board in a shared site office offer a co-located project team?
o: It captures the tone and body language of the author
It provides a searchable digital archive of all the messages
It provides constant, at-a-glance visibility of key information to everyone present
It automatically notifies remote members of every update
14.w: A physical display gives everyone in the shared space continuous, at-a-glance access to key project information.

14.q: An agile team forecasts remaining effort by extrapolating from its established average sprint velocity. Which estimating method does this represent?
o: Parametric estimating
Three-point estimating
Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
14.w: Applying a known unit rate, such as story points per sprint, to extrapolate a total is a form of parametric estimating.

14.q: During initiation the project manager drafts cost and risk information while the sponsor decides on strategic justification. What does this show?
o: The two roles collaborate, with the manager informing and the sponsor owning the case
The two roles entirely duplicate each other's responsibilities and effort
The project manager holds ultimate accountability for the whole investment
The sponsor is responsible only for producing the detailed cost estimates
14.w: Developing the business case is collaborative: the project manager provides delivery information while the sponsor owns and justifies the investment.

14.q: Why is face-to-face communication often the most suitable method for delivering sensitive or difficult news to a stakeholder?
o: It allows tone, empathy and immediate reassurance to be conveyed in person
It creates a permanent written record of exactly what was said
It reaches large, geographically dispersed audiences at the lowest cost
It removes the need to follow the conversation up afterwards
14.w: Face-to-face communication conveys tone and body language and allows immediate, empathetic two-way response, suiting sensitive messages.

14.q: When a project team lists what is 'in scope' and 'out of scope', which discipline are they applying?
o: Scope management
Risk management
Quality management
Procurement management
14.w: Defining what is in and out of scope sets the boundaries of the project's work, which is a core part of scope management.

14.q: A contract must be signed and kept as lasting evidence of what both parties agreed. Which method best suits this?
o: A brief telephone call
A live video conference
A physical, printed document
An instant-messaging chat
14.w: A physical, printed document provides a durable, signable record, an advantage where formal evidence of agreement is required.

14.q: Which statement best defines project management as understood within the APM Body of Knowledge?
o: The routine monitoring of daily operational activities within a permanent department
The application of processes, methods and knowledge to achieve defined project objectives
The forecasting of resource requirements across the whole organisation each year
The assignment of repetitive tasks to staff within ongoing business functions
14.w: Project management is the application of processes, methods, knowledge, skills and experience to achieve the project objectives within agreed constraints.

14.q: A stakeholder asks whether the latest test script represents the most current version. Which configuration activity provides the answer?
o: Configuration identification
Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration planning
14.w: Status accounting records the version history, current status and location of each controlled item, allowing such questions to be answered.

14.q: What is one benefit of defining clear success criteria at the beginning of a project?
o: They remove the need to produce a stakeholder map
They guarantee that the schedule cannot slip
They avoid the need for a post-project review
They provide a clear benchmark for evaluating performance
14.w: Clear success criteria give a measurable benchmark for judging whether objectives were achieved and for justifying decisions.

14.q: What is a common issue with relying solely on virtual communication platforms?
o: They are vulnerable to internet outages or system failures
They remove the need for any project documentation
They function without issue in every geographic region
They require no training for people to use them
14.w: Poor connectivity or system failures can disrupt communication entirely when it depends only on virtual platforms.

14.q: A project manager maintains a risk management process throughout delivery. What is this mainly intended to achieve?
o: Better-informed decisions by anticipating and managing uncertainty
A permanent record of every completed project activity
The removal of any need for quality management
A reduction in the total number of project stakeholders
14.w: Ongoing risk management supports informed decision-making by anticipating uncertainty and planning responses.

14.q: Why might a project manager carry out a PESTLE analysis during the initiation of a project?
o: To identify external factors that could influence the project
To map out the internal work breakdown structure
To set the payment schedule agreed with contractors
To evaluate the team's internal communication styles
14.w: PESTLE analysis is used to identify external, macro-environmental factors that may affect the project.

14.q: Why does having an agreed communication plan actually save the project manager effort during the delivery of a project?
o: It automatically resolves all of the disagreements between stakeholders
It removes the need to maintain a detailed underlying schedule
It eliminates every one of the project's risks well in advance
Communication decisions are agreed once rather than repeated each time
14.w: With communications agreed in advance, the project manager avoids reconsidering who, what, when and how for each message, saving effort.

14.q: How do change control and configuration management together protect the integrity of a project's deliverables?
o: One trains the users; the other reviews the benefits realised
One ensures changes are properly authorised; the other keeps items consistent and correctly versioned
One identifies risks; the other transfers them to a supplier
One fixes the budget; the other sets the delivery schedule
14.w: Change control ensures only authorised changes proceed, while configuration management keeps deliverables consistent and correctly versioned.

14.q: What is the role of configuration management once a scope change has been formally approved?
o: To carry out the approval of the original change request
To redefine the project's chosen life cycle for delivery
To ensure the approved change is applied and documented correctly
To communicate the approved change out to the stakeholders
14.w: After change control approves a change, configuration management ensures it is implemented, recorded and reflected in the controlled products.

15.q: Which statement best characterises how estimate tolerance behaves as a project moves through the estimating funnel?
o: Tolerance stays constant from concept through to delivery
Tolerance widens steadily as the project progresses
Tolerance is only ever expressed as a single fixed value
Tolerance narrows progressively as knowledge and detail increase
15.w: Estimate tolerance narrows progressively through the funnel as increasing knowledge and detail reduce uncertainty.

15.q: A learner confuses scope management with schedule management. Which statement correctly explains how the two disciplines differ?
o: Scope management sequences the work, while schedule management defines what is required
Scope management controls cost, while schedule management controls quality
Both are simply identical processes operating under two different names
Scope management defines the work required, while schedule management sequences it in time
