15.w: Scope management defines what work is required, whereas schedule management arranges that work in time; they are distinct disciplines.

15.q: Within the wider hierarchy of managing change, which statement best defines what 'programme management' actually involves?
o: The management of a single temporary endeavour to produce one defined output
The coordinated management of related projects to deliver benefits not achievable separately
The routine supervision of continuing operational services and business functions
The selection of all organisational investments to reflect strategic priorities
15.w: Programme management coordinates related projects to deliver benefits beyond what individual projects could achieve alone; the distractors describe a single project, portfolio management and operations.

15.q: Quality management is best understood as an umbrella covering which combination of activities?
o: Estimating, scheduling and procurement
Quality planning, quality assurance and quality control
Identification, analysis and risk response
Concept, definition and handover
15.w: Quality management encompasses quality planning, quality assurance and quality control.

15.q: What is regarded as the primary objective of communication within a project?
o: To remove the need for formal project documentation
To ensure that all identified project risks are mitigated
To support shared understanding among the project's stakeholders
To reduce the total number of meetings that are held
15.w: The purpose of communication is to ensure that everyone involved understands the relevant information and expectations.

15.q: A project team uses a probability and impact matrix to assess its risks. What are they doing?
o: Creating the risk register
Performing risk analysis
Prioritising the lessons learned
Carrying out risk identification
15.w: A probability and impact matrix is a standard method of carrying out qualitative risk analysis.

15.q: Which of the following would not typically be the responsibility of a project team member?
o: Providing progress updates to the project manager
Contributing specialist technical expertise
Delivering assigned tasks to the agreed specification
Tracking organisational benefits after handover
15.w: Tracking benefits after handover is a sponsor responsibility, not part of a team member's delivery role.

15.q: What is the primary purpose of the risk identification stage?
o: To capture and record potential future events that may affect objectives
To assign risk owners and set aside their mitigation budgets
To resolve every open issue before project execution begins
To remove all uncertainty from the project management plan
15.w: Risk identification focuses on uncovering and recording potential future events that could affect the project's objectives.

15.q: A team inspects completed deliverables to confirm they meet the agreed requirements; which process are they performing?
o: Quality planning of outputs
Quality control of outputs
Risk management activity
Stakeholder management work
15.w: Quality control involves inspecting and testing deliverables to verify they meet the agreed quality requirements.

15.q: Which of the following best defines leadership in a project context?
o: Recording risks and issues in the relevant registers
Enforcing compliance with procurement procedures
Monitoring the budget and updating the schedule
Providing vision, motivation and direction to the team
15.w: Leadership is about inspiring and guiding people towards achieving the project's objectives, rather than administering controls.

15.q: In the context of project management, how is a 'procurement strategy' best defined?
o: A schedule showing when each supplier's work will take place
A record of the threats and opportunities affecting suppliers
A matrix assigning internal team members to each work package
The overall approach to obtaining goods and services from suppliers
15.w: A procurement strategy sets out the overall approach a project will take to acquiring the goods and services it needs.

15.q: The project's actual spend has now exceeded its approved budget and finance has flagged it. How is this best classified?
o: A dependency
A risk
A tolerance
An issue
15.w: A confirmed overspend that has already happened and needs action is an issue, not a risk, which remains only a possibility.

15.q: In a typical linear project life cycle, at which phase are the detailed schedule, budget and project management plan normally finalised?
o: Definition
Concept
Development
Handover
15.w: The definition phase is where the detailed plans, schedule and budget are developed and baselined before delivery begins.

15.q: A team switching from a linear to an iterative approach asks how their deployment baseline will now behave. What is the best answer?
o: It will be locked for the entire project duration
It will be updated as requirements emerge each iteration
It will be removed because iterative work has no plan
It will be signed off only at the concept stage
15.w: Iterative delivery updates the deployment baseline as requirements emerge and are prioritised in each iteration, rather than locking it once.

15.q: How does the estimating funnel help justify revisiting cost estimates at each stage of a project?
o: It demonstrates that later estimates are inherently less trustworthy
It confirms estimates should only ever be produced at project closure
It proves that the first estimate given should be treated as final
It shows that increasing knowledge legitimately allows estimates to be refined over time
15.w: The funnel shows that greater knowledge at each stage legitimately allows estimates to be refined, justifying revisiting them.

15.q: After a challenging delivery, an organisation holds a structured session on what went well and what could improve; what is this?
o: A post-project review
A risk assessment
A quality control check
A cost benefit analysis
15.w: A post-project review allows the team and stakeholders to reflect on and learn from the project experience.

15.q: A project manager analyses delivery options and their associated risks for the business case. How does this help the sponsor?
o: It improves the credibility and delivery accuracy of the business case
It guarantees the sponsor's independence from delivery
It allows the project manager to approve the project budget
It removes the need for any governance review of the case
15.w: By supplying delivery detail, the project manager helps the sponsor produce a credible, evidence-based justification.

15.q: A project fails to meet its key success criteria at a gate review; what is the likely outcome?
o: New scope is added without any assessment
The project may be paused or stopped
The project budget is increased without review
The team proceeds automatically to the next stage
15.w: Decision gates allow the organisation to pause, redirect or stop a project based on its current performance and alignment.

15.q: What advantage does video conferencing offer when compared with a voice-only call?
o: It removes the possibility of any technical problems arising
It is more formal and removes the need for a meeting agenda
It guarantees that no message can ever be misinterpreted
It conveys visual cues such as facial expressions and gestures
15.w: Video adds non-verbal context to a conversation, helping to clarify tone and intent.

15.q: A project manager arranges a backup supplier agreement in case the main vendor fails to deliver. Which risk response is this?
o: Risk acceptance
Risk transfer
Contingency planning
Risk avoidance
15.w: Preparing a fallback to be used only if the risk occurs is a contingency (fallback) response.

15.q: Which action by a team leader is most likely to boost performance during project execution?
o: Ignoring team conflicts to keep focus on delivery
Setting unrealistic deadlines to create a sense of urgency
Assigning every complex task to one individual
Coaching team members and providing development opportunities
15.w: Coaching and development raise capability and motivation, which directly improves team performance.

15.q: Which review is specifically concerned with confirming whether the intended benefits have actually materialised?
o: A project audit
A decision gate
A benefit review
A post-project review
15.w: A benefit review checks whether the forecast benefits have actually been realised, usually after closure.

15.q: Which statement best describes the shared responsibility of the sponsor and project manager in developing the business case?
o: The project manager owns it and the sponsor merely signs it off
The sponsor owns it and the project manager contributes delivery detail
The finance team writes it without involving either role
The PMO is solely responsible for writing and approving it
15.w: The sponsor owns the business case while the project manager supports its development with delivery-focused content.

15.q: In the context of scope management, how is 'change control' best defined?
o: The process for levelling resources across the project schedule
The process for closing risks once they no longer apply
The process for formally requesting, assessing and approving changes to scope
The process for identifying and recording all project stakeholders
15.w: Change control is the process by which changes to scope are formally requested, evaluated and authorised.

15.q: Which of the following best describes the purpose of a project milestone?
o: To track the unresolved risks within the project
To assign specific tasks to individual project team members
To measure product quality against the baseline specification
To mark a significant point or achievement within the schedule
15.w: Milestones are zero-duration events that flag key points such as phase completions or major approvals within the schedule.

15.q: Which word most accurately captures the essential nature of a project risk?
o: Certainty
Deliverable
Milestone
Uncertainty
15.w: A risk is fundamentally an uncertain event, distinguishing it from certainties, deliverables or milestones.

15.q: Which of the following best describes the role of a change control board on a project?
o: A group authorised to review and approve or reject scope changes
An external panel appointed to audit the project's accounts
A working group responsible for the project's external marketing
A team that decides on the project's team-building activities
15.w: A change control board is the body with the authority to evaluate change requests and decide whether to approve or reject them.

15.q: At the start of a project a team decides the naming conventions, tools and responsibilities for managing controlled items. Which configuration management activity is this?
o: Verification audit
Configuration planning
Identification
Status accounting
15.w: Configuration planning establishes how items will be managed, including conventions, tools and responsibilities.

15.q: In which type of project life cycle is time boxing most commonly applied?
o: Linear
Iterative or Agile
Extended
Sequential
15.w: Time boxing is a core practice of iterative and Agile approaches, where time is fixed and the scope delivered is flexible.

15.q: Which of the following would you typically expect to find within a well-structured business case?
o: The project closure checklist and lessons learned
Options analysis, investment appraisal and success criteria
A record of every risk the project has identified
A detailed daily stand-up schedule for the team
15.w: A business case typically sets out the options considered, the investment appraisal and the success criteria that justify proceeding.

16.q: What is a key benefit of summarising a verbal discussion in a follow-up email?
o: It guarantees the eventual success of the whole project
It removes the need for the original discussion to take place
It removes every possibility of the message being misread
It provides a record of what was agreed and the next steps
16.w: A written summary creates a record and reinforces shared understanding of what was agreed verbally.

16.q: Which of the following is least likely to form part of a business case?
o: The investment appraisal
The project rationale
The options analysis
A detailed stakeholder engagement matrix
16.w: Detailed stakeholder engagement planning sits within the project management plan rather than the business case.

16.q: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of critical path analysis?
o: Identifying the longest sequence of dependent activities
Revealing which activities have float available
Justifying the project's investment to the sponsor
Determining the shortest possible project duration
16.w: Critical path analysis addresses scheduling, not investment justification, which is the role of the business case.

16.q: Two departments received different updates and the sponsor asks why. How does the communication plan help the project manager respond?
o: It requires every department to receive identical content
It prevents the two departments from working together
It removes the manager's need to answer such questions
It records how communications were tailored and the reasons why
16.w: The plan documents who receives which information and why, allowing variations in the communication approach to be justified.

16.q: Which of the following best defines a project issue?
o: A problem that has already occurred and requires resolution
A possible delay that could arise during execution
An uncertain event that may affect the project in future
A threat for which a mitigation strategy must be planned
16.w: In APM terms an issue is an event that has already happened, or is happening now, and must be resolved, unlike a risk which is an uncertain future event.

16.q: How does critical path analysis help a project manager decide where to concentrate limited resources?
o: By ranking stakeholders according to their influence
By showing which activities have the greatest cost
By highlighting the activities that cannot afford to slip
By listing the risks with the highest impact scores
16.w: By highlighting zero-float activities, critical path analysis shows where resources must be protected to avoid delaying the project.

16.q: Why is risk analysis carried out before deciding on responses in the risk management process?
o: So that every identified risk can be immediately closed
So effort can be focused on the most significant risks first
So that the responses can be chosen at random for fairness
So that the project budget can be finalised and fixed
16.w: Analysis prioritises risks by probability and impact so that responses target the most significant threats.

16.q: What is a benefit of using email for communication on a project?
o: It is always a fully secure and completely private channel
It provides a written trail that can be referred to later
It functions without any need for an internet connection
It removes the need to hold project meetings altogether
16.w: Email creates an auditable written record that is easy to store and refer back to throughout the project.

16.q: Before delivery begins, a project manager defines the standards the outputs must meet and how conformance will be checked. Which process is this?
o: Quality planning
Configuration management
Quality control
Quality assurance
16.w: Setting the required standards and how conformance will be checked, ahead of delivery, is quality planning.

16.q: A project team uses the RACI model to assign responsibilities. Which type of tool are they using?
o: An organisational breakdown structure
A work breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
A product breakdown structure
16.w: RACI (responsible, accountable, consulted, informed) is a common form of responsibility assignment matrix used to clarify roles.

16.q: What is the purpose of producing a risk response plan?
o: To document the acceptance criteria for the project's final deliverables
To define how the team will react once issues have been logged
To develop the project's work breakdown structure
To set out the actions that will reduce, avoid, transfer or accept each risk
16.w: A risk response plan records the agreed action for each risk, whether to reduce, avoid, transfer or accept it.

16.q: A schedule shows that two activities must finish before testing can begin. What does this illustrate?
o: A task dependency
A work breakdown structure
A project benefits map
A scope verification check
16.w: A dependency exists where one activity cannot start until another is complete; scheduling identifies these relationships.

16.q: A manager defines communication as sending a message from sender to receiver 'with feedback'. Why is the feedback element important?
o: It confirms the receiver has received and understood the message
It formally records the message within the communication plan
It sets out the agreed scope for the project's deliverables
It introduces the technical terminology the team will use
16.w: Feedback confirms that the message has been received and understood, which is central to effective communication.

16.q: A supplier fails to deliver components on time, delaying the schedule. What is the role of issue management in this situation?
o: To revise the scope so the affected tasks are removed
To document the issue, assign ownership and track its resolution
To plan the resources needed for the next project phase
To reassess the project's future risks and update tolerances
16.w: Issue management handles real disruptions such as a missed delivery by logging them, assigning an owner and tracking them through to resolution.

16.q: Why does benefits management typically continue after a project has been formally closed?
o: Because outstanding project risks can only be reviewed after closure
Because many benefits are realised during operational use rather than during delivery
Because the project baseline must be recalculated once delivery ends
Because the next phase of delivery must be planned after handover
16.w: Benefits such as cost savings or improved service are usually realised once outputs are in operational use, so benefits management extends beyond project closure.

16.q: A project sets up a version-controlled folder with controlled access for all configuration items. Which activity does this address?
o: Configuration identification
Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration control
16.w: Configuration control includes the procedures that govern controlled access and the storage of approved item versions.

16.q: A stakeholder submits a formal request to alter a key deliverable. What is the first step in the change control process?
o: Escalate the matter straight to the project board
Implement the requested change to the deliverable immediately
Log the change request and assess its likely impact
Update the configuration baseline before any review
16.w: The first stage of change control is to log the request and assess its impact on time, cost, quality and risk before any decision.

16.q: Why should the project sponsor be actively involved as a stakeholder in agreeing the project management plan?
o: Because the sponsor owns the business case and provides direction
Because the sponsor writes each work package personally
Because the sponsor tests each deliverable for quality
Because the sponsor performs the day-to-day delivery tasks
16.w: The sponsor owns the business case and provides strategic direction, so their agreement ensures the plan aligns with the organisation's aims.

16.q: Why is the sponsor, rather than the project manager, held accountable for the business case throughout the project?
o: Because the sponsor produces the detailed cost estimates used in delivery
Because the sponsor manages the project's day-to-day activities and tasks
Because the sponsor writes the technical specification of the product
Because the sponsor owns the investment and is answerable for its benefits
16.w: The sponsor owns the investment and is accountable for realising its benefits, which is why the business case sits with them, not the project manager.

16.q: When reviewing a colleague's draft business case, which of the following would you expect to be a core component?
o: The finalised test scripts to be used in verifying each deliverable
The individual holiday schedules of every member of the project team
The minutes of every project progress meeting held to date
The expected benefits, costs, timescales and risks of the proposed investment
16.w: A business case sets out the anticipated benefits, costs, timescales and risks of the investment; test scripts, holiday schedules and meeting minutes are not core content.

16.q: A late supplier delivery has caused a critical delay. What is the most appropriate first action for the project manager?
o: Notify procurement that the project will be cancelled
Assess the impact and update the risk register and schedule
Escalate straight to the sponsor without any analysis
Reassign the whole project to the product owner
16.w: The project manager should first assess the impact and update the relevant records before recommending action or escalating.

16.q: If change control operated without any configuration management, what problem would most likely arise?
o: The project would be unable to identify any of its stakeholders
Approved changes might be made without the resulting versions being recorded or traceable
No change could ever be authorised because there would be no approval route
The business case could not be written before delivery began
16.w: Without configuration management, authorised changes would not be recorded, so version control and traceability of items would be lost.

16.q: A deadline is fixed and cannot move, but resource peaks must be reduced. Which optimisation technique should the project manager apply?
o: Crashing, adding cost to shorten the critical path
Resource levelling, accepting a later completion date
Fast tracking, overlapping activities to save time
Resource smoothing, using float without changing the end date
16.w: When the end date must hold, smoothing evens out resource peaks using available float without delaying completion.

16.q: Which statement best describes the way in which regular progress reporting supports effective control of a project?
o: It transfers accountability from the sponsor to users
It fixes the deployment baseline permanently in place
It measures progress so deviations can be corrected
It records lessons only after the project has closed
16.w: By measuring progress against plan, reporting exposes deviations so the project manager can take corrective action, supporting control.

16.q: Members drawn from several departments are struggling with unclear communication and low trust. Which challenge does this illustrate?
o: Difficulties with procurement planning
Cross-functional team dynamics
Work breakdown structure confusion
Disengagement of the project sponsor
16.w: Cross-functional teams frequently face communication and cohesion challenges arising from differing priorities and norms.

16.q: A project team has reached the adjourning stage of Tuckman's model. Which leadership action is most appropriate?
o: Introduce fresh team norms and ground rules
Increase the workload to sustain performance
Recognise the team's achievements and support the transition
Drive the team straight into a new forming phase
16.w: Adjourning marks disbandment, so the leader should acknowledge contributions and help members transition smoothly.

16.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between a PBS and a WBS?
o: The PBS defines the deliverables and the WBS defines the work to create them
The PBS defines the risks and the WBS defines the risk responses
The PBS sets the budget and the WBS sets the time limits
The PBS defines the costs and the WBS defines the people involved
16.w: The PBS identifies the product's deliverables, while the WBS defines the work needed to produce those deliverables.

16.q: How does configuration management help to maintain the integrity of project deliverables?
o: By automatically approving every change that stakeholders request
By removing change restrictions so the team can work more flexibly
By ensuring changes to deliverables are reviewed, approved and documented
By allocating individual team members to specific project tasks
16.w: Configuration management provides formal control over deliverables so that any change is identified, controlled and recorded, keeping items consistent with requirements.

16.q: How can a project team leader positively influence the performance of their team?
o: By withholding feedback in order to avoid any conflict
By micromanaging tasks and limiting the team's autonomy
By setting clear goals and recognising individual contributions
By delegating all responsibility to external suppliers
16.w: Clear goals and genuine recognition improve motivation and alignment, which raises team performance.

16.q: Which of the following is NOT a standard step in the issue resolution process?
o: Analysis
Closure
Rescheduling
Identification
16.w: Rescheduling may be a consequence of resolving an issue but is not itself a formal step in the issue resolution process, which runs from identification to closure.

17.q: A project manager needs a standard risk register template and guidance on preparing for a gateway review. Which role usually provides this support?
o: The scrum master
The project sponsor
The project governance board
The project management office (PMO)
17.w: The PMO provides templates, tools, assurance and support to help projects plan and prepare for reviews.

17.q: How does the timing of change control differ from that of configuration management on a project?
o: Change control acts when a change is requested, whereas configuration management runs continuously to keep records current
Change control runs continuously, whereas configuration management acts only at project closure
Both operate only once, during the concept phase, and then stop
Both operate only after the outputs have been handed over to operations
17.w: Change control is triggered by each change request, while configuration management is an ongoing activity keeping item records up to date.

17.q: Which advantage does a recorded virtual meeting offer that a face-to-face meeting usually does not?
o: It removes any possibility of a technical failure
It guarantees immediate emotional reassurance to all
It can be replayed later by those who could not attend
It always conveys body language much more clearly
17.w: A recorded virtual meeting can be stored and replayed, giving absent members access to the discussion later.

17.q: Why are risks and issues typically tracked separately on a project?
o: Risk tracking is optional, whereas issue tracking is mandatory
Issues must always be resolved before the project can start
They follow different lifecycles and require different treatment
Only risks can be escalated to senior management for a decision
17.w: Risks are analysed and planned for as uncertain future events, while issues are resolved as current problems, so they need separate processes and records.

17.q: Infrastructure is delivered using a linear model while customer-facing features are developed and adjusted during delivery. What is this model called?
o: Extended
Agile
Hybrid
Waterfall
17.w: Mixing sequential and iterative components within one project is the defining characteristic of a hybrid life cycle.

17.q: Why does an effective issue management process assign a clear owner to each logged issue?
o: So that the issue can be ignored until the project closes
So that responsibility for resolving the issue is unambiguous and it is progressed
So that no record of the issue needs to be kept
So that the issue is reclassified as a future risk
17.w: Assigning an owner makes resolution responsibility unambiguous, ensuring the issue is actively progressed to closure.

17.q: At a decision gate review, who typically decides whether the project proceeds to the next phase?
o: An external team of auditors
The project manager acting alone
The governance board or sponsor
The project team collectively
17.w: Gate decisions are made by the governance board or sponsor to provide objective oversight and strategic alignment.

17.q: Against what standard should a project deliverable's quality ultimately be judged in practice?
o: The requirements and needs it was created to satisfy
The total budget that was spent on producing it
The number of premium features it happens to contain
Its ranking against rival products in the marketplace
17.w: Quality is judged against the requirements and needs the deliverable was created to satisfy, not cost or market position.

17.q: A risk plan notes that poor weather may delay construction. What benefit does identifying this early provide?
o: It removes the impact of every environmental risk on the project
It gives the team time to prepare responses before any delay occurs
It removes the need for configuration control during the project
It guarantees that the project will remain within its agreed scope
17.w: Identifying risks early is the purpose of risk management: it allows responses to be planned before problems arise.

17.q: What is a limitation of virtual communication methods when engaging project stakeholders?
o: It always guarantees full understanding of the message
It allows the physical handover of deliverables in person
It supports the same rich non-verbal cues as being present
It can reduce emotional connection and weaken rapport
17.w: Virtual settings can hinder relationship-building because of reduced physical presence and informal interaction.

17.q: A quality assurance review shows that a key process is not being applied consistently; what should happen next?
o: The findings should be ignored by the team
The project should be closed down immediately
Corrective actions should be identified and implemented
The product should be delivered without change
17.w: Quality assurance identifies process shortfalls so that corrective actions can realign work with quality standards.

17.q: When developing the communication content of a project management plan, which group most needs clearly defined roles and timely updates in order to deliver the work?
o: The project team members
The regulatory authorities
The general public
The external suppliers
17.w: Project team members carry out the work, so they require clear responsibilities and regular, relevant updates to perform effectively.

17.q: Why does an identified project issue demand immediate management attention rather than monitoring alone?
o: Because it is a problem that has already occurred and is affecting the project
Because it is a benefit expected only after the project closes
Because it is a constraint that was fixed at the project's outset
Because it is an uncertain event that has not yet happened
17.w: An issue has already occurred and is affecting the project, so it demands action now, unlike a risk which is only monitored as a possibility.

17.q: Two experienced specialists on a project team repeatedly clash over how the work should be done. What leadership challenge is this?
o: Managing interpersonal conflict between strong team members
Ensuring every member holds an identical opinion
Removing the need for any communication between members
Guaranteeing that no member ever contributes an idea
17.w: Reconciling conflict between strong individuals is a genuine leadership challenge when developing a team.

17.q: In an iterative life cycle, what is typically produced at the end of each cycle of work?
o: A partial or improved increment of the overall solution
The final, fully complete product ready for closure
A fixed baseline that can never afterwards be revised
A complete business case covering the whole programme
17.w: Each iteration delivers an increment that adds to or improves the evolving solution.

17.q: Which of the following is most likely to be included in a project communication plan?
o: A list of the sponsors of previous, unrelated projects
Escalation routes for unresolved communication issues
The individual salaries of the project team members
The technical hardware specifications of the deliverables
17.w: A communication plan commonly sets out how communication issues are escalated if they cannot be resolved.

17.q: A team decides to take no pre-emptive action against a possible delay to key components. Which risk response is this?
o: Transfer
Acceptance
Avoidance
Mitigation
17.w: Acceptance means acknowledging a risk and taking no pre-emptive action unless it actually materialises.

17.q: A project manager must define 'configuration management' for a new starter. Which description is correct?
o: The technical and administrative control of a project's deliverables and their versions
The formal process for requesting and approving changes to scope
The identification and engagement of the project's stakeholders
The evening out of resource demand across the schedule
17.w: Configuration management is the technical and administrative control of deliverables, their status and their versions.

17.q: Why is a post-implementation review an essential part of the change control process?
o: To ensure the change was recorded within the supplier contract
To validate that all stakeholders were formally consulted first
To confirm the change achieved its intended outcomes without adverse effects
To determine the payment terms owed to the supplier
17.w: The review confirms the change was effective and has not introduced new problems in other areas of the project.

17.q: How does setting clear and achievable objectives for team members influence their performance?
o: It transfers accountability for delivery entirely to the team
It guarantees that no risks will affect their work
It gives them focus and a shared sense of direction, improving performance
It removes any need for the leader to monitor progress
17.w: Clear, achievable objectives focus effort and give direction, which lifts individual and team performance.

17.q: A sponsor asks for a summary of how the project is performing against its key milestones. Which document best provides this?
o: The work breakdown structure
The project progress report
The lessons learned log
The project risk register
17.w: The progress report summarises current status against milestones, budget and performance indicators for decision-makers.

17.q: Which of these statements describes a genuine project risk rather than a current problem?
o: Adverse weather might delay outdoor work next month
The budget was exceeded during the last reporting period
A team member resigned from the project last week
A supplier has already failed to deliver essential materials
17.w: Only the weather statement is an uncertain future event; the others have already occurred and are issues.

17.q: Which of the following best explains the value of carrying out a PESTLE analysis at the start of a large project?
o: It helps anticipate external influences on the project's success
It defines the individual responsibilities within the team
It identifies the project's key delivery milestones
It estimates the cost baseline used for procurement
17.w: PESTLE surfaces external threats and enablers early, helping the project anticipate factors beyond its direct control.

17.q: What is the key difference in timing between issues and risks?
o: Both issues and risks relate only to events after project delivery
Risks relate to the future, whereas issues occur in the present or past
Both issues and risks are recorded only once lessons are learned
Issues relate to the future, whereas risks occur in the present or past
17.w: Risks are anticipated future events, whereas issues are events that have already happened and are affecting the project.

17.q: What is the primary purpose of quality control within a project?
o: To document the interests of the stakeholders
To confirm outputs conform to specifications through inspection
To produce a detailed and costed business case
To manage the contracts held with suppliers
17.w: Quality control verifies outputs through inspection, measurement and testing to confirm they meet requirements.

17.q: Which statement best describes how a risk register is used across the life of a project?
o: It is completed once at initiation and then archived
It is a living document reviewed and updated throughout
It is produced only after the project has closed
It is used solely to record issues that have occurred
17.w: A risk register is a living document, reviewed and updated throughout delivery as risks change, close or newly emerge.

17.q: A project without any issue management process is most likely to experience which of the following?
o: A permanent reduction in all project risks
Unresolved problems that grow and threaten objectives
A guaranteed increase in delivered benefits
An automatic improvement in team morale
17.w: Without issue management, problems go unaddressed and can escalate to threaten the project's objectives.

17.q: What is the primary purpose of a business case in the context of project management?
o: To define the engagement approach for each stakeholder
To justify the investment by weighing benefits, costs and risks
To schedule the daily activities of the delivery team
To assign roles and responsibilities across the project team
17.w: The business case provides the justification for investment, setting out expected benefits against the associated costs and risks.

17.q: What is the key distinction between a programme and a portfolio?
o: A programme coordinates related projects; a portfolio oversees all projects and programmes
A programme contains only unrelated projects, while a portfolio does not
A programme is aligned to strategy, whereas a portfolio is not
A portfolio is always smaller in scale than a programme
17.w: A programme manages a set of related projects, while a portfolio spans the organisation's entire collection of projects and programmes.

17.q: What is the primary purpose of project management within an organisation?
o: To take over the responsibilities of programme management
To standardise every routine operational procedure in use
To provide a controlled framework for delivering unique objectives
To remove the need for any risk and issue management
17.w: Project management exists to provide structure, control and clarity so that defined, unique objectives are delivered.

18.q: At what point during project delivery does the quality control process principally take place?
o: Only after the project has been formally closed down
When deliverables have been produced and can be inspected or tested
Before any work starts, when standards are being set
Continuously, by auditing the management processes in use
18.w: Quality control takes place once deliverables exist and can be inspected or tested against their requirements.

18.q: During delivery, a scope change is identified that will affect cost and schedule. What is the first step the project manager should take?
o: Continue as planned and ignore the change
Reassign the work without recording it
Compare the proposed change against the deployment baseline
Notify stakeholders that the project will close
18.w: Proposed changes are first assessed against the deployment baseline to determine their impact and whether approval is required.

18.q: At which point in a project is analogous estimating typically most useful?
o: Late in delivery when every work package is fully specified
Early on, when little detail exists but similar past projects do
Only after the critical path has been finalised
Only once the product has been handed over to operations
18.w: Analogous estimating draws on similar completed projects, making it valuable early when detailed information is scarce.

18.q: When identifying the stakeholders of a project management plan, which of the following would not normally be included?
o: An external auditor
The product owner
A project team member
The project sponsor
18.w: The project management plan focuses on delivery stakeholders; an external auditor is not typically among them.

18.q: What is the main purpose of risk management on a project?
o: To improve the chance of meeting objectives by managing uncertainty
To eliminate every possible risk before the project begins
To transfer all responsibility for the project to the sponsor
To replace the need for a project management plan
18.w: Risk management aims to increase the likelihood of achieving objectives by identifying and responding to uncertainty, not to remove all risk.

18.q: A project needs a specialised system that only two suppliers can provide. What should guide the selection of a supplier?
o: The stakeholder communication plan
The lessons learned log
The project issue log
The procurement strategy
18.w: The procurement strategy sets out the supplier selection criteria and contract preferences that inform such a decision.

18.q: A project manager is planning a new construction project. Who should be consulted to ensure operational handover requirements are captured in the plan?
o: The wider project team
The programme director
The end users
The project management office
18.w: End users define the operational needs that must be met for a successful handover into use.

18.q: Which statement correctly describes a project issue?
o: It is an uncertainty relating to the project business case
It is an unplanned event that has occurred and needs management attention
It is a scheduled event that is recorded in the risk register
It is a constraint that has been imposed by the project sponsor
18.w: An issue is an actual, unplanned event affecting the project that requires management action to resolve it.

18.q: A project manager sets up processes to ensure the final product meets the agreed requirements. What is the main purpose of quality management?
o: To make the project's procurement arrangements simpler
To reduce the number of stakeholders involved in the project
To ensure outputs are delivered to a consistent and acceptable standard
To increase the overall speed at which the product is delivered
18.w: Quality management exists to ensure that project outputs consistently meet the agreed standards and are fit for purpose.

18.q: In an iterative life cycle, what term is commonly used for the short, time-boxed development cycles the team works in?
o: Milestones
Gateways
Phases
Sprints
18.w: Sprints are the short, time-boxed iterations used to deliver increments of the product in iterative and agile approaches.

18.q: During the early planning of a project with little detailed information, which estimating method is most appropriate?
o: Parametric estimating
Three-point estimating
Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
18.w: Analogous estimating suits early planning, using high-level comparison with previous projects when detail is scarce.

18.q: Which of the following is a key outcome of performing critical path analysis?
o: A detailed quality assurance plan for deliverables
An understanding of which tasks have scheduling flexibility
A stakeholder influence and interest chart
A revised procurement contract for the main suppliers
18.w: Critical path analysis distinguishes tasks with float from those without, showing where the schedule has flexibility.

18.q: How does a milestone differ from an ordinary task within a project schedule?
o: Milestones consume project resources, whereas ordinary tasks do not
Milestones are used only within quality control activities on a project
Milestones must be repeated within every phase of the project life cycle
Milestones have zero duration and mark significant events, unlike tasks
18.w: A milestone is a zero-duration marker of a significant event or decision point, whereas a task represents work that consumes time and resource.

18.q: A change board has approved a deliverable change. Which process now ensures the new version is recorded and the old one withdrawn?
o: Benefits management
Configuration management
Risk management
Change control
18.w: Once a change is authorised, configuration management records the new version and controls withdrawal of the superseded one.

18.q: Testing reveals a flaw and the team wants to modify a deliverable. Which process ensures the change is formally evaluated and approved?
o: Risk assessment
Benefits management
Change control
Schedule control
18.w: Change control ensures any alteration to scope or a deliverable is formally reviewed and authorised before it is implemented.

18.q: Why is stakeholder analysis important during the planning phase of a project?
o: It removes all project risks before delivery begins
It ensures all project tasks are assigned to the project manager
It identifies stakeholder interests so engagement can be tailored accordingly
It completes the procurement documentation ahead of time
18.w: Stakeholder analysis reveals interest and influence, enabling engagement to be targeted for smoother delivery.

18.q: A linear project has delivered and installed new equipment and has trained the staff who will operate it. Which phase is being completed?
o: Definition
Handover and closure
Concept
Development
18.w: Handover and closure is where the deliverables are transitioned to the users and the project is formally brought to an end.

18.q: When resource smoothing is applied and the project end date must not change, what typically happens to the schedule?
o: Non-critical tasks are rescheduled within their float to even out resource demand
All tasks are moved onto the critical path so delivery is faster
The scope of several tasks is reduced to lower overall resource demand
Additional staff are recruited so that the work can be shortened
18.w: Smoothing keeps the end date fixed by rescheduling non-critical activities within their available float to level resource demand.

18.q: What is the primary responsibility of the product owner in an agile environment?
o: Producing the detailed technical documentation
Monitoring the delivery team's performance metrics
Prioritising the product backlog according to business value
Negotiating and managing the supplier contracts
18.w: The product owner ensures the most valuable features are delivered by managing and prioritising the backlog.

18.q: A project manager revises the likelihood rating of an existing risk after new information arrives. Where is this recorded?
o: In the project issue log
In the stakeholder register
In the risk register
In the schedule baseline
18.w: The risk register is kept up to date throughout the project to reflect changes in likelihood, impact and status.

18.q: A stakeholder demands that an issue be escalated before any assessment has been made. What should the project manager do?
o: Close the issue without recording any further detail
Assign the issue to a team member without logging it
Analyse the issue first to decide whether escalation is needed
Escalate the issue immediately as the stakeholder requests
18.w: The issue should be analysed first so the project manager can judge whether it genuinely exceeds project authority and warrants escalation.

18.q: Which of the following would typically be discussed during a post-project review?
o: Lessons learned and performance against objectives
Plans for procuring brand new suppliers
Estimates for the costs of a new product
Detailed technical rework of the product
18.w: Post-project reviews cover overall performance, stakeholder feedback and lessons learned to inform future projects.

18.q: Which sequence correctly reflects the stages of a typical issue resolution process?
o: Analysis, then identification, then escalation, and finally resolution
Identification, then analysis, then resolution, and finally closure
Identification, then resolution, then analysis, and finally closure
Escalation, then identification, then resolution, and finally closure
18.w: Issues are first identified and logged, then analysed, resolved through agreed action and finally closed once addressed.

18.q: What is the primary purpose of a milestone in a project schedule?
o: To mark the completion of a significant stage or deliverable
To allocate the project budget across its work packages
To record the daily effort logged by each team member
To calculate the total float available on the critical path
18.w: A milestone is a key point in the schedule, usually marking the completion of a significant deliverable or stage; it has zero duration.

18.q: Which of the following best defines configuration management in the context of a project?
o: Measuring the project's performance against its agreed baselines
Planning the allocation of resources across the packages of work
Estimating the level of budget reserve the project should hold
Identifying, controlling and tracking the project's products and their changes
18.w: Configuration management is the technical and administrative activity of identifying, controlling, accounting for and verifying a project's products throughout their life.

18.q: Why should an early-stage estimate be presented as a range rather than a single figure, according to the estimating funnel?
o: Because the range will always prove more accurate than the final cost
Because presenting a range removes the need for any later estimates
Because limited information at that stage means the estimate carries wide uncertainty
Because single-figure estimates are never permitted under APM guidance
18.w: At an early stage limited information means the estimate carries wide uncertainty, so the funnel shows it is best expressed as a broad range.

18.q: Which statement best defines a 'risk' in the context of project management?
o: A confirmed problem that requires immediate resolution by the team
An uncertain event that, should it occur, would affect the project's objectives
A completed task that is currently waiting for formal approval
A cost overrun that has already occurred and cannot be recovered
18.w: A risk is an uncertain future event that may have a positive or negative effect on project objectives.

18.q: According to the APM, a project is best understood as a unique, transient endeavour undertaken primarily to achieve which of the following?
o: Balanced returns from a managed collection of investments
Steady outputs delivered through repeatable routine tasks
Planned objectives that bring about beneficial change
Coordinated benefits realised across several linked projects
18.w: A project is a unique, transient endeavour undertaken to achieve planned objectives, defined in terms of outputs, outcomes or benefits.

18.q: A linear project fixes all deliverables before work starts, while an iterative project adapts them over time. What does this show about scope management?
o: Iterative projects carry out no planning before delivery
Linear projects are inherently less reliable than iterative ones
Iterative projects manage scope incrementally as understanding grows
Iterative projects fail to define their scope at all
18.w: Iterative projects manage scope in increments, refining it as understanding of the requirements improves.

18.q: Critical path analysis shows a non-critical task has five days of float. What does this tell the project manager?
o: The task can slip up to five days without delaying completion
The task must be finished five days earlier than planned
The task lies directly on the project's critical path
The task should be removed from the schedule entirely
18.w: Float is the time an activity can be delayed without affecting the project end date; five days of float means that much slippage is tolerable.

19.q: A total cost is built up from detailed specifications and individual work package estimates. Which estimating method does this describe?
o: Analytical (bottom-up) estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
Parametric estimating
19.w: Analytical, or bottom-up, estimating aggregates detailed estimates from individual work packages to produce the overall figure.

19.q: A schedule is revised to delay a task by three days so a shared specialist can finish another job first. Which technique is this?
o: Time boxing
Resource levelling
Resource smoothing
Risk transfer
19.w: Resource levelling resolves a resource conflict by moving task timings to match availability, even where this affects the schedule.

19.q: Which of the following best describes the primary purpose of scheduling within a project?
o: To track the project's risks and open issues
To confirm that the business case is financially viable
To identify the key stakeholders of the project
To sequence activities and allocate time for their completion
19.w: Scheduling sequences activities and assigns durations so the project can be planned and delivered within an agreed timeframe.

19.q: A critical activity is forecast to overrun by two days. According to critical path analysis, what is the likely effect?
o: The project end date slips by two days unless recovered
The project end date is unaffected because of float
Only non-critical activities are delayed by two days
The project baseline automatically re-sets itself
19.w: A slip on a zero-float critical activity pushes out the project completion date unless corrective action recovers the time.

19.q: A software defect has been fixed, tested and verified. What is the final step in the issue resolution process?
o: Escalation of the issue to a higher authority
Closure of the issue, recording it as complete
Reassessment of the issue's potential impact
Reopening the issue for further investigation
19.w: Once an issue has been resolved and verified, it is formally closed and recorded as complete.

19.q: What information is typically contained within a formal project progress report?
o: A complete list of the project's suppliers
Progress against plan, key risks, issues and forecast to complete
A post-project analysis of the benefits realised
The scope baseline and a full stakeholder map
19.w: A progress report typically sets out current status against the plan, key risks and issues, and a forecast of the outcome.

19.q: An app is being built in agile using short sprints, with priorities changing after each review. What does this mean for the deployment baseline?
o: It is defined fully at the start and never altered
It does not exist on agile projects
It is flexible and reviewed frequently
It contains only the cost baseline
19.w: In iterative and agile approaches the baseline is flexible and reviewed regularly as the project progresses.

19.q: The team agrees and carries out corrective actions to remove the effect of a logged issue. Which stage of issue resolution does this describe?
o: Identification
Resolution
Logging
Escalation
19.w: Agreeing and carrying out the corrective actions to deal with the issue is the resolution stage.

19.q: In a project to digitise patient records, which activity best demonstrates benefits management?
o: Tracking supplier invoices during the system rollout
Identifying, measuring and realising improvements in access to patient data
Ensuring clinical staff are trained before the system goes live
Producing the project's quality register
19.w: Benefits management focuses on identifying, measuring and realising value, such as improved access to patient data.

19.q: A data breach has just occurred and is disrupting the project. In risk terminology, how is this event now best classified?
o: An issue, because it has already occurred and requires action
A risk, because it might affect the project
A constraint, because it limits the project
An assumption, because it was anticipated
19.w: An event that has already occurred and is affecting the project is an issue requiring resolution, not a future uncertainty.

19.q: During quality planning, a team agrees to follow recognised industry standards to guide development; what does this represent?
o: Selecting the quality measures for the project
Avoiding risk by outsourcing the work
Assigning the procurement roles for the team
Reducing project cost through standardisation
19.w: Choosing standards during quality planning helps define the measures used to verify that deliverables meet requirements.

19.q: Midway through a project a client requests several enhancements to the agreed product. What should the project manager do first?
o: Add the changes to the next iteration in order to save time
Submit a formal change request for the change to be reviewed
Update the work breakdown structure and proceed with the changes
Amend the entries in the configuration log to reflect the changes
19.w: The first step is to raise a change request so the change can be logged and its impact assessed before any implementation.

19.q: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of establishing success criteria at the start of a project?
o: It aligns the expectations of the project stakeholders
It removes the need for formal project governance
It guides decisions about scope and quality
It provides clear measures for evaluating performance
19.w: Success criteria support evaluation, alignment and decision-making, but they do not replace the need for governance structures.

19.q: A trade union group with a history of resisting change is assessed as high influence and high interest. What is the most suitable engagement strategy?
o: Delay engagement until executive approval is granted
Withhold project documents from them
Assign a junior team member to manage the relationship
Engage them early and involve them in planning to address concerns
19.w: High-influence, high-interest stakeholders should be engaged closely and early to reduce resistance and gain their input.

19.q: Delivered equipment has arrived damaged and cannot be installed, stopping the next task. Why is this an issue rather than a risk?
o: Because it has already happened and is now impacting delivery
Because it relates purely to a much later delivery phase
Because it has no measurable effect on the project at all
Because it is at this stage still only a future possibility
19.w: The event has occurred and is affecting the project now, which makes it an issue; a risk would still only be a potential event.

19.q: How does understanding stakeholders' interests through analysis improve project communication?
o: It removes the need to consider how messages are received
It allows the same generic message to be issued to everyone
It enables messages to be shaped to each group's needs and concerns
It ensures only good news is ever shared with stakeholders
19.w: Knowing each group's interests allows communications to be shaped to their needs, supporting more effective engagement.

19.q: A development team is waiting for its next batch of prioritised work. Who is responsible for keeping the backlog updated and correctly ordered?
o: The project manager
The product owner
The scrum master
The project sponsor
19.w: The product owner maintains the backlog and ensures the most valuable items are ready for the team to develop.

19.q: Why does describing a project as 'transient' matter when defining what a project actually is?
o: It confirms the work will always exceed its planned budget
It signals the work has a defined start and finish
It shows the work will never involve any external suppliers
It guarantees the work produces identical repeated outputs
19.w: Transience means a project has a defined beginning and end, unlike the continuous nature of operational business-as-usual work.

19.q: The development team reports a defect that is preventing key features from working. How should this be treated?
o: As an issue, because it is already affecting the project
As a change request, because the scope has altered
As a constraint, because it limits the design
As a risk, because it may affect the project later
19.w: A defect that is actively preventing features from working has already occurred, so it is an issue that must be managed and resolved.

19.q: A project team includes members who only work part-time on the project. Which leadership challenge does this most likely create?
o: They will always prioritise the project above all other work
Their limited availability may conflict with their other duties
They will never need any direction from the project manager
They automatically remove all risk from the project
19.w: Part-time members split their time, so availability clashes with their other duties are a common challenge.

19.q: In a fast-paced project with several stakeholder groups, what benefit does a communication plan provide?
o: It removes the need to carry out any risk management
It maps who needs what, keeping communication relevant and manageable
It guarantees that all communication happens in real time
It automatically prevents any changes to project scope
19.w: A good plan helps the project manager manage the volume and relevance of communication across diverse stakeholder groups.

19.q: Why does a risk register support effective communication about risk on a project?
o: It records only the risks the sponsor wishes to see
It replaces the need for any progress reporting
It provides a shared, consistent record all parties can reference
It hides risk information from the wider stakeholders
19.w: By holding risk information in one consistent place, the register gives stakeholders a shared reference for discussing and reviewing risk.

19.q: During delivery a planned milestone is not achieved on its target date. What does this most usefully signal to the project manager?
o: That the project's budget has automatically been increased
That progress may be slipping and corrective action may be needed
That the project's scope has been formally reduced
That the risk register no longer needs to be maintained
19.w: A missed milestone is an early signal that progress is slipping, prompting the project manager to consider corrective action.

19.q: A supplier has failed to deliver a critical component, halting project work. How should this be classified?
o: An issue, because the problem has already occurred
An assumption, because it was expected during planning
A risk, because it might affect the project later
A milestone, because it marks a point in the schedule
19.w: A problem that has already happened and is affecting the project is an issue, not a risk.

19.q: A team agrees its delivery scope, timeline and budget, and this is recorded and approved before work begins. What has been established?
o: A procurement strategy
A risk threshold
A communication plan
A deployment baseline
19.w: An agreed and approved reference for scope, time and cost before execution describes the deployment baseline.

19.q: Which factor most commonly makes it difficult to build trust within a newly assembled project team?
o: Members already know each other's strengths perfectly
Members are unfamiliar with one another's ways of working
Members have no individual roles to fulfil
Members have a long shared history of working together
19.w: In a new team, members are unfamiliar with each other's styles, so trust takes time to establish.

19.q: A sponsor asks the project manager to refresh the cost and benefit figures within the business case. Why is this appropriate?
o: The manager is taking over ownership of the case from the sponsor
The manager alone now decides whether the project should continue
The manager supplies delivery information so the sponsor can keep it current
The manager becomes accountable for the realisation of the benefits
19.w: The project manager provides updated delivery information to help the sponsor keep the business case current; ownership and accountability remain with the sponsor.

19.q: When an organisation talks about 'portfolio management', which statement best captures what that discipline is concerned with?
o: The coordination of routine business activities to sustain steady operational performance
The selection, prioritisation and control of projects and programmes to meet strategic goals
The delivery of a group of related projects to achieve a single change outcome
The day-to-day control of one project's scope, cost, schedule and quality
19.w: Portfolio management selects, prioritises and controls the organisation's projects and programmes to align them with strategy; the others describe a programme, a single project and operations.

19.q: A team holds a brainstorming session to work out what could prevent successful delivery. Which risk management stage is this?
o: Risk analysis
Risk response
Risk closure
Risk identification
19.w: Brainstorming is a common technique used during risk identification to surface possible risks.

19.q: A deliverable is completed on time and within budget, yet the customer is dissatisfied. Which success criteria were most likely overlooked?
o: Measures reflecting the schedule's baseline dates
Measures reflecting the supplier payment terms
Measures reflecting the project's risk tolerance
Measures reflecting user acceptance and satisfaction
19.w: Success criteria should capture user acceptance and satisfaction, not only time and cost, so that the outcome genuinely meets the customer's needs.

20.q: A sponsor of a linear construction project asks how often the deployment baseline will change during delivery. What is the most accurate reply?
o: Rarely, and only through formal change control
Weekly, as part of routine iteration planning
Never, even where formal changes are approved
Constantly, after every single working day
20.w: In a linear life cycle the baseline is fixed early and only altered through formal change control, so changes are infrequent.

20.q: A project team is discussing whether their final product meets the definition of 'quality'. Which statement best defines quality?
o: Every project risk was successfully avoided during delivery
The final cost of the product came in below the initial budget
The deliverable includes as many additional features as possible
The output meets the defined requirements and serves its intended purpose
20.w: Quality means the deliverable satisfies its agreed specifications and is suitable for its intended use.

20.q: A project manager uses critical path analysis to find which tasks must finish on time to avoid delaying the project. What is being managed?
o: Critical path activities
The quality of project resources
The overall project budget
Formal stakeholder approval
20.w: Critical path activities have zero float, so they must be completed on time to prevent the project end date from slipping.

20.q: Which of the following is the weakest description of communication in a project setting?
o: A process aimed at building shared understanding
An exchange of information involving feedback
A two-way flow between sender and receiver
A one-off transmission that needs no confirmation
20.w: Communication requires feedback and shared understanding, so a one-way transmission needing no confirmation is the weakest description.

20.q: A project posts updates only on a physical noticeboard, and remote staff never see them. Which disadvantage of this method does this reveal?
o: It reaches only those physically present
It provides no permanent written record
It is far too fast for considered messages
It prevents any interpretation of tone
20.w: Physical, paper-based communication only reaches people at the location, excluding remote or dispersed stakeholders.

20.q: A project manager regularly shares the vision, encourages initiative and supports team learning. Which leadership quality is being demonstrated?
o: Inspirational leadership that aligns the team
Purely reactive decision-making
Detailed cost and budget management
A command-and-control leadership style
20.w: Inspirational leaders energise and align their teams around a shared sense of purpose.

20.q: In a project, what is quality management fundamentally intended to ensure about the deliverables?
o: That they involve the fewest possible team members
That they are produced at the lowest possible cost
That they are fit for purpose and meet the agreed requirements
That they are delivered before the agreed schedule
20.w: Quality management ensures deliverables meet agreed requirements and are fit for purpose.

20.q: A project manager derives the work breakdown structure directly from the product breakdown structure. What benefit does this bring?
o: It removes the need for any change control process
It ensures the planned work aligns with the required deliverables
It fixes the responsibilities of each team member
It guarantees the project finishes ahead of schedule
20.w: Deriving the WBS from the PBS ensures the work planned maps directly to the deliverables required, reducing the chance of missed scope.

20.q: A team switches from a linear to an iterative approach. What should they expect to change about scope management?
o: Scope will now be locked permanently at the start
Scope will be decided solely by the project sponsor
Scope will now be reviewed and adjusted each cycle
Scope will no longer need any prioritisation
20.w: Moving to iterative delivery means scope is reviewed and reprioritised in each cycle rather than fixed once.

20.q: Why is it important to formally close risks during the risk management process?
o: To prevent risks from being escalated to the project’s stakeholders
To transfer the lessons learned directly into the project issue log
To reduce the number of meetings the project team must hold
To keep the risk register accurate and focused on active threats
20.w: Closure removes risks that are no longer relevant, keeping the risk register current and focused on active threats and opportunities.

20.q: Which of the following would be the weakest choice of project success criterion?
o: Delivery within the approved budget tolerance
Achievement of the required technical specification
Stakeholder satisfaction above an agreed threshold
An improvement in team morale during the project
20.w: Team morale is subjective and not directly tied to the project's deliverables, making it a poor, hard-to-measure success criterion.

20.q: Which of the following is not a characteristic of a project?
o: An objective to deliver a unique output
A permanent team structure that continues indefinitely
A temporary nature, disbanding once objectives are met
A defined start point and a defined end point
20.w: Projects are staffed by temporary teams assembled for the objective and disbanded on completion, so a permanent structure is not a project characteristic.

20.q: What is the main advantage of adopting a hybrid life cycle on a project with mixed requirements?
o: It removes the need for any change control because everything is planned upfront
It guarantees the project will finish earlier than a purely linear approach
It applies predictable planning where requirements are stable and flexibility where they evolve
It allows the team to avoid producing a deployment baseline at any stage
20.w: The hybrid approach matches the method to the work, giving predictability to stable elements and adaptability to uncertain ones.

20.q: Which of the following activities best reflects the sponsor's particular role in relation to the project's business case?
o: Testing the completed deliverables against their acceptance criteria
Championing and defending the investment at senior decision-making levels
Maintaining the project's day-to-day risk and issue registers
Producing the detailed schedule and resource plan for the delivery work
20.w: The sponsor champions and defends the business case at senior level; scheduling, testing and register maintenance are project manager or team responsibilities.

20.q: When is a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) most useful during a project?
o: When defining the project's overall scope and its schedule
When conducting the project's lessons learned review at closure
When assigning clear ownership of deliverables and decision-making
When establishing the communication channels with stakeholders
20.w: The RAM is most valuable when ownership and accountability for deliverables and decisions must be made explicit.

20.q: Which of the following activities would appear within an extended life cycle but not within a standard one?
o: Producing the detailed project management plan
Reviewing whether forecast benefits have been realised in operational use
Defining the project's scope during the concept phase
Approving the deployment baseline before delivery begins
20.w: Reviewing realised benefits after handover is characteristic of the extended life cycle, which continues beyond delivery of the outputs.

20.q: At handover a customer claims the product is unacceptable while the team believes it is complete. Which reference best resolves this dispute?
o: The agreed success criteria
The procurement strategy
The communication plan
The risk register
20.w: Pre-agreed success criteria give an objective standard against which acceptance at handover can be judged, resolving such disputes.

20.q: How does active listening help a project leader to improve team performance?
o: It slows down necessary project decision-making
It builds trust and allows issues to be addressed early
It removes the need for any formal reporting
It promotes a culture of blame within the team
20.w: Active listening creates a safe environment where concerns can be raised and resolved before they escalate.

20.q: What benefit does a communication plan provide when conflict arises from misunderstood expectations?
o: It provides an agreed record of communication responsibilities
It guarantees that every team member is satisfied
It delays resolving the matter until project closure
It removes the need to involve stakeholders at all
20.w: Documented communication methods and responsibilities reduce ambiguity and provide a reference point that supports conflict resolution.

20.q: An audit is carried out to assess whether the project's quality procedures are being applied correctly; which process is this?
o: Project scheduling activity
Quality assurance of processes
Requirements gathering work
Risk assessment activity
20.w: Audits are a form of quality assurance used to confirm that established quality procedures are being followed.

20.q: During which phase of a typical linear life cycle is the initial idea first tested for feasibility and strategic fit?
o: Transition
Deployment
Concept
Definition
20.w: The concept phase tests the initial idea for feasibility and strategic fit before detailed planning begins.

20.q: A team recognises that a supplier might fail to meet its deadlines. Which stage of risk management does this demonstrate?
o: Risk identification
Risk acceptance
Risk avoidance
Risk exploitation
20.w: Spotting a potential future threat before it materialises is an example of risk identification.

20.q: A manager arranges a peer review of the team's process to confirm agreed procedures are being followed; what is this an example of?
o: Quality assurance of processes
Scope verification activity
Change control process
Quality control of outputs
20.w: Quality assurance confirms that project processes are being followed correctly so that quality outputs are produced.

20.q: Why might a project manager use models such as Belbin and Tuckman when developing a team?
o: To calculate the project's overall budget
To understand team roles and development stages and adapt their approach
To replace the need for a project schedule
To decide the project's procurement strategy
20.w: Such models help the manager understand behavioural roles and development stages, so leadership can be adapted to support the team.

20.q: A project manager finds the team has no Monitor Evaluator among its Belbin roles. Which risk is this most likely to create?
o: A shortage of new and creative ideas
Too great a reliance on outside stakeholders
Excessive attention to minor details
Weaker critical analysis and poorer decision-making
20.w: The Monitor Evaluator supplies objective, analytical judgement; without one the team may reach poorly considered decisions.

20.q: Of quality planning, assurance and control, which is the only one performed on the finished or in-progress deliverables themselves?
o: Quality control
Quality assurance
Quality governance
Quality planning
20.w: Quality control is performed on the deliverables themselves through inspection and testing; planning and assurance act on standards and processes.

20.q: A project manager lists each recipient, message, channel and timing in a communication plan. Which further detail should be added?
o: The detailed critical path of the schedule
Who is responsible for issuing each communication
The project's complete cost breakdown
The full risk register scoring
20.w: A communication plan should also record who is responsible for issuing each communication, alongside recipient, message, channel and timing.

20.q: A project manager combines a per-square-metre rate with a similar building's actual cost to sense-check figures. Which two methods are being used?
o: Bottom-up and comparative estimating
Qualitative and residual estimating
Parametric and analogous estimating
Analytical and Delphi estimating
20.w: Applying a unit rate is parametric, while comparing against a similar building's actuals is analogous estimating.

20.q: Which underlying principle lies at the very heart of the time boxing scheduling technique?
o: The time available is fixed and the scope is adjusted to fit it
The scope is fixed and the time is extended until it is complete
The cost is fixed and the quality is reduced to meet it
The team size is fixed and the deadline moves to suit it
20.w: Time boxing fixes the period and flexes the scope to fit, rather than extending time to complete a fixed scope.

20.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between project, programme and portfolio management?
o: Programme management replaces portfolio management in smaller organisations
Projects are managed independently of any portfolio or programme structure
Portfolio management provides strategic alignment, while programmes coordinate related change
There is no meaningful overlap between the three disciplines
20.w: Portfolio management aligns all projects and programmes to strategy, while programmes coordinate related change and projects deliver defined outputs.

21.q: What is a typical output of applying resource optimisation techniques to a project?
o: An updated communication plan for the project’s stakeholders
A revised schedule that balances resource demand against availability
An approved business case setting out the project’s justification
A prioritised list ranking the project’s stakeholders by influence
21.w: Resource optimisation produces a revised schedule in which resource demand is balanced against the resources available.

21.q: Which of the following is typically recorded during the closure stage of issue resolution?
o: The stakeholder responsibility matrix for the project
The proposed escalation route for the issue
The date the issue was resolved and the actions taken
The estimated likelihood of the issue recurring later
21.w: At closure the resolution date and a summary of the actions taken are recorded to confirm the issue is complete.

21.q: An auditor physically checks delivered products against the configuration records to confirm they match. Which activity is this?
o: Verification audit
Status accounting
Configuration identification
Configuration planning
21.w: A verification audit confirms that the recorded configuration matches the actual products, checking the records are accurate.

21.q: A project team recognises potential cyber-attacks as a threat to delivery. What has this activity achieved?
o: It has identified a risk
It has closed the risk
It has analysed the risk's impact
It has accepted the risk
21.w: Recognising cyber-attacks as a possible future threat means the team has successfully identified a risk.
