21.q: Midway through an iterative project, stakeholders reprioritise features. What effect does this typically have on the deployment baseline?
o: It invalidates the baseline, so it must be deleted
It freezes the baseline until the project closes
It has no effect, as the baseline is permanently fixed
It updates the baseline to reflect the revised priorities
21.w: An iterative deployment baseline is expected to evolve, so reprioritised features are absorbed by updating the baseline for the next iterations.

21.q: How does a risk register support accountability within a project's risk management?
o: By assigning an owner responsible for each risk
By removing the need to assign any risk owners
By recording only risks that have already occurred
By listing the project's stakeholders and their interests
21.w: The register names a risk owner for each entry, making individuals accountable for monitoring and responding to their risks.

21.q: Which characteristic best distinguishes a hybrid life cycle from other project life cycles?
o: It postpones all delivery until every requirement is agreed
It deliberately combines plan-driven and adaptive methods in one approach
It relies solely on adaptive methods with no fixed structure
It follows one rigid sequence with no scope for iteration
21.w: The defining feature of a hybrid life cycle is its deliberate combination of plan-driven and adaptive methods within a single project.

21.q: When applying resource smoothing to a schedule, which constraint must always be respected?
o: The stakeholder analysis must be fully revised before smoothing begins
The project sponsor must approve each individual resource change first
The risk register must be cleared of all entries before smoothing starts
The available float must not be exceeded, so the completion date is protected
21.w: Resource smoothing works only within available float; the critical path and the project end date must remain unchanged.

21.q: Midway through planning, a team realises part of the scope is fixed and part is unclear. Why might a hybrid life cycle suit them?
o: It ensures no changes will ever be requested during delivery
It combines predictable planning with adaptive delivery within one project
It replaces the need for a project manager to coordinate the work
It lets them skip defining any requirements until the very end
21.w: A hybrid life cycle accommodates both fixed and evolving work by combining plan-driven and adaptive approaches in one project.

21.q: A sponsor insists that stakeholder feedback be included as a success measure. What does this illustrate about effective success criteria?
o: They must always be expressed in financial terms
They should include both objective and subjective elements
They should exclude any measure of user experience
They are best defined at project closure
21.w: Good success criteria combine measurable, objective outcomes with subjective elements such as stakeholder satisfaction.

21.q: The board reviews every current project across IT, finance and HR to reallocate funding by business priority. What process is this?
o: Configuration management
Programme planning
Change control
Portfolio management
21.w: Portfolio management provides strategic oversight, prioritisation and resource balancing across all of an organisation's initiatives.

21.q: An agile team reviews scope at the start of each sprint and updates priorities from user feedback. How does this reflect iterative scope management?
o: The deliverables are set upfront and reviewed only monthly
The product evolves through ongoing review and stakeholder input
The team proceeds without defining any scope at all
The scope is fixed at the start and is never revisited
21.w: In iterative projects the scope evolves as work progresses, guided by continual review and stakeholder feedback.

21.q: A project manager keeps a single document listing each risk, its owner and its planned response. What is this document?
o: The quality plan
The communication plan
The business case
The risk register
21.w: A risk register is the central record of identified risks, their assessment, owners and planned responses, supporting ongoing risk management.

21.q: What key benefit does effective scheduling provide to a project manager?
o: Improved levels of motivation across the project team
Easier negotiation with influential project stakeholders
Reduced financial risk within the project business case
Clarity on task dependencies and the overall project duration
21.w: Scheduling makes dependencies visible and establishes how long the project will take, supporting sound planning and control.

21.q: Which of the following is commonly used as a tool for identifying project risks?
o: SWOT analysis, examining strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
Critical path analysis, identifying the longest sequence of activities
Earned value analysis, comparing planned and actual project performance
MoSCoW prioritisation, ranking requirements by their relative importance
21.w: SWOT analysis is a recognised technique during the identification stage of the risk management process for surfacing threats and opportunities.

21.q: What best distinguishes a project audit from a post-project review carried out after closure?
o: Audits are informal discussions, whereas reviews are formal inspections
Audits apply only to iterative projects, whereas reviews apply to linear ones
Audits assess benefits, whereas reviews assess only the schedule
Audits check compliance and governance, whereas reviews capture performance and lessons
21.w: Audits examine whether the project complied with organisational processes and governance, while post-project reviews focus on results and lessons learned.

21.q: At closure, a team wants to confirm whether the expected objectives and benefits have been achieved. Which element should they refer to?
o: The stakeholder matrix
The work breakdown structure
The success criteria agreed during initiation
The change control log
21.w: The success criteria agreed at initiation provide the benchmark for evaluating whether outcomes and benefits have been delivered.

21.q: A linear project finalised its scope during the concept phase. What is the likely consequence when new requirements emerge during delivery?
o: The change will be managed through strict change control
The scope will be re-planned freely at every stage
The change will be absorbed into the work automatically
The team will simply reprioritise its next sprint
21.w: Linear projects fix scope early, so new requirements arising later are handled through a formal, strictly controlled change process.

21.q: What is an advantage of using physical, paper-based communication in certain project environments?
o: It prevents any form of miscommunication from occurring
It gives a tangible, lasting record that does not depend on technology
It is always the quickest way to distribute project information
It guarantees that recipients will actually read the information
21.w: Physical communication provides a reliable, permanent record in environments where technology access is limited.

21.q: On a rural community project, high unemployment and low digital literacy threaten delivery. These are examples of which PESTLE factor?
o: Technological
Environmental
Political
Sociological
21.w: Demographic and social conditions such as unemployment and literacy are sociological factors that affect adoption and delivery.

21.q: A possible delay to delivery is identified because a supplier may be overloaded with work. How should this be classified?
o: As a milestone, because it marks a delivery point
As a risk, because it has not yet happened
As a change request, because the plan must alter
As an issue, because it is affecting the project now
21.w: The delay is only a possibility that has not yet occurred, so it is an uncertain future event and is therefore a risk.

21.q: In a linear project the baseline for time, cost and scope is set at the start. What is the key challenge if significant changes are later needed?
o: There is no means of tracking the change
The whole project has to be restarted
Baselines cannot be documented at all
Any change must pass through formal change control
21.w: In a linear life cycle changes to the fixed baseline must be formally assessed and approved through change control.

21.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between change control and configuration management?
o: They are the same process operating under two different names
Change control governs whether changes happen; configuration management maintains records of items and versions
Configuration management authorises changes; change control audits the schedule
Both processes apply only after the project has been formally closed
21.w: Change control decides on changes while configuration management keeps the record of controlled items and their versions; the two are complementary.

21.q: An extended life cycle includes a final phase covering the safe retirement of the delivered asset at the end of its useful life. What is this phase called?
o: The concept and feasibility phase
The termination or disposal phase
The delivery and integration phase
The initiation and mobilisation phase
21.w: The extended life cycle concludes with a termination or disposal phase, managing the retirement of the asset once its benefits are exhausted.

21.q: Which of the following statements best describes the main outcome of carrying out critical path analysis on a project?
o: It identifies which activities directly control the project duration
It calculates the financial return forecast for the project
It assigns responsibilities using a RACI matrix
It documents the change requests raised during delivery
21.w: Critical path analysis identifies the activities that control the overall duration, distinguishing them from those with float.

21.q: A construction project introduced quality procedures early and monitored them regularly; what benefit does this bring?
o: It removes the need to obtain stakeholder approval
It increases the likelihood that deliverables meet their specifications
It guarantees that no changes will occur during delivery
It reduces the amount of planning the team must do
21.w: Applying quality management consistently helps ensure deliverables meet agreed specifications and reduces the likelihood of rework.

21.q: What is the main purpose of a procurement strategy in project management?
o: To schedule the internal resources needed to complete project tasks
To identify and document the risks that face the project
To define how goods and services will be acquired from external suppliers
To assign roles and responsibilities to project team members
21.w: A procurement strategy sets out how external products, services and resources will be obtained to support delivery.

21.q: A sponsor requests a rough cost estimate while the project is still at the concept stage. Where in the estimating funnel does this sit?
o: A narrow-tolerance estimate at the bottom of the funnel
A detailed bottom-up estimate stage
A final validated estimate stage
A wide-tolerance estimate near the top of the funnel
21.w: The top of the estimating funnel produces high-level, wide-tolerance estimates because little detail is yet available.

21.q: A retailer runs related projects for online ordering, a mobile app and supply-chain automation. What ensures they are aligned for maximum benefit?
o: Programme management
Quality assurance
Change control
Portfolio management
21.w: Programme management coordinates related projects so their combined benefit exceeds what each project could achieve alone.

21.q: A team defines, plans and controls its processes so that outputs satisfy customer expectations; what is the purpose of this?
o: To provide the cheapest possible product to the customer
To shorten the overall project life cycle
To ensure deliverables meet stakeholder-defined standards
To transfer quality responsibility across to the suppliers
21.w: The purpose of quality management is to define the agreed quality requirements and ensure they are met throughout the project.

22.q: In what way can parametric estimating help to improve the accuracy of a project estimate?
o: By applying historical cost-per-unit data and scaling it to the work required
By relying on group brainstorming sessions to reach an agreed figure
By assigning a single fixed cost to every stage of the project
By comparing the whole project against one broadly similar completed project
22.w: Parametric estimating applies measured historical rates per unit of work, which can be scaled to give a more accurate and defensible estimate.

22.q: A project manager wants to know whether current progress is ahead of or behind plan. Which tool most directly supports this?
o: The stakeholder matrix
The risk register
The schedule
The business case
22.w: The schedule provides the time baseline against which actual progress is measured, showing whether work is ahead of or behind plan.

22.q: Midway through delivery, a steering group relies on progress reports to make decisions. Which benefit of reporting does this best illustrate?
o: It removes all risk from the project entirely
It enables informed, timely decision-making
It guarantees the project finishes ahead of time
It replaces the project's governance arrangements
22.w: Progress reporting gives stakeholders timely, accurate information, enabling informed decisions and effective control.

22.q: A project manager omits the senior user when producing the project management plan. What is the most likely consequence?
o: Delivery costs will automatically increase tenfold
The plan may not reflect genuine user requirements
The sponsor loses all accountability for benefits
The schedule will no longer require any milestones
22.w: The senior user represents those who will use the output; omitting them risks a plan that does not reflect real user needs.

22.q: A reviewer evaluates whether the design procedure in use will reliably yield acceptable results. Is this assurance or control?
o: Control, because it corrects a defect found in the product
Assurance, because it counts the number of finished items produced
Assurance, because it examines the process rather than a finished output
Control, because it inspects a completed deliverable against its specification
22.w: Examining whether a process will reliably yield acceptable results is quality assurance, which is process-focused.

22.q: Why might a project manager include milestones within a project schedule?
o: To provide clear checkpoints for monitoring and reporting progress
To increase the total number of activities shown on the plan
To remove the need for a formal project management plan
To guarantee that the project finishes ahead of schedule
22.w: Milestones give recognisable checkpoints against which progress can be monitored and reported to stakeholders.

22.q: Why does a linear life cycle generally require tighter scope control than an iterative one?
o: Because it welcomes unlimited change at any point in delivery
Because it has no defined deliverables that need protecting
Because its baseline is fixed early, so change disrupts the plan
Because scope is only ever agreed after delivery has ended
22.w: A linear baseline is set early, so uncontrolled change threatens the plan and demands rigorous control.

22.q: In a linear life cycle the scope, timeline and budget are fixed at the start and rarely change. What does this indicate about the deployment baseline?
o: It changes on a daily basis
It is used only after the project closes
It is set early and used to manage performance
It is created during the benefits review
22.w: In a linear life cycle the deployment baseline is fixed early and used as a stable reference for controlling delivery.

22.q: Which outcome would a project manager most reasonably expect from completing a PESTLE analysis?
o: A complete list of the project's internal stakeholders
A signed-off configuration baseline for all deliverables
A finalised critical path for the project schedule
A clearer view of the external context influencing the project
22.w: PESTLE produces an understanding of the external context; the other outputs come from scheduling, configuration and stakeholder work.

22.q: Several workstreams must all reach a common checkpoint before integration testing begins. How is this checkpoint best represented in the schedule?
o: As a milestone
As the critical path
As a resource histogram
As a work package
22.w: A shared checkpoint marking a key point that workstreams must reach is represented as a milestone; it has no duration itself.

22.q: Which of the following is an example of the risk response known as avoidance?
o: Removing a high-risk feature from the project's scope entirely
Accepting the possibility of a small delay to final delivery
Buying insurance to cover possible damage to project equipment
Increasing the budget to cope with late supplier deliveries
22.w: Avoidance removes the threat completely, for example by taking the risky element out of scope.

22.q: In a linear project, when is the scope of work normally fixed?
o: Early on, and then controlled through formal change control
Only after the product has been handed over
Continuously throughout each delivery cycle
At the very end, once all work is complete
22.w: Linear projects define scope early and thereafter manage any changes through formal change control.

22.q: Which of the following statements best describes what a schedule provides to those delivering a project?
o: A record of quality standards the outputs must meet
A list of stakeholders and their communication needs
A justification of why the project should be funded
A time-based plan of activities, dependencies and resources
22.w: A schedule is a time-based plan showing activities, their dependencies, durations and required resources.

22.q: What is the primary purpose of critical path analysis in project scheduling?
o: To identify the sequence of tasks that determines the project's duration
To define the overall scope of work for the project
To establish the stakeholder communication methods
To allocate team roles and responsibilities to members
22.w: Critical path analysis identifies the longest chain of dependent tasks with zero float, which sets the minimum project duration.

22.q: Which activity is most characteristic of the concept phase within a typical linear project life cycle?
o: Defining the business need and justification for change
Completing the post-project benefit reviews
Allocating detailed work packages to the delivery team
Producing and signing off the final test results
22.w: The concept phase articulates the need, high-level options and justification for the project before detailed planning begins.

22.q: A business case compares 'do nothing', 'do the minimum' and 'do something' approaches. Why is this comparison valuable?
o: It defines the criteria for project handover
It reduces the overall scope of the project
It demonstrates value for money and the case for change
It accelerates the procurement of suppliers
22.w: Comparing these options shows the value of proceeding and supports the strategic case for change.

22.q: A team regularly reviews the work completed so far, checking each output against its specification; which process is this?
o: Risk assessment activity
Resource optimisation activity
Communication planning work
Quality control of outputs
22.w: Quality control includes regular reviews and inspections to ensure deliverables meet their agreed specifications.

22.q: Which scenario best illustrates poor stakeholder engagement caused by inadequate analysis?
o: A key regulator halted work because it was not consulted during planning
A quality report was produced in the wrong format
A supplier failed to deliver a component on time
The team did not complete the project risk register
22.w: Overlooking a key regulator during analysis and engagement planning can lead to serious blocks on delivery.

22.q: A team agrees, at the outset, the tolerances and acceptance criteria their deliverables must satisfy. This activity is an example of what?
o: Benefits management forecasting the project's value
Quality control checking against those criteria
Quality planning defining those criteria upfront
Quality assurance auditing the applied processes
22.w: Defining tolerances and acceptance criteria in advance is part of quality planning, which sets the requirements to be met.

22.q: A communication plan helps the project manager manage stakeholder expectations during delivery mainly because it does which of the following?
o: It fixes the scope so that no further changes can ever occur
It sets out clearly what will be communicated, to whom and how often
It guarantees that all stakeholders will actively support the project
It removes the need to record any of the project's risks
22.w: By defining what is communicated, to whom and how frequently, the plan sets consistent expectations and reduces surprises for stakeholders.

22.q: A risk on a healthcare project is patient resistance to digital appointment systems. Which PESTLE category does this best fit?
o: Sociological
Economic
Technological
Legal
22.w: Public attitudes and cultural acceptance of change fall under the sociological category of PESTLE.

22.q: A newly formed project team is polite but hesitant and unsure of its direction. According to Tuckman's model, what should the leader mainly do?
o: Encourage members to work independently straight away
Avoid setting expectations to see how the team develops
Step back and let the team organise itself immediately
Provide clear direction and define the team's goals and roles
22.w: In the forming stage the team looks to the leader for direction and structure to build its early confidence.

22.q: After stakeholder analysis, the project manager groups stakeholders for communication purposes. Why is this important?
o: It removes low-priority stakeholders from the project records
It establishes distinct categories of project risk
It creates a new reporting hierarchy within the project team
It tailors communication and engagement methods to each stakeholder type
22.w: Grouping stakeholders lets communication be made relevant, timely and appropriate to each group's level of involvement.

22.q: A charity plans a major national campaign. Why might its project manager use PESTLE rather than rely on internal information alone?
o: Because it records lessons learned from earlier campaigns
Because it sets out the quality tolerances for each deliverable
Because it surfaces external forces that internal planning would otherwise overlook
Because it decomposes the campaign into manageable work packages
22.w: PESTLE looks beyond the organisation, revealing external factors that internally focused planning tends to miss.

22.q: A project manager reviews risks at every team meeting rather than only at the outset. What benefit does this ongoing review bring?
o: It removes the need to maintain a risk register
It transfers all accountability for risks to the sponsor
It provides early warning of new and changing risks so responses stay current
It guarantees that no risks will materialise during delivery
22.w: Reviewing risks regularly gives early warning of new and changing risks, keeping planned responses current throughout delivery.

22.q: Which group of stakeholders should contribute to a project management plan to ensure the delivered output can be operated after handover?
o: Regulatory auditors external to the organisation
Competitors within the same market sector
End users and operational staff
Members of an unrelated project's team
22.w: End users and operational staff must contribute so the plan reflects requirements needed for successful operation and handover.

22.q: Midway through delivery a team spots a new threat that was not previously listed. Which stage does the process return to?
o: Analysis
Identification
Response
Closure
22.w: Risk management is iterative; a newly spotted threat re-enters the process at the identification stage before being analysed and responded to.

22.q: Which activity is most closely associated with quality control on a project?
o: Defining the quality standards the project will need to meet
Inspecting completed deliverables against their agreed acceptance criteria
Planning how the quality assurance processes will be carried out
Conducting the post-project review once delivery is complete
22.w: Quality control inspects, tests or reviews completed deliverables against defined acceptance criteria to confirm they conform.

22.q: In Belbin's model, which team role is most focused on turning ideas and plans into practical, workable actions?
o: Implementer
Resource Investigator
Plant
Monitor Evaluator
22.w: The Implementer is disciplined and reliable, converting concepts and plans into organised, practical action.

22.q: A project has quality procedures in place but never reviews whether the team follows them; what is missing?
o: Risk management activity
Scope management activity
Issue control activity
Quality assurance of processes
22.w: Without checks to verify process adherence, quality assurance is not being properly implemented.

23.q: One event may happen next quarter; another has already stopped work today. How should each be classified respectively?
o: The first as an issue; the second as a risk
Both as risks, since both affect the project
The first as a risk; the second as an issue
Both as issues, since both are recorded
23.w: A possible future event is a risk; one that has already occurred and stopped work is an issue.

23.q: What does version control help to ensure within the configuration management process?
o: That outdated documents are clearly identified and replaced
That the project's tasks are placed in the correct sequence
That the project's procurement rules are properly followed
That the entries in the risk register are correctly prioritised
23.w: Version control ensures that only the latest approved versions of documents and products are in use, and older versions are withdrawn.

23.q: What is the role of success criteria when they are set out within a business case?
o: To set performance targets for individual team members
To clarify the benefits the project must deliver to be considered worthwhile
To record the communication preferences of the team
To track the duration of each scheduled task
23.w: Success criteria define what the project must achieve to justify the investment and deliver worthwhile value.

23.q: A project manager decides to buy in specialist development work from an outside supplier. Which document guides this approach?
o: The change request log
The risk register
The work breakdown structure
The procurement strategy
23.w: The procurement strategy defines whether work is delivered internally or bought externally, and the criteria for doing so.

23.q: Which aspect of a team does Belbin's model primarily help a project manager to understand?
o: The reporting lines shown in an organisational breakdown structure
The balance of behavioural roles within the team
The order in which risks should be addressed
The stages a team moves through as it matures
23.w: Belbin's model describes behavioural team roles, helping the manager build a balanced and effective team.

23.q: A team is building a new mobile app through short development cycles with regular end-user feedback. Which life cycle is most likely being used?
o: Extended
Hybrid
Iterative
Linear
23.w: An iterative life cycle delivers in small increments and refines the product through repeated cycles of stakeholder feedback.

23.q: Which of the following best explains the distinction between change control and configuration management?
o: Change control evaluates proposed changes, and configuration management ensures approved changes are correctly implemented
Change control tracks scheduling milestones, and configuration management carries out product testing
Change control plans the use of resources, and configuration management defines the project team's roles
Change control manages procurement, and configuration management handles the project's budget reporting
23.w: Change control is the gatekeeper that assesses and approves changes; configuration management ensures approved changes are applied and maintained.

23.q: A client asks what calling their deliverable 'quality' actually guarantees about it. What is the best answer?
o: That it conforms to its agreed requirements and is fit for its purpose
That it is the most advanced and expensive option available
That it includes every possible additional feature
That it was delivered faster than originally scheduled
23.w: Quality means conformance to agreed requirements and fitness for purpose, not maximum cost, features or speed.

23.q: A PMO introduces a lessons learned process across all completed projects. What is the primary benefit of doing this?
o: It identifies who to blame for previous project failures
It speeds up future procurement decisions
It supports continuous improvement across the project portfolio
It justifies staff changes within the delivery teams
23.w: Capturing lessons learned helps future projects avoid repeat mistakes and adopt proven good practice.

23.q: A client wants a fixed upfront cost and schedule for deployment but also wants to evolve features after go-live. Which approach best fits?
o: Extended
Iterative
Hybrid
Linear
23.w: A hybrid approach allows a predictable, planned deployment while retaining iterative flexibility to evolve features later.

23.q: How does the deployment baseline relate to the project management plan?
o: It replaces the plan once the project enters the delivery phase
It is the approved reference set for scope, time and cost drawn from the plan
It is produced by operations after the outputs are handed over
It records only the risks and issues identified during planning
23.w: The deployment baseline is the fixed, approved set of scope, time and cost derived from the project management plan and used to control delivery.

23.q: Which statement best corrects the misconception that risk management removes all risk from a project?
o: It guarantees the project will meet every objective
It ensures no threats will ever materialise
It manages uncertainty to acceptable levels rather than removing it entirely
It transfers every risk to an external supplier
23.w: Risk management reduces and controls uncertainty to acceptable levels; it cannot eliminate all risk from a project.

23.q: What is a key benefit of a communication plan to the project manager?
o: It prevents any conflict from arising within the team
It ensures consistent, structured messaging reaches the right people
It guarantees that the project will be delivered successfully
It removes the need to maintain any project documentation
23.w: A communication plan helps deliver the right message, to the right people, at the right time in a consistent format.

23.q: Two team members carried out a task differently after a briefing because neither confirmed what was meant. Which aspect of communication failed?
o: There was no feedback to confirm shared understanding
The message was too short to be archived
The message was sent to too many recipients
The wrong communication medium was chosen
23.w: Without feedback to confirm shared understanding, the message was interpreted differently, so the communication was not effective.

23.q: A customer is uncertain whether the final deliverable meets their original needs. Which early activity would most likely have prevented this?
o: Holding more frequent team retrospective meetings
Assigning additional members to the project team
Producing a more detailed schedule as a Gantt chart
Defining the success criteria collaboratively with the customer
23.w: Agreeing success criteria with the customer early ensures a shared, documented understanding of the intended outcome.

23.q: A project manager maintains a risk register and reviews it each week. How does this best support project success?
o: It removes all remaining assumptions from the project management plan
It allows risks to be monitored continuously and responses to be actioned
It ensures the lessons learned are all documented before work begins
It prevents any further change requests from being raised during delivery
23.w: Regular review of the risk register lets the team act on emerging threats and opportunities before they escalate.

23.q: Why is it important to tailor progress reports to different stakeholder groups?
o: To provide information relevant to each group's interest and influence
To remove the need for formal governance meetings
To avoid carrying out any project audits
To reduce the amount of communication within the team
23.w: Stakeholders have differing interests and influence, so tailoring reports ensures each group receives meaningful and relevant information.

23.q: A developer implements a change to a deliverable before it has been reviewed or authorised. Which stage of the change control process has been omitted?
o: Post-implementation review
Benefits review
Configuration audit
Impact assessment
23.w: Impact assessment evaluates the effect of a proposed change on time, cost, quality and risk before it can be approved and implemented.

23.q: A project manager notices discrepancies between the latest deliverable and the configuration baseline. Which process should be reviewed first?
o: Procurement management
Scheduling control
Communication planning
Configuration management
23.w: Configuration management keeps deliverables aligned with the current approved baseline, so it should be reviewed when discrepancies appear.

23.q: As your project's outputs are handed over to the operational team, what role does benefits management play?
o: It becomes irrelevant once the project has closed
It ensures the expected value outcomes continue to be tracked in operations
It finalises the outstanding contract negotiations
It replaces the project's risk register
23.w: Benefits are often realised after handover, so benefits management ensures value continues to be tracked in operation.

23.q: Which combination of elements is typically fixed within a project's deployment baseline?
o: Quality standards, audits and benefit reviews
Scope, schedule and cost agreed for delivery
Team roles, supplier contracts and lessons learned
Stakeholder interests, risks and communication channels
23.w: The deployment baseline captures the approved scope, schedule and cost that define what will be delivered.

23.q: Why might a deployment baseline change more frequently in an iterative life cycle than in a linear one?
o: Change control is not used on iterative projects
Requirements evolve throughout the development
Schedules are disregarded in iterative delivery
Project governance is not required at all
23.w: Iterative life cycles use feedback and evolving requirements, so the baseline is regularly updated.

23.q: Which stakeholder is primarily responsible for ensuring that the project management plan aligns with the organisation's strategic objectives?
o: A project team member
A supplier
The project sponsor
The product owner
23.w: The sponsor owns the business case and ensures the project remains aligned with the organisation's strategic goals.

23.q: Why are both change control and configuration management needed together in scope management?
o: To evaluate and approve changes and then maintain them in the outputs
To prevent any changes at all from being made to the project
To provide the project's budget approval and procurement sign-off
To handle only the external modifications made to contracts
23.w: Change control evaluates and approves changes, while configuration management ensures those approved changes are correctly applied and maintained.

23.q: The sponsor is concerned that delivery risks are under-represented in the business case. What should the project manager do?
o: Remove the risk section and emphasise the benefits
Work with the team to supply accurate risk data and mitigation plans
Transfer ownership of the business case to governance
Wait until the next stage gate before raising it
23.w: The project manager supports the sponsor by providing accurate delivery risk information to inform the case.

23.q: In which type of life cycle is the deployment baseline expected to evolve frequently as the solution develops?
o: Linear
Iterative
Waterfall
Extended
23.w: In iterative life cycles the baseline evolves as understanding grows and the solution is progressively refined.

23.q: An audit confirms that versioning rules were followed and only approved changes were made. What does this outcome confirm?
o: That all of the planned benefits have been realised
That the stakeholder requirements have changed
That the agreed project baseline has since changed
That configuration control and verification were effective
23.w: A satisfactory audit demonstrates that changes were properly controlled and that items conform to their approved configuration.

23.q: A manager lists features of project work to contrast it with business as usual. Which feature genuinely applies only to projects?
o: Continuing indefinitely with no planned closure
Being run by a permanent operational department
Delivering a steady, repeatable stream of outputs
Being temporary, with a defined start and end
23.w: A project is temporary, with a defined start and end, whereas business as usual is repetitive and ongoing.

23.q: A finance team updates spreadsheets and processes invoices every day. How should this work most appropriately be classified?
o: Business-as-usual, because it involves regular, repeatable tasks
Business-as-usual, because it has a sponsor and a budget
A project, because it is constrained by time and cost
A project, because it is carried out by a skilled team
23.w: Regular, repeatable work that maintains an ongoing service is business-as-usual, not a project.

23.q: At what point should a project's deployment baseline normally be agreed and approved?
o: During the concept phase, before any planning is done
After the project has been formally closed
Before delivery begins, at the end of planning
Only when a change request is first raised
23.w: The baseline is set and approved once planning is complete and before delivery begins, so performance can be measured from that point.

24.q: Short, fixed-length cycles such as sprints in an iterative delivery are an application of which scheduling technique?
o: Resource levelling
Parametric estimating
Time boxing
Critical path analysis
24.w: Sprints are fixed-length cycles, a direct application of time boxing within iterative delivery.

24.q: Why is it important to carry out regular configuration audits during a project?
o: To ensure that all project work is completed ahead of schedule
To confirm that only authorised changes have been implemented and recorded
To speed up the procurement processes used by the project
To reduce the number of team members the project requires
24.w: Configuration audits verify that only authorised changes have been made and that the deliverables and records match the approved configuration.

24.q: A project team has reached the performing stage of Tuckman's model. Which leadership approach is most appropriate at this point?
o: Reassign the work frequently to keep the team stimulated
Revisit the ground rules and reset the team's agreed norms
Provide firm direction and closely define every role and task
Delegate and allow autonomy while monitoring for emerging issues
24.w: A performing team is capable and self-managing, so the leader can delegate and facilitate rather than direct closely.

24.q: A construction firm pours foundations in a fixed sequence but develops the building's smart controls in short cycles. Which life cycle is this?
o: Linear life cycle
Iterative life cycle
Hybrid life cycle
Extended life cycle
24.w: Combining a linear sequence for fixed work with iterative cycles for evolving elements within one project is a hybrid life cycle.

24.q: A project manager wants to show how the project's work is distributed across the organisation's departments and teams. Which tool suits this?
o: A cost breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
A product breakdown structure
An organisational breakdown structure
24.w: An OBS structures the project's people resources into the organisational units responsible for the work.

24.q: A client requests an urgent change to a critical deliverable. What should the project manager do first?
o: Implement the change straight away to meet expectations
Include the change within the next routine progress report
Email the project team and proceed with it immediately
Raise and assess a change request through the formal procedure
24.w: Every change, however urgent, is raised and assessed through the formal change control procedure so its impact is understood before any decision.

24.q: Which of the following would you NOT normally expect to find recorded in a risk register?
o: The actual durations recorded for completed project tasks
A clear description of each identified risk
The probability and impact scores for each risk
The named person who owns each identified risk
24.w: Actual task durations belong to the schedule, not the risk register, which focuses on uncertainty and responses.

24.q: Two projects run side by side: one linear, one iterative. Which difference in their deployment baselines should the project manager expect?
o: The linear baseline flexes weekly; the iterative stays fixed
Both baselines remain completely unchanged throughout
The iterative baseline flexes; the linear stays largely fixed
Neither project establishes a baseline at any point
24.w: The iterative project's baseline evolves with each iteration, while the linear project's baseline is largely fixed after early approval.

24.q: A team defines the improvements expected, then tracks whether they materialise after go-live. Which discipline are they applying?
o: Quality control
Configuration management
Critical path analysis
Benefits management
24.w: Defining expected improvements and tracking their realisation is the essence of benefits management.

24.q: During which stage would a project manager draw on lessons learned from earlier projects to spot potential risks?
o: Risk acceptance
Risk response
Risk closure
Risk identification
24.w: Lessons learned from previous projects are a useful input to risk identification, helping surface recurring or overlooked risks.

24.q: How does a risk differ from an assumption on a project?
o: A risk is always true; an assumption is always false
A risk is an uncertain future event; an assumption is taken to be true
There is no difference between the two terms
A risk has occurred; an assumption cannot occur
24.w: A risk is an uncertain event that might happen, while an assumption is something accepted as true for planning.

24.q: A project board wants assurance that a new initiative will meet its aims without exceeding budget or deadline. Which discipline directly serves this purpose?
o: Project management, which delivers objectives within agreed constraints
Business-as-usual management, which sustains ongoing repeatable services
Facilities management, which maintains the organisation's physical assets
Operational supervision, which oversees continuous daily production
24.w: Delivering objectives within the agreed constraints of time and cost is the defining purpose of project management.

24.q: How does a communication plan help to reduce misunderstandings on a project?
o: By reducing the amount of stakeholder engagement needed
By clarifying who communicates what, when and how
By transferring all communication tasks to suppliers
By restricting the team to informal conversations only
24.w: Clear responsibilities and defined channels support accurate, consistent communication throughout the project.

24.q: Quality assurance is often described as 'process-focused'. What does this mean in practice?
o: It concentrates on ensuring the methods used can produce quality, rather than checking each output
It records risks and issues as they arise during delivery
It inspects every finished output and rejects those that fail
It focuses only on controlling the project's overall budget
24.w: Being process-focused, quality assurance ensures the methods used are capable of producing quality rather than inspecting each output.

24.q: What challenge might a project manager face when trying to build motivation in a high-pressure delivery environment?
o: The team being consistently underloaded with work
Stress and burnout reducing morale and engagement
Receiving too much interest from stakeholders
Spending excessive time on detailed planning
24.w: Sustained pressure can lead to burnout, which the project manager must manage to keep the team effective and motivated.

24.q: On a new IT project you gather requirements, attend progress meetings and support testing. Which role are you performing?
o: Project sponsor
Product owner
End user
Project team member
24.w: A project team member completes assigned tasks and contributes specialist or technical input to the delivery of the project.

24.q: What key function does the deployment baseline serve in relation to change control?
o: It sets the duration of the supplier contract
It provides a reference point for evaluating proposed changes
It guarantees that no changes will ever be permitted
It allows stakeholders to be removed without approval
24.w: All proposed changes are compared against the baseline so their impact can be assessed and approval sought.

24.q: How does effective risk management benefit a project?
o: It removes all uncertainty from the project environment
It shifts every decision onto the individual team members
It reduces the impact of threats and helps exploit opportunities
It allows the project to ignore its business case
24.w: Managing risk reduces the effect of threats and helps the project take advantage of opportunities, improving the chance of success.

24.q: Considering how projects define their terms, which of the following situations most clearly represents an issue?
o: A supplier might raise its component prices next quarter
A required approval has been refused, halting the next stage
Bad weather could delay some outdoor work later in delivery
A team member may possibly leave before delivery ends
24.w: A refused approval that has halted progress has already happened, making it an issue; the others are uncertain future events, or risks.

24.q: As soon as a problem is confirmed to be affecting the project now, where is it first recorded in the resolution process?
o: In the benefits plan at closure
In the business case during escalation
In the risk register during analysis
In the issue log at the identification stage
24.w: A confirmed issue is first recorded in the issue log as part of the identification stage of the process.

24.q: A company produces a one-off prototype for a client using a new design method. How is this effort correctly classified?
o: Business-as-usual, because it involves routine manufacturing
A project, because it is a unique activity with defined outcomes
A project, because it forms part of regular production
Business-as-usual, because the client places orders frequently
24.w: Creating a unique prototype with defined outputs is a time-bounded, one-off endeavour, which makes it a project.

24.q: Before handover is approved, the board requires confirmation that all deliverables meet the agreed scope and quality standards. What mechanism is this?
o: A risk escalation process
A work package authorisation
An issue log update
A decision gate review
24.w: A decision gate lets governance confirm that agreed criteria are met before the project is authorised to proceed.

24.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the phases of a typical linear project life cycle?
o: Deployment
Definition
Optimisation
Concept
24.w: The four phases of a typical linear life cycle are concept, definition, deployment and transition; optimisation is not one of them.

24.q: Which statement best describes the purpose of carrying out a benefit review on a project?
o: An evaluation of whether the expected business benefits have been delivered
A report on the availability of the team once the project ends
A discussion of scope changes held with the project’s suppliers
An internal audit of the time-tracking systems used by staff
24.w: A benefits review assesses whether the anticipated benefits set out in the business case have actually been realised.

24.q: Which of the following is not normally an activity within the configuration management process?
o: Status accounting
Configuration procurement
Configuration identification
Configuration planning
24.w: Procurement is not part of configuration management; the recognised activities include planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification.

24.q: Why is it important that a business case documents its key assumptions and constraints?
o: They define the decision-making authority of governance
They remove the need for ongoing performance tracking
They are legally binding on all parties to the project
They help stakeholders judge feasibility and where risk may lie
24.w: Stated assumptions and constraints let stakeholders assess how realistic the proposal is and where key risks are concentrated.

24.q: For a quick decision needing input from team members across three time zones, which method offers the greatest advantage?
o: A physical noticeboard in the site office
A single face-to-face meeting at head office
A virtual meeting or video conference
A printed memo posted to each location
24.w: Virtual methods connect geographically dispersed members quickly and cheaply, without the time and cost of bringing everyone together in person.

24.q: Which statement correctly separates the responsibilities of the project sponsor from those of the project manager?
o: The sponsor delivers the work packages while the manager owns the business case
Both roles share identical accountability for producing the deliverables
The sponsor owns the business case and benefits; the manager delivers the outputs
The manager secures funding while the sponsor schedules daily tasks
24.w: The sponsor is accountable for the business case and benefits realisation, while the project manager is responsible for day-to-day delivery of the outputs.

24.q: Which of the following best explains how a product breakdown structure supports scope definition?
o: It lists all stakeholders and their communication preferences
It defines the product deliverables in a structured hierarchy
It records the planned and actual cost of each activity
It organises the reporting structure of the project team
24.w: The PBS sets out the product's deliverables in a structured hierarchy, giving a clear understanding of the required scope.

24.q: Resource levelling is most accurately described as which kind of scheduling technique?
o: Resource-limited, adjusting the schedule to available resources
Scope-limited, deleting tasks until demand is affordable
Time-limited, never allowing the completion date to change
Quality-limited, adjusting specifications to save resources
24.w: Resource levelling is resource-limited, adjusting the schedule to fit the resources available, which may extend the duration.

25.q: Stakeholders disagree over the project's success criteria partway through delivery. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Proceed with the original criteria and ignore the concerns
Revise and agree updated criteria through change control
Suspend all activity until full consensus is achieved
Replace the success criteria with the business case
25.w: Success criteria may need revising as expectations evolve, and any change should be agreed through the formal change control process.

25.q: A deliverable is altered without going through the change control process. What is the most likely outcome?
o: More efficient approval of the change by the control board
Reduced cost and improved satisfaction among stakeholders
Stronger compliance with the project's quality standards
Increased risk of scope creep and unplanned rework
25.w: Unauthorised changes bypass assessment of their impact, leading to scope creep, misalignment with the baseline and likely rework.

25.q: How does adapting leadership style to the team's needs and maturity help influence its performance?
o: It provides the right level of support and direction to keep the team effective
It removes the requirement to set any objectives
It ensures the team never needs feedback again
It hands day-to-day control to the project sponsor
25.w: Adapting style to the team's maturity gives the appropriate balance of support and direction, sustaining effective performance.

25.q: A team leader recognises a member's contribution during a sprint review. What effect is this most likely to have?
o: It boosts morale and encourages continued high performance
It delays the delivery of future sprints
It demotivates the remainder of the team
It reduces collaboration across the team
25.w: Recognition reinforces positive behaviour and lifts morale, which can drive further high performance.

25.q: Which of the following best defines an 'issue' in a project?
o: A technique used to break down the scope of the work
A planned milestone marking the end of a project stage
An uncertain event that may or may not happen in future
A problem that has occurred and requires management action
25.w: An issue is a problem that has already happened and needs resolving now, unlike a risk, which is an uncertain future event.

25.q: During which stage of the risk management process are risks assessed for probability and impact so that they can be prioritised?
o: Identification
Response
Analysis
Closure
25.w: Risk analysis assesses probability and impact, enabling risks to be prioritised for attention.

25.q: On a software project the team decides all deliverables must comply with a recognised standard; which aspect of quality planning is this?
o: Creating the change control procedures
Selecting the relevant quality standards
Defining the overall budget baseline
Documenting the lessons learned so far
25.w: Quality planning includes selecting the standards that will guide development and testing of deliverables.

25.q: Which of the following is not normally a responsibility of an end user during a project?
o: Controlling the project budget and schedule
Taking part in user acceptance testing
Providing feedback on usability and functionality
Adopting the new system or process after handover
25.w: Controlling budget and schedule is a project management responsibility and falls outside the end user's role.

25.q: Where would a project manager typically record and track a problem that has already arisen during delivery?
o: In the risk register
In the issue log
In the communication plan
In the business case
25.w: A problem that has arisen is an issue and is recorded and tracked in the issue log, distinct from the risk register used for potential events.

25.q: You are running a construction project with a linear life cycle and fully defined requirements. What is the correct sequence of phases?
o: Concept, Definition, Development, Handover and Closure
Concept, Definition, Deployment, Closure
Initiation, Development, Execution, Review
Concept, Feasibility, Deployment, Handover
25.w: A typical APM linear life cycle runs through Concept, Definition, Development, and Handover and Closure.

25.q: The project manager has supplied updated risk analysis for the business case. Who decides whether the case is formally revised?
o: The project sponsor, as owner of the business case
The project manager, as author of the analysis
The project team, as producers of the work
The end users, as recipients of the benefits
25.w: The project manager provides the analysis, but the sponsor owns the business case and decides whether it is formally revised.

25.q: A director reviews the organisation's entire collection of projects and programmes to decide which to fund, pause or stop. Which discipline is this?
o: Programme management
Portfolio management
Project management
Operational management
25.w: Selecting, prioritising and controlling the whole collection of projects and programmes for strategic value is portfolio management.

25.q: After logging an issue, the project manager works out how seriously it affects cost, time and quality. Which stage of issue resolution is this?
o: Closure
Escalation
Identification
Assessment
25.w: Determining the effect of a logged issue on the project's objectives is the assessment stage.

25.q: Which of the following activities most accurately represents what project management involves when delivering a project's objectives?
o: Delivering identical outputs repeatedly to satisfy steady and predictable customer demand
Planning, monitoring and controlling all aspects of a project to meet its objectives
Directing a coordinated set of projects to realise combined organisational benefits
Selecting which proposed initiatives should receive investment in each financial year
25.w: Project management plans, monitors and controls all aspects of a project to achieve its objectives; the others describe business as usual, programme and portfolio management.

25.q: In an agile project, which stakeholder clarifies the acceptance criteria and ensures user needs are reflected in the plan?
o: The PMO analyst
The product owner
The scrum master
The project sponsor
25.w: The product owner represents the customer and defines the requirements, including what acceptable delivery looks like.

25.q: At what point in the issue resolution process is ownership of the issue formally assigned?
o: During the analysis of the issue
Only if the issue is escalated
During the closure of the issue
Immediately after the issue has been logged
25.w: Once an issue has been identified and logged, ownership is promptly assigned so that resolution can be driven and tracked.

25.q: A work breakdown structure contains items such as 'code user interface' and 'test module'. What does this structure help to define?
o: The procurement process for the external suppliers
The financial framework underpinning the project
The structure of the client's own organisation
The work required to produce each project deliverable
25.w: The WBS breaks the scope into the work required to complete each deliverable, expressed as manageable work packages.

25.q: Why does a project adopt quality management rather than relying on inspection alone?
o: To eliminate the need for any project documentation
To guarantee the project finishes ahead of schedule
To build quality in through planning, assurance and control
To remove the sponsor's involvement in the project
25.w: Quality management builds quality in through planning, assurance and control rather than depending on end inspection.

25.q: When developing a business case, which pairing of responsibilities to roles is correct?
o: Owning and championing it — the sponsor; providing information to develop it — the manager
Owning it — the manager; approving the funding — the sponsor
Producing the estimates — the sponsor; deciding strategic fit — the manager
Approving it — the end users; writing it — the project team
25.w: The sponsor owns and champions the business case, while the project manager provides the information needed to develop it.

25.q: When comparing the two, which pairing correctly matches each structure to what it represents?
o: PBS = responsibilities; WBS = risks
PBS = activities; WBS = products
PBS = deliverables; WBS = the work to create them
PBS = costs; WBS = timescales
25.w: A PBS represents the deliverables (products), whereas a WBS represents the work required to create those deliverables.

25.q: What is one benefit of applying a standard estimating funnel across an organisation's projects?
o: It replaces the need for bottom-up estimating
It fixes all estimates at the start of each project
It promotes consistent refinement of estimates across project phases
It removes the need for any contingency planning
25.w: A standard funnel provides a consistent approach to refining estimates as knowledge grows, aiding comparison across projects.

25.q: Staff using a newly delivered finance system report confusion over some features and ask for more training. What is the most appropriate project response?
o: Log the feedback and assess the options for supporting the users
Disregard the request because the project has already closed
Escalate the concern straight to the governance board
Amend the business case to add the requested features
25.w: End user feedback should be acknowledged and addressed through support, training or further improvement to aid successful adoption.

25.q: How does a communication plan help when several stakeholder groups with differing needs are involved?
o: It allows senior leadership to be left out of all updates
It restricts every communication to a single email channel
It requires the same message to be sent to every group
It lets the manager tailor messages to each audience's needs and influence
25.w: Communication plans support stakeholder-specific approaches, improving the relevance and effectiveness of engagement.

25.q: Resource smoothing evens out resource peaks by rescheduling activities within which scheduling allowance?
o: Their mandatory dependencies
Their available float
The project's cost baseline
The critical path duration
25.w: Resource smoothing reschedules activities within their available float, evening out demand without moving the end date.

25.q: A bank runs daily transaction processing and, separately, a one-off move to new premises. Which statement about these two activities is correct?
o: The processing is operations; the move is a project
The processing is a project; the move is operations
Both are business as usual because both are essential
Both are projects because both consume resources
25.w: Repetitive daily processing is business as usual, whereas the unique, time-bounded office move is a project.

25.q: The team records that adverse weather might delay outdoor work next month. How is this best classified?
o: An issue, because it is affecting delivery now
A change, because it alters the agreed scope
A risk, because it is uncertain and may occur in future
A constraint, because it limits the schedule
25.w: An uncertain future event that may or may not happen is a risk, distinguishing it from an issue that has occurred.

25.q: What does a well-structured communication plan help a project team to ensure during delivery?
o: That the right people receive the right information at the right time
That only face-to-face meetings are used throughout the project
That all identified project risks are resolved automatically
That every project meeting is cancelled to save time and cost
25.w: A communication plan sets out who needs what information, when and how, so the right people are kept informed at the right time.

25.q: Which communication method is most effective for detailed discussions that need clarification and negotiation?
o: Holding a face-to-face meeting
Issuing a monthly written status report
Sending a one-way recorded video message
Circulating a general group email
25.w: Face-to-face meetings allow complex points to be discussed and clarified immediately through two-way dialogue.

25.q: What does the quality planning process mainly set out to establish before delivery of a project begins?
o: The quality standards required and how they will be met
The defects found in completed deliverables
The market price of each project deliverable
The behavioural roles within the project team
25.w: Quality planning determines the relevant quality standards and requirements and defines how they will be achieved during the project.

25.q: Beyond simply issuing orders, effective project leadership is best characterised by which behaviour?
o: Focusing solely on the project's budget and schedule
Issuing detailed instructions and requiring strict compliance
Enabling and empowering people to contribute their best towards the goal
Avoiding contact with the team to remain impartial
25.w: Leadership enables and empowers people to contribute their best, going beyond merely issuing orders.

26.q: Which activity is most closely associated with the extended project life cycle?
o: Monitoring benefit delivery over time
Defining the work breakdown structure
Procuring the development resources
Identifying the initial user requirements
26.w: The extended life cycle focuses on tracking benefit delivery, often long after the deliverables have been handed over.

26.q: A project manager uses a milestone to record the formal approval of the completed design phase. What does this milestone provide?
o: A checklist of quality requirements
An overview of team responsibilities
A schedule marker that shows progress
A register of the project stakeholders
26.w: A milestone marks a significant scheduled event, such as a phase completion or approval, providing a clear indicator of progress.

26.q: Which estimating method would give the most accurate figure once detailed design information is available?
o: A high-level judgement made at the concept gate
Analytical (bottom-up) estimating of each work package
Analogous estimating based on a past project
A rough order-of-magnitude estimate
26.w: Bottom-up estimating uses detailed component information, so it is most accurate once that detail exists.

26.q: In Belbin's team role model, which role is most concerned with meeting deadlines and checking work thoroughly for errors?
o: Resource Investigator
Completer Finisher
Plant
Coordinator
26.w: The Completer Finisher is conscientious and detail-focused, ensuring work is finished thoroughly and on time.

26.q: A change initiative coordinates a new system, revised processes and staff training so that together they transform customer service. What is this?
o: Benefits realisation management
Portfolio management
Project management
Programme management
26.w: Coordinating related projects so that combined they deliver a shared transformation is programme management.

26.q: A team implemented a change straight after it was requested, without evaluating its effect on cost, time and quality. Which stage was skipped?
o: Closing the completed project
Impact assessment of the proposed change
Implementing the approved change
Logging the initial change request
26.w: Implementing straight after the request skipped the impact assessment stage, where effects on cost, time and quality are evaluated before a decision.

26.q: Which process ensures that a project delivers only the work required to meet its objectives?
o: Cost management
Change control
Stakeholder management
Scope management
26.w: Scope management defines and controls the work included in the project so that it delivers only what is necessary to meet its objectives.

26.q: A configuration audit finds that several different versions of the same document are in active use. Which activity has failed?
o: Configuration identification
Configuration control
Verification audit
Configuration planning
26.w: Configuration control should prevent unauthorised or duplicate versions from being released and used across the project.

26.q: Beyond audience, method and frequency, which further detail strengthens a communication plan?
o: The colour scheme used in every report
The supplier's internal reporting lines
The daily attendance of every team member
A means of gathering feedback from recipients
26.w: Including a feedback mechanism ensures communication is two-way, confirming messages are received and understood.

26.q: Which of the following is typically included in a benefits management plan?
o: The ownership, timing and measurement of each benefit
The baseline schedule data for the project
The list of items excluded from scope
The communication escalation procedures
26.w: A benefits management plan sets out who owns each benefit, when it is expected and how it will be measured.

26.q: What is a downside of relying too heavily on informal verbal communication?
o: It guarantees that information is always communicated accurately
Agreements may go undocumented and be misunderstood later
It removes the need for any defined escalation routes
It substantially increases the volume of project documentation
26.w: Informal verbal communication relies on memory, so agreements can be forgotten or misunderstood unless confirmed in writing.

26.q: Which of the following would you normally expect to find recorded against each entry in a risk register?
o: The exact wording of the project's business case
The full technical specification of every deliverable
The behavioural role of the person raising it
The risk's probability, impact and planned response
26.w: Each register entry typically records the risk description, its probability and impact, a risk owner and the agreed response.

26.q: A project manager brings in an expert to supply in-depth knowledge the team currently lacks. Which Belbin role does this describe?
o: Specialist
Shaper
Team Worker
Coordinator
26.w: The Specialist provides deep, focused expertise in a specific area that the rest of the team does not possess.

26.q: Which characteristic of scope management is more typical of iterative than linear projects?
o: A single formal acceptance of scope at project handover
A detailed scope baseline agreed once and rarely altered
Complete avoidance of stakeholder involvement in scope
Flexibility to adjust deliverables in response to regular feedback
26.w: Iterative scope management is characterised by flexibility to adjust deliverables as feedback arrives.

26.q: Which document typically captures the details of a proposed scope change before it is formally reviewed?
o: Change request form
Stakeholder matrix
Configuration item log
Communication plan
26.w: A change request form initiates the process, recording the proposed change and its rationale so it can be assessed and a decision made.

26.q: Why are benefit reviews often carried out well after a project has finished?
o: To give the project team time to recover
To reduce the overall costs of the project
To allow benefits time to emerge and be measured
To avoid any pressure coming from the sponsors
26.w: Some benefits take time to materialise, so reviews after implementation assess whether those outcomes were achieved.

26.q: A sponsor is frustrated that the concept-stage estimate later changed. How does the estimating funnel explain this?
o: The original estimate should never have been shared with the sponsor
Estimates are fixed once given and any change indicates poor planning
Early estimates are broad and refine as project detail increases
Later estimates are always less reliable than earlier ones
26.w: The funnel shows that early estimates are indicative and legitimately refine as more detail emerges through the life cycle.

26.q: What is normally the first step in a typical issue resolution process?
o: Escalating the issue directly to the project board
Closing the issue as soon as it has been recorded
Implementing a resolution before any assessment is made
Identifying and logging the issue in the issue register
26.w: The issue must first be identified and formally logged so that it can then be assessed, owned and tracked to resolution.

26.q: Which of the following scenarios best illustrates work that would be classified as a project?
o: Answering routine user queries on a support helpdesk each day
Processing the organisation's payroll at the end of every month
Maintaining a client's existing software system throughout the year
Implementing a new customer relationship management system over six months
26.w: A time-bounded initiative delivering a unique output, such as a new CRM system, is a project; the others are ongoing, repeatable business-as-usual tasks.

26.q: Why is a single, tightly controlled deployment baseline more workable in a linear life cycle than in an iterative one?
o: Linear projects have no stakeholders to satisfy
Linear projects deliver nothing until the very end
Linear requirements are defined and stable up front
Linear projects never encounter any change requests
26.w: Linear life cycles define requirements up front and expect them to remain stable, so a single controlled baseline is appropriate; iterative requirements evolve.

26.q: What is a recognised disadvantage of using analogous estimating during a project?
o: It can only be applied once the project is nearing completion
It is based on judgement and can therefore be subjective and less accurate
It demands fully detailed specifications before any estimate is produced
It requires extensive historical unit-rate data to be collected first
26.w: Analogous estimating relies on comparison and expert judgement, so it is quick but tends to be subjective and less accurate than data-driven methods.

26.q: At its lowest level, what does a work breakdown structure typically break the work down into?
o: High-level phases only, without further detail
Individual products and their raw materials
Work packages that can be assigned, estimated and controlled
Departments responsible for the project
26.w: A WBS decomposes work to the level of manageable work packages that can be assigned, estimated, scheduled and controlled.

26.q: How can a leader who addresses conflict within the team promptly and fairly influence performance?
o: It guarantees that the project will meet its budget
It removes the need to hold any team meetings
It transfers responsibility for morale to the sponsor
It restores focus and cooperation, protecting performance
26.w: Handling conflict promptly and fairly restores cooperation and focus, protecting the team's performance.

26.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between progress reporting and stakeholder confidence?
o: Frequent reports remove the need for stakeholder input
Clear, honest reports build trust and transparency
Reports should be withheld to avoid raising concerns
Reporting is the main cause of project scope creep
26.w: Transparent and honest reporting keeps stakeholders informed and engaged, which builds trust and confidence in the project.

26.q: What is a benefit of using several different communication methods on a project?
o: It removes the need to plan communication in advance
It reliably leads to information overload for stakeholders
It allows the project manager to reduce stakeholder engagement
Stakeholders receive information in the format that best suits them
26.w: Tailoring the method to each stakeholder's needs increases the likelihood that information is received and understood.

26.q: A sponsor wants the value of a new asset to be monitored for years after handover until it is retired. Which life cycle supports this?
o: Hybrid life cycle
Iterative life cycle
Extended life cycle
Linear life cycle
26.w: Only the extended life cycle spans beyond delivery to include benefits realisation and eventual disposal, matching the sponsor's requirement.

26.q: What is the primary focus of configuration management within scope management?
o: Selecting the most suitable procurement route
Estimating the total cost of each work package
Approving or rejecting individual requests for change
Maintaining the integrity and consistency of the project's products
26.w: Configuration management maintains the integrity and consistency of the project's products and their versions.

26.q: In which situation should analytical (bottom-up) estimating be preferred over analogous or parametric methods?
o: When only high-level assumptions are available
When detailed work package data is available
When an estimate is needed very quickly
When no historical data exists
26.w: Analytical estimating gives the most accurate result when detailed task and resource data at work package level is available.

26.q: What is the main difference between a product breakdown structure and a work breakdown structure?
o: The PBS shows the deliverables and the WBS shows the work to create them
The PBS sets the deadlines and the WBS sets the budgets
The PBS shows the work and the WBS shows the associated costs
The PBS supports communication and the WBS supports risk management
26.w: The PBS defines what the project must produce, while the WBS defines the work needed to produce those deliverables.

26.q: A plan setting out the agreed scope, cost, schedule and resources for delivery, signed off by the stakeholders, is known as what?
o: The benefit profile
The change request log
The work breakdown structure
The deployment baseline
26.w: The deployment baseline records the agreed parameters for delivery, including scope, cost and schedule.
